# Language Models Part: Plan

**Plan for the Language Models part of Dive into Deep Learning. Last updated 6 November 2026.**

**Checks.** Every book label cited in this front matter and in the closing sections was checked against `chapter_*/` on 6 November 2026 and resolves; labels of the form `*_lm_*` belong to this part and do not exist yet.

## How to use this plan

This plan is a specification for the agents and authors who will write the chapters and for instructors who will teach from them. It is not book text.

**Entry format.** Every section entry has the shape below. Entries are written in full sentences where that is clearer; there is no telegraphic shorthand.

```text
### N.M Noun-Phrase Title · T<k>
**Idea:** one jargon-free sentence.
**Opening:** the reader's starting point, one concrete example, the open question the section answers.
**Teaches:** 3 to 6 bullets: the mechanism in full; relatives only with their one difference.
**Derivation:** the derivation, with its smallest numeric case, or "none".
**Notebook:** numbered steps: the question, model and data, the check against a reference (with tolerance),
  the claim that survives run-to-run noise, reused `d2l` pieces, the reduced T1 configuration for T2+ sections.
**Figures:** 1 to 3 ids, each with a phrase saying what it shows; "(plot)" marks a computed plot.
**Restate / forward:** labels restated in one sentence each (never re-derived); at most one forward reference.
**Exercises:** count, then the load-bearing ones by kind (check, derive, measure, open).
**Writer notes:** what an authoring agent must know and would otherwise get wrong.
**Sources:** Papers; Code and documentation; Courses, tutorials and blogs (each with a URL and its role).
```

A chapter block precedes the entries: label, hook, route (one question per section), out of scope (with the owner labels), writer notes (running models, shared artifacts and `d2l` exports, the hosted assignment, compute, consistency points), teaching sources, and the FR topics.

**What is binding.** Writer notes and Sources are binding inputs to the authoring agent, in the same way as the Teaches and Notebook lines: a writer who departs from a Writer note (a tolerance, an owner label, a reserved `d2l` name, a hardware fallback) records the departure in the chapter's hand-off note. Sources are the verified reading list of the section; a writer may add a source only after verifying it (an arXiv title on its abstract page; any other page by loading it) and never invents a URL or an arXiv identifier. Where an entry and the book source disagree, the book source wins and the writer notes it.

**Blueprints.** The per-chapter blueprints in `docs/llm/blueprints/` carry detail an entry cites as "blueprint chNN §x" (autograder fixtures, artifact schemas, microbenchmark contracts, decisions numbered in `blueprints/README.md`). They use their own section numbering; `docs/llm/blueprints/README.md` maps blueprint sections to the sections of this plan. Where a blueprint and this plan disagree, this plan wins. The blueprints for Chapters 4 to 9 and 11 to 14 differ most from this plan's structure and must be read through the entries here; those for Chapters 1 to 3 and 10 need only targeted edits.

**Verification duties per section.** Before a section is declared written, its author checks: (1) every label it cites resolves (`grep -r ':label:\`X\`' chapter_*/*.md`, likewise `:eqlabel:` and `:exlabel:`), and every `*_lm_*` label it defines is in the registry exactly once; (2) every URL in its Sources loads and every arXiv title matches its abstract page; (3) every number quoted in prose, tables and slides survives re-execution (rounded to the run-to-run noise of the store, ranges and qualitative statements preferred, no conclusion from a difference inside the noise); (4) the notebook runs one experiment, checks it against a reference with a stated tolerance, and has a T1 or T0 path; (5) no run of three hyphens and no em-dash (U+2014) in the text, no section or chapter numbers in book text (labels only), and no tier label in a heading.

**Compute.** No section may assume interactive access to A100 machines. A T2+ section is finished when it meets the campaign readiness list in "Compute campaigns"; its full-scale run happens later, in a campaign. Paid API calls from notebooks are listed with their caps in "Paid API calls"; a notebook that calls an API replays its committed cache in every build.

## Goal

The part teaches how modern language models are built, scaled across machines, adapted, aligned, extended to tools and multi-step tasks, compressed and served, and how current architectures depart from the transformer built in Advanced. It starts where Advanced stops. Parsing and structured prediction are out of scope; translation and summarization appear only through their scoring conventions in 1.4. By then a reader can:

- build a GPT with RoPE, GQA, RMSNorm and mixture-of-experts layers (`sec_gpt`, `sec_kv-cache`, `sec_moe`);
- train it with AdamW or Muon under a WSD schedule (`sec_adamw`, `sec_muon`, `sec_scheduler`);
- reason about rooflines, KV caches and data-parallel training (`sec_perf_model`, `sec_hardware`, `sec_multi_gpu`);
- derive policy gradients, PPO, DPO and the KL-regularized optimum (`chap_reinforcement_learning`, `chap_deep_rl`, `sec_rl_sequences`).

Every section here is either new material or applies those tools at a scale where new problems appear.

## Size

14 chapters, 97 sections and 4 FR notebooks: 101 units. A section runs 2,000 to 3,500 prose words with one notebook experiment; an FR notebook 1,000 to 2,000 words with no training run. The written part is therefore bounded at about 194,000 to 340,000 prose words of sections plus 4,000 to 8,000 words of FR notebooks, which is the constraint the owner set and the size the owner has accepted; there is no cap or headroom language. Basics has 58 sections and Advanced 72.

The part is organized in seven arcs, so a course can take whole arcs:

| Arc | Chapters | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| I. Using and measuring | 1 Working with Pretrained Language Models, 2 Encoders, Embeddings and Retrieval | What does a trained model do, and how do we measure it? |
| II. Building a base model | 3 Data for Language Models, 4 Pretraining | How is a base model made? |
| III. Scaling out | 5 Hardware for Training and Inference, 6 Parallelism Beyond One Node | What hardware do training and serving need, and how does training run on many machines? |
| IV. Post-training | 7 Fine-Tuning, 8 Preference Optimization and Reinforcement Learning, 9 Distillation and Reasoning | How does a base model become useful? |
| V. Acting | 10 Agents and Tool Use | How does a model use tools and act over many steps? |
| VI. Deploying | 11 Model Compression, 12 Efficient Inference, 13 Serving Systems | How is it run cheaply and fast? |
| VII. Architecture | 14 Advanced Architectures | Which architectural changes do current models make, and what does each buy? |

## Teaching approach

The part targets an advanced undergraduate or first-year graduate course at a research university. The prerequisites are Basics plus the Advanced chapters on attention, transformers, optimization, computational performance and reinforcement learning; the Mathematics part is a reference that sections cite by label.

**Section shape (the writing guide).** A section opens with 150 to 300 words from the reader's starting point and one concrete example, ending on the open question it answers; the body is two to five `##` subsections on one mechanism, with the derivation where one exists; a closing paragraph, a summary and exercises follow. One idea per section. One experiment per notebook: a single seeded run checked against a reference or a prediction; any second measurement is a cell on a committed artifact or an exercise. Restated facts carry the owner label in one sentence and are never re-derived or re-implemented. No "Builds on" lines, no learning objectives, no assignment blocks and no tier labels in the book text; headings are noun phrases; at most one forward reference per section.

**Instructor-facing apparatus.** Objectives, assignments and course paths live only in this front matter. Chapters carry none of them.

### Assignments

Instructor-facing. Every target is a committed number with a noise floor stated in the grader (floors from staff runs with their seed spread; paired-bootstrap intervals where two systems are compared); every assignment has a T1 path. Labels are `sec_lm_a<n>` unless stated.

| # | Assignment | Chapters (host) | Tier | Checkable target |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Run, port and measure: Qwen3.5 through Transformers, Qwen3-0.6B into the book's code, the evaluation harness with error bars | 1 (end of chapter) | T1 | Logits of the port within a stated bf16 tolerance; the harness reproduces one published score within its interval |
| A2 | RAG system over the book | 2 (end of chapter) | T1 | Recall@10 and answer accuracy above committed floors with paired-bootstrap intervals; the grading split is regenerated per term |
| A3 | Data pipeline: extraction, MinHash deduplication, quality classifier, a checkable manifest | 3 (end of chapter) | T0 to T1 | Deduplication F1 on labelled pairs within a margin of the staff solution; manifest hash reproducible from the rebuilt documents; MinHash bit-exact to the specification |
| A4 | Pretrain a small model with packing, document masks and WSD | 4 (end of chapter) | T1 (T2 full) | Ten autograder checks with exact tolerances; validation loss inside a band of three staff seeds at a fixed token budget; throughput at least 0.9 of the staff pipeline |
| A5 | Scaling-law fit on 4.2's committed ladder logs | 4 (4.6) | T0 | Exponents within a tolerance set from the bootstrap over ladder points; one lifetime-cost prediction |
| A6a | Calibrated performance model of a chip, a node and a cluster, plus a Triton FlashAttention-2-style forward kernel (`sec_lm_a6a`) | 5 (5.3, with 5.2's kernel task) | T1 on one 16 GB GPU within 14 GiB; the all-reduce task graded in reference mode from committed logs | Parameters and FLOPs counted exactly; step time, prefill latency and decode throughput predicted within 15% on at least 80% of held-out configurations; ring, tree and hierarchical all-reduce times predicted from committed logs; the kernel within 5.2's tolerance against SDPA and reported as a fraction of the calibrated matmul peak |
| A6b | Tensor- and pipeline-parallel blocks verified against one process, a schedule simulator, and a kill-and-resume on a different world size (`sec_lm_a6b`) | 6 (6.3 and 6.4, with 6.9's task) | T1 on 2 to 4 gloo CPU ranks in under 10 minutes; T3 for the BF16 band | Outputs and every gradient within 1e-9 relative in float64; collective bytes equal to the formulas; the simulated bubble within 10% of a measured four-stage run; the resumed run's sample order and loss match the reference |
| A7 | SFT, then DPO, then GRPO on Qwen3-0.6B (`sec_lm_a7`; part 1, the SFT stage `sec_lm_a7_sft`, is hosted by 7.2) | 7 (7.2) and 8 (end of chapter) | T1 to T2 | Float64 unit tests for `dpo_loss`, `group_advantages`, `ppo_loss` and `token_logprobs`; a T1 integration test on trainer-against-sampler log-probabilities; win rate and verifiable accuracy above floors published at half the reference gain after five staff seeds |
| A8 | Safety and red-teaming | 8 (8.7) | T1 | Refusal and over-refusal rates on the published category set; attack success under the jailbreak families; memorization extraction rate on a small model; floors from the staff run with the noise stated |
| A9 | Agent harness: the reader's loop of 10.3 on the fixed `repair30` set | 10 (10.3) | T1 | pass^k above a committed floor at a fixed token budget; sandbox self-test, gold patches pass the grader, turn masks match per-turn gradients to 1e-5; the grader resamples tasks, never trials |
| A10 | Inference engine: a scheduler (13.2's policies plus 13.5's admission control and preemption), paged cache, prefix cache, optional speculative decoding, end to end on a fixed trace (`sec_lm_a10`) | 12 (hooks) and 13 (13.3) | T1 | Allocator invariants; exact logits; batch invariance under 12.3's `det_mode`; hit-rate equality with an oracle; throughput and tail-latency targets on the committed trace `lm-a10-trace` against `lm-a10-reference` |

| Capstone | Design under a budget (`sec_lm_capstone`) | 14 (FR notebook) | Any (scenario B is T1) | Hand-derived claims checked to 0.5% by `d2l.config_stats` and 5.3's decode model; one measured baseline (peak memory within 15%, decode tokens per second within 25% of prediction, or a profile that localizes the gap); one rejected design with a pre-registered rule; a dossier |

**Project scaffold** (the 11-711 and CS288 pattern, two paragraphs in the instructor material): a proposal naming the claim and the baseline; a baseline reproduction with error bars using 1.5's reproduction protocol; an ablation protocol fixed before the runs; a report at the precision that survives re-execution. T1 by default.

## Compute tiers

| Tier | Hardware | Budget per notebook | How it runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| T0 | CPU | Minutes | Any build host |
| T1 | One 16 GB GPU: two scheduler slots, at most 15 GiB | About 15 min | The existing scheduler |
| T2 | One A100 40 GB (about 38 GiB usable); "T2 pair": two A100 with an NVLink bridge | A few hours | New resource class |
| T3 | One 8x A100 40 GB node | About 2 h (4.2's reference run plus its ladder: about 2.5 h) | New resource class, once per release |
| T4 | Two 8x A100 nodes | About 1 h | Cluster launch; the notebook analyzes committed logs |

Per-tier section counts are in the chapter overview. A100 is the target for T2 to T4 (H100 is unlikely to be available). There is no standing access to A100 machines: T2, T3 and T4 runs happen in three targeted campaigns, T2 first, then T3, then T4, each opened only after every notebook it covers is written and ready (see "Compute campaigns" below). FP8 stays native on the Ada build box; NVFP4 and MXFP4 stay simulated.

**Rules for T2 and above.** Every T2+ notebook has a reduced configuration that runs at T1 with the same code (a config flag); analysis cells run on committed artifacts (logs, traces, small checkpoints) through `d2l.DATA_HUB`, pinned by commit hash, never `main`. T3 and T4 notebooks are re-executed per release, not per build.

**Hardware limits.** FP8 is native on Ada and Hopper, not on A100 (4.3's native arm runs on the build box's Ada cards; the A100 runs the simulated arms). NVFP4 and MXFP4 are simulated on Ada and A100 and native on Blackwell; the prose says that frontier open models are pretrained in NVFP4 and the simulation is a teaching device, not a research framing. The build box runs no GPU-to-GPU traffic (no NVLink, unreliable peer-to-peer), so every T1 twin of a systems notebook uses one GPU, host-device copies, or a gloo loopback group in float64, and two-GPU measurements run on the T2 pair. Triton compiles on Ampere and Ada; a cell whose kernel fails to compile on the reader's driver prints the error and loads the committed series.

**Tier allocation in the systems chapters.** Chapter 5: about 5 A100-hours (5.1, 5.2's twin, 5.3, 5.8's clock sweep), about 3 node-hours (5.4, 5.5), and one two-node allocation of about 2 node-hours shared by 5.6 and 5.7 as its only T4 job. Chapter 6: every section has a T0 or T1 path; T3 jobs run once per release; the T4 jobs are 6.1, 6.7 and 6.10's committed logs. Chapter 13: every T3 section (13.7, 13.8) has a T2-pair live reduction and a T1 path on committed logs.

**Build system.** T2 to T4 resource classes in `runtime_env.notebook_resource`; a `d2l.launch` helper that submits a `%%writefile` script with `torchrun --nnodes` or SLURM and collects the logs (6.1 owns it); dedicated hosts for T2 to T4 with committed outputs.

## Compute campaigns

A100 time is granted in three bounded windows, not as interactive access, and only once the notebooks are written. Everything that can be settled without an A100 is settled before a window opens, so each window is spent on runs, not on configuration and experiments.

**Phase 0: write everything at T0 and T1.** All 97 sections and 4 Further Reading notebooks are written, executed and committed on the build box before any campaign. A T2+ section is written around its reduced T1 configuration (the same code, behind one config flag): every cell runs, every check passes, and the analysis cells run on T1-produced artifacts that have exactly the schema the full run will produce, so swapping in the campaign artifact is a data change, not a code change. Prose that quotes a T2+ result is drafted against the predicted outcome stated in the entry and marked with an HTML comment `<!-- campaign: <artifact key> -->` on the sentence, so the post-campaign pass can find every claim that depends on a campaign run.

**Campaign readiness (per T2+ section).** A section enters a campaign only when all of these hold:

1. The T1 reduced run passes its checks and is committed.
2. The full-scale job is a script, not a notebook session: a `%%writefile` script plus a launch entry (`d2l.launch` for T3 and T4) with the exact configuration, seed, model and data revisions pinned.
3. A smoke mode exists (a flag that runs the first few minutes: model load, a few steps, one checkpoint save and resume, one artifact write) and has been run at T1 or on the T2-pair-sized reduction.
4. Peak memory and runtime are predicted from the T1 measurement with the section's own FLOP and byte model, and the prediction is written into the manifest; the job stops itself at 1.5 times the predicted time.
5. The job checkpoints and resumes, so a failure costs the time since the last checkpoint, not the whole run.
6. The artifact it produces has a `DATA_HUB` key, a schema, and an analysis cell that already runs on the T1 stand-in.

**The campaign manifest.** One file, `tools/lm_campaigns.yaml`, lists every T2+ job: section, tier, command, predicted hours and memory, outputs, and dependencies (4.2's reference model and ladder feed 4.4 to 4.6 and assignment A5; 7.2's SFT checkpoint feeds Chapter 8; Chapter 8's checkpoints feed 9.2 to 9.4; 6.1's launch recipe gates every T3 and T4 job). Jobs run in dependency order within a campaign.

**Campaign 1: T2 (single A100s and the T2 pair).** About 20 sections, 45 to 60 A100-hours of planned runs; budget about 80 A100-hours including smoke runs and reruns. With four A100s this is one to two days. Order: smoke every job first (about 2 hours in total), then the full runs by dependency.

**Campaign 2: T3 (one 8x A100 node).** About 17 jobs (16 sections plus 4.2's ladder), 25 to 30 node-hours planned; budget about 40 node-hours, so two days on one node. The first two hours validate the node: `nccl-tests` all-reduce bandwidth against 5.5's prediction, the 6.1 launch recipe, and the pinned environment image. Jobs are batched by chapter (Chapter 6 alone is about 66 GPU-hours).

**Campaign 3: T4 (two 8x A100 nodes).** About 4 jobs (5.6 with 5.7, 6.1, 6.7, 6.10's logs), about 7 node-hours planned; budget one day on two nodes, of which the first half is fabric validation (`ib_write_bw` per rail, two-node `nccl-tests`, the 6.1 hang drills), since multi-node setup is the main risk. 6.1's two-node launch is rehearsed beforehand as a two-"node" job on one host (`torchrun --nnodes 2` over loopback), so only the fabric is new on the day.

**After each campaign.** Commit the artifacts and logs, re-execute the analysis cells at T0 and T1, run the freshness gate, and revise every sentence marked `<!-- campaign: ... -->` to the precision the run supports. A job that fails or overruns its window keeps its T1 artifacts and a sentence saying what the full run would show; it goes into the next campaign's manifest.

**Totals.** About 80 A100-hours (T2), 40 node-hours (T3) and one two-node day (T4): roughly 550 to 650 A100-hours in three windows, against roughly 300 to 350 A100-hours for a clean re-run at each later release.

## Paid API calls

Three places call a paid API, and nothing else in the part does. Every call goes through 1.7's `d2l.ChatAPI`, so the same rules hold everywhere: builds run in `mode='replay'`, where a cache miss raises `d2l.ReplayMiss` instead of reaching the network; a recording runs in `mode='record'` under a cost cap (`COST_CAP_USD`, a notebook or script constant) and stops with `d2l.CostCapExceeded`; the committed cache, its manifest and the dated price listing are the artifact.

| Where | Model | Calls per recording | Cap | Estimate | Re-recorded |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.7 notebook | DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, Qwen3.8-27B | About 750 (probe 20, Experiment 1 300, Experiment 2 60, Experiment 3 320, effort cell 15) | $5 | Under $2 | When 1.7 changes or the snapshot retires |
| 9.6 notebook (the effort dial) | DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 | About 4,500 (1,500 problems at three settings; `max_tokens` 16,384) | $25 | $5 to $15 | When 9.6 changes |
| 2.5 question set (authoring script) | DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (drafter) | About 4,500 (two candidates per anchor, 1.8 times oversampling) | $20 | $3 to $8 | Once |
| 2.5 answer check (authoring script) | Qwen3.8-27B | About 4,500 | $15 | About $3 | Once |

The estimates use the OpenRouter listing of 2026-11-06 (the flagship at $0.15 per million input and $0.60 per million output tokens on DeepSeek's own route, less on several FP8 providers; Qwen3.8-27B at $0.15 and $1.875) and assume about 4,000 reasoning tokens per call in 9.6 and 1,000 in 1.7. A full re-recording of both notebooks costs about $10 to $20; the sum of the caps, $65, bounds the whole part.

**Rules for a recording.**

1. Smoke first: 10 requests per model in `record` mode against a scratch cache, checking the served model id, the provider, the fields the experiment needs (`logprobs`, `seed`, the reasoning text) and the cost per call against the estimate.
2. Pin the dated snapshot and one provider per model with fallbacks off; record the served id and provider with every response, and snapshot the price listing with its date (`lm-api-listing-v1`).
3. Cap every call with `max_tokens`, which also bounds reasoning tokens, so one runaway trace cannot spend the budget.
4. Record outside the weekday windows in which DeepSeek's own route doubles its price (01:00 to 04:00 and 06:00 to 10:00 UTC), or pin a provider with flat pricing.
5. The API token lives in an environment variable outside the repository and never enters the hash, the cache or the logs.

Readers run every notebook in replay mode by default; `mode='live'` is opt-in, and the live exercises of 1.7 cost cents.

## Conventions

- **PyTorch only**, a deliberate exception to Advanced's PyTorch+JAX policy, with the RL chapter as precedent; PyTorch-only symbols from Advanced (`generate_cached`, FlexAttention, `d2l.torchrun`, `fully_shard`) are therefore unproblematic. Stated once in the part intro.
- **Reader floor:** one 16 GB GPU (two scheduler slots, at most 15 GiB): the judge is Qwen3.5-4B in bf16, the QLoRA headline is Qwen3-8B in NF4 within 15 GiB, and no T1 notebook claims a whole 24 GB card.
- **Models:** the Qwen3 dense ladder in the book's own code, Qwen3.5 as the current small generation, Gemma 4 E2B as the one deliberate second family; the remaining names live in Chapter 14's data file and FR notebook.
- **The Tools appendix is linked, never absorbed.** `sec_model_serving`, `sec_training_systems`, `sec_software_ecosystem`, `sec_hardware_buyers` and `sec_cloud_instances` own usage, the engine landscape, pinning, licences and buying; this part owns mechanisms and measurements.
- **Scope.** Parsing and structured prediction are out of scope for this part; translation and summarization appear only through their scoring conventions in 1.4.
- **Paid APIs, licences and downloads.** Three places make paid API calls through OpenRouter (or a similar aggregator): the notebooks of 1.7 (the API section itself) and 9.6 (the effort dial), and the authoring script that builds 2.5's question set. Each recording runs under a fixed cost cap and is committed, so every build replays it; "Paid API calls" lists the calls, caps and estimates. The hosted models are DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and Qwen3.8-27B; 2.5's questions are drafted by DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (outside the Qwen3 family) and ship with the book. Qwen-Scope may be used (academic use). gpt-oss-20b appears only in 11.5, where its MXFP4 tensors are read by range request and a local run is optional.
- **Experiments.** One per notebook; single seeded runs; no conclusion from a difference within run-to-run noise; prose quotes only the precision that survives re-execution.
- **Technical reports** are read in depth only in Chapter 14; elsewhere a method is cited by its origin paper plus one current exemplar. Numbers that sources dispute are never printed in prose.
- **Names and numbers.** Benchmark names, model rows and dollar figures live in per-edition data files (`data/lm_benchmarks.json`, `lm-arch-registry`, dated CSV rows), never in prose. The list of benchmarks is the data file `data/lm_benchmarks.json`, approved by the owner per edition. Running models are called by name ("Qwen3-0.6B", "the reference model"); no coined names.
- **Private authoring sources** (the ETH slide decks) stay out of bibliographies.
- **Cross-references** use labels only (`chap_lm_<topic>`, `sec_lm_<topic>`); book text never names a chapter or section number. Tier labels never appear in a heading.
- **Prose rules for the plan and the book:** no em-dashes, no question or wh-clause headings, noun-phrase section titles.

## References policy

- **Per section:** a Sources list in three groups, Papers; Code and documentation; Courses, tutorials and blogs, with at least one entry in each, every entry with a URL and a phrase on its role. No section-end Further Reading tails in the book text; the reading lives in the plan's Sources, in the chapter's teaching sources and in the four FR notebooks (Chapters 2, 8, 11, 14), which say what each work adds.
- **Per chapter:** an annotated teaching-sources list (courses, lecture notes, tutorials, blogs, code bases) that teach the chapter well.
- **Bibliography:** every Source in the entries was verified between 28 October and 6 November 2026 on its primary page. "verify" in an entry marks what the writer must confirm before citing. Nothing is cited by an invented URL or arXiv identifier; what could not be verified was dropped and is reported in the chapter's hand-off note.
- **Cited by title** (landing pages that block scripted checks or have none): Robertson and Zaragoza's BM25 monograph; Levy and Goldberg (2014), already in the book's bibliography as `Levy.Goldberg.2014`; Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher (2009) on reciprocal-rank fusion; the Meta and Alibaba network papers from SIGCOMM 2024; Young (1974) and Daly (2006) on checkpoint intervals; Tillet, Kung and Cox (2019) on Triton.
- **Freshness:** course links are refreshed to the 2026 to 2027 offerings before publication; benchmark and model names live in per-edition data files.

## Chapter 1 Working with Pretrained Language Models

**Label:** `chap_lm_pretrained`. Seven sections, T0 to T1. The chapter turns released checkpoints into instruments and builds the scoring and comparison tools that every later notebook of the part imports.
**Hook:** The reader has trained the GPT of `sec_gpt` on a few hundred megabytes of text and has seen released models answer questions that model cannot. This chapter loads such a model, runs the same tensors in the book's own code, scores it under explicit conventions, opens it, and reaches the models that no local machine can hold.
**Route:** What is in a released checkpoint, and how much memory and speed follow from its configuration file (1.1)? Do its tensors run the same in the book's code, layer by layer (1.2)? How much of a score does the prompt decide (1.3)? Can two scoring conventions rank two models differently (1.4)? When does a measured difference survive a paired test, and what does a judge add (1.5)? How is a claim about what a model computes tested rather than read off (1.6)? What can a hosted model be made to measure, and what does it withhold (1.7)?
**Out of scope:** No fine-tuning (`chap_lm_finetuning`), no serving beyond one local endpoint (`chap_lm_serving`), no architecture beyond reading a configuration (`chap_lm_architectures`); usage, pinning, licences and buying stay in the Tools appendix (`sec_software_ecosystem`, `sec_model_serving`, `sec_hardware_buyers`), which this chapter links and never absorbs.
**Writer notes:**
- Running models (Table 5): the current small Qwen generation is Qwen3.5 (0.8B, 2B, 4B; Apache-2.0); the book's own code runs the Qwen3 dense ladder (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B), chosen because Qwen3 is the last pure-transformer Qwen ladder; Gemma 4 E2B is the one deliberate second family (1.1 comparison, exercise elsewhere); the hosted models of 1.7 are DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and Qwen3.8-27B, reached only through the API; the judge is Qwen3.5-4B in bf16 (not the Qwen3.5-9B judge of blueprint ch01 Decision 5, which needs a 24 GB card). Every memory claim says what fits a 15 GiB scheduler slot; no T1 notebook claims a whole 24 GB card.
- Shared artifacts the chapter produces: the Qwen3-0.6B checkpoint loaded into the book's code (1.2; `d2l.Qwen3GPT`, `d2l.load_qwen3`), the harness (1.4 `d2l.score_choices`, `d2l.pass_at_k`, `d2l.extract_answer`, `d2l.bits_per_byte`; 1.5 `d2l.EvalSuite`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`, `d2l.judge_pairwise`), the client `d2l.ChatAPI` (1.7), `d2l.load_hf`, `d2l.config_memory`, `d2l.config_params` (1.1), `d2l.fewshot_prompt` (1.3), `d2l.intervene`, `d2l.TopKSAE` (1.6).
