- Courses, tutorials and blogs: [ICML 2026 poster, Stable Asynchrony](https://icml.cc/virtual/2026/poster/62012); [RLHF Book](https://rlhfbook.com/) (its chapters on constitutional AI and over-optimization).
## Chapter 9 Distillation and Reasoning

**Label:** `chap_lm_reasoning` (6 sections, T1 to T3; no Further Reading notebook).
**Hook:** The reader has a 1.7B model that solves the arithmetic family after the reinforcement learning of Chapter 8, and a 0.6B model that does not. This chapter moves the capability into the smaller model, and then shows how to buy accuracy at the moment of answering with tokens instead of parameters.
**Route:** What can a student learn from the teacher's distribution that it cannot learn from the teacher's samples (9.1)? Why does scoring the student's own samples help (9.2)? What do supervised fine-tuning on traces, reinforcement learning from a base model and distillation each change in a reasoning model (9.3)? What does a step-level scorer see that an outcome scorer cannot (9.4)? Why do more samples stop helping (9.5)? How is a reasoning budget set at inference or trained in (9.6)?
**Out of scope:** Tool calls inside a reasoning trace and interleaved thinking are `chap_lm_agents` (10.3). Chain-of-thought monitorability is the one paragraph in 1.6 (`sec_lm_interpretability`). Reward models for preferences and the GRPO trainer are Chapter 8 (`sec_lm_reward_models`, 8.4); reward hacking is restated from `subsec_rl_sequences_hacking`, not re-derived. No single named efficient-reasoning method is taught in prose (the field turns over in months); 9.6 teaches length penalties generically and cites one current exemplar in its Sources only. Technical reports are read in depth only in Chapter 14.
**Writer notes:**
- *Running models.* Students are Qwen3-0.6B-Base and Qwen3-1.7B-Base; teachers are Qwen3-1.7B (T1) and Qwen3-8B (T2 and T3), all Apache-2.0 and all on the Qwen3 tokenizer (vocabulary 151,936). The one cross-tokenizer example is Qwen3.5-2B (vocabulary 248,320), used only to show why logit distillation needs a shared vocabulary (9.1 exercise). The trace teacher of 9.3 is Qwen3.5-4B in thinking mode (the judge model of Table 5; the blueprint's Qwen3-8B is not used): traces are text and are re-tokenized, so the vocabulary mismatch is harmless there and harmful only for logit matching. The effort-level model of 9.6 is DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 behind the API (1.7's client; recorded once and replayed at T0). Reading-only references at T1: Qwen3-1.7B in thinking mode, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (MIT).
- *Shared artifacts and the compute unit.* 9.1 defines the chapter's compute unit, FLOPs counted from tokens by `d2l.ComputeLedger` (2 N_ne per token processed in a forward pass, generated or scored, and 6 N_ne per token trained, with N_ne the non-embedding parameter count of the model that processed the token, from `sec_scaling-laws`). Attention FLOPs are excluded and the exclusion is stated at every use. Every plot with a token or FLOP axis also reports wall-clock for the same run, because decode is memory-bound and prefill compute-bound (`sec_kv-cache`), and the text says when the two orderings disagree. When every model in a comparison is the same size the unit reduces to generated tokens, counting all generated tokens including discarded samples and thinking tokens. Teacher-trace and pool generation costs are reported as "amortized" and included in an "all-in" column.
- *Problem generator.* 9.1 exports `d2l.make_problems(family, n, seed, split, difficulty=None)` with splits `train`, `test_seen_templates`, `test_unseen_templates`, `test_harder`; the `chain` family has 24 templates and 2 to 6 reasoning steps (templates 0 to 15 train; 16 to 23 unseen; `test_harder` is templates 0 to 15 with 7 or 8 steps). Items carry `question`, `prompt` and `answer` so they pass straight to `d2l.grpo_train` as `tasks`. Every training experiment in the chapter uses these generated families (the idea of GSM-Symbolic; the notebook builds its own generator and does not redistribute `apple/GSM-Symbolic`, whose card is CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0). Public sets (GSM8K test, MATH-500, AIME 2024 and 2025) appear only as "public, possibly seen" reality checks with paired, within-model comparisons; Qwen3 was trained after they were public.
- *Formats and templates.* Both models in every pair render prompts with 7.2's `d2l_chatml_v1` (`d2l.render_chat`), so teacher and student see identical token ids; Qwen's own template is used only when a teacher generates offline samples, and those are stored without the empty `<think></think>` block that Qwen3's non-thinking template inserts. `<think>...</think>` is a response-text convention of this chapter (7.2 keeps think blocks out of `d2l_chatml_v1`); the answer format is `#### <integer>`, taught by a short SFT warm-up (9.2's S0) and checked by `d2l.format_reward` (9.3). `d2l.verify_math` (8.4) composes 1.4's `d2l.extract_answer(kind='boxed')` with `d2l.canonical_answer`.
- *Library exports introduced here* (all `#@save`, signatures in the section entries): `d2l.nonembedding_params`, `d2l.ComputeLedger`, `d2l.make_problems`, `d2l.kd_loss`, `d2l.topk_compress`, `d2l.kd_topk_loss`, `d2l.uld_loss` (9.1); `d2l.opd_loss`, `d2l.OnPolicyDistiller`, `d2l.privileged_prompt` (9.2); `d2l.format_reward`, `d2l.grpo_train_with_reset`, `d2l.rejection_sample`, `d2l.behavior_stats`, `d2l.eval_families`, `d2l.compute_matched_grid` (9.3); `d2l.split_steps`, `d2l.mc_step_labels`, `d2l.ProcessScorer`, `d2l.scorer_loss`, `d2l.aggregate_prm`, `d2l.ece`, `d2l.auroc`, `d2l.select_by_score` (9.4); `d2l.load_tts_pool`, `d2l.answer_classes`, `d2l.majority_vote`, `d2l.accuracy_vs_cost`, `d2l.maj_accuracy_indep`, `d2l.maj_error_bound`, `d2l.coverage_beta`, `d2l.fit_beta_mle` (9.5); `d2l.budget_force`, `d2l.vote_lead_stop`, `d2l.greedy_allocate`, `d2l.AllocationPolicy`, `d2l.fit_allocation`, `d2l.evaluate_policy`, `d2l.length_reward`, `d2l.overthinking_stats`, `d2l.pareto_front`, `d2l.match_budget`, `d2l.amortized_breakeven` (9.6; `pareto_front` is consumed by 10.5 as `d2l.agent_pareto`'s base). Consumed from earlier chapters: `d2l.sft_train`, `d2l.render_chat`, `d2l.sft_collate` (7.2), `d2l.LoRALinear`, `d2l.add_lora` (7.4), `d2l.token_logprobs`, `d2l.RewardModel` (8.1), `d2l.grpo_train`, `d2l.group_advantages`, `d2l.sample_responses`, `d2l.verify_math`, `d2l.canonical_answer` (8.4), `d2l.sync_weights` (8.5), `d2l.pass_at_k`, `d2l.extract_answer`, `d2l.score_choices` (1.4), `d2l.EvalSuite`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap` (1.5), `d2l.launch` (6.1). A T2 or T3 notebook prints its own ledger; GPU-hours are not quoted beyond the tier budgets.
- *Assignment.* The chapter hosts the optional distillation mini-assignment (`sec_lm_a9_mini`, blueprint ch09 "Assignment"): 9.2's T1 reduction, continuing from the reader's A7 part 1 SFT checkpoint (`sec_lm_a7_sft`) or the staff checkpoint `lm-sft-qwen3-0p6b`, graded on the correctness of the estimator code (`opd_loss` fixture to 1e-10, the two toy checks) and a written report, never on a gain threshold, because 40 online steps on a 0.6B model give an accuracy change that noise can swamp. Estimated 6 to 8 student hours, entirely T1.
- *Compute notes.* T1 means two scheduler slots and at most 15 GiB: the 9.1 training cell never loads the teacher (it trains from the cached top-k file); 9.2's T1 teacher scoring fits only with rollout batches of at most 32 and responses of at most 256 tokens, which the config enforces. T2 is one A100 40 GB with a target of at most 38 GiB: 9.2's memory plan is a LoRA (rank 16) on a frozen bf16 1.7B student (3.44 GB) plus a second student copy in the rollout engine plus the 8B teacher (16.38 GB), about 23.3 GB resident, with teacher scoring in micro-batches of at most 8 sequences and a chunked log-softmax; full fine-tuning of the student does not fit beside the teacher. 9.3's T3 job runs once per release on one 8x A100 node (three arms on two GPUs each, one rollout GPU and one training GPU, the remaining two GPUs generating teacher traces beforehand), at most about 2 hours; full fine-tuning state of the 1.7B student is 27.5 GB, so gradient checkpointing, micro-batches of a few thousand tokens and 4.1's `d2l.chunked_lm_loss` are mandatory. No section uses T4.
- *Noise discipline (chapter-wide).* Three seeds wherever a trained arm fits the tier; a difference is stated only if the paired-bootstrap 95% interval over problems (clustered by template on the unseen split) excludes zero and each arm's seed range is smaller than the gap; otherwise the table says "not resolved". T3 single-seed runs may be compared only if the difference exceeds twice the maximum seed spread measured at the T2 reduction. The `n_trials` subset noise of 9.5 is not problem-level noise and is never reported as such.
- *Cross-chapter consistency.* Chapter 8 is cited by this plan's numbers: 8.1 reward models, 8.4 RL with verifiable rewards (GRPO, the verifier, the `lm-grpo-qwen3-0p6b` and `lm-grpo-qwen3-1p7b-base` checkpoints; the blueprint calls this 8.5), 8.5 RL systems (`d2l.sync_weights`; the blueprint's 8.6). `tab_rl_notation` (owner `sec_mdp`) is the notation table; `tab_rl_notation_contract` in the blueprints does not exist. GKD's mixing coefficient is written alpha (beta is the KL coefficient in this part); the distillation temperature is written kappa (T is the horizon). N denotes test-time samples and K the training group size, never interchanged.

- Courses: [Stanford CS224N, Winter 2026](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/) (two reasoning lectures; the shape of a one-semester treatment), [Stanford CS336, Spring 2026](https://cs336.stanford.edu/) (assignment A5, SFT and RL on math, the model for the chapter's verifier-based experiments), [CMU 11-711, Spring 2026](https://cmu-l3.github.io/anlp-spring2026) (fine-tuning and distillation, test-time scaling lectures), [Berkeley CS288, Spring 2026](https://cal-cs288.github.io/sp26) (test-time compute and reasoning models lecture).

### 9.1 Knowledge Distillation · T1
**Idea:** A student can learn from the teacher's whole distribution over next tokens, not only from the teacher's samples, and the choice between the two is a choice of what the student sees and what it costs to store.
**Opening:** The reader fine-tuned a 0.6B model on a 1.7B model's answers in Chapter 7 and got a weaker copy. A student trained on the teacher's answers sees one token per position; the teacher's distribution at that position holds a probability for every one of 151,936 entries, including the alternatives it nearly chose. The concrete example is one position of one GSM8K solution with the teacher's top five tokens and their probabilities next to the single sampled token. The open question: what do the samples never show, and is it worth 300 KB per token to keep it?
**Teaches:**
- The three decisions that define a distillation method (`tab_lm_kd_design`): who generates the prefixes (teacher, human data or student), what labels each position (a hard token, the full distribution, a top-k slice), and which divergence is minimized. Sequence-level distillation (SFT on teacher samples) and token-level distillation (matching the teacher's distribution at the teacher's own prefixes) are the two worked representatives.
- The divergence table: forward KL (mass-covering; one-sample estimator is SFT on teacher samples; token-level full-vocabulary matching is its Rao-Blackwellized form; logit gradient q minus p at kappa equal to 1), reverse KL (mode-seeking; needs student samples; score-function gradient), generalized Jensen-Shannon with mixing alpha (interpolates). Each row says where it is used (SFT, GKD, MiniLLM, on-policy distillation of 9.2); none is re-derived.
- Top-k teacher logits as storage: tail-bucket coarsening into k plus 1 cells is a lower bound on the full divergence, monotone in k; renormalized top-k is not a coarsening and can over- or under-estimate; m sampled tokens per position give an unbiased alternative with variance 1 over m. Storage arithmetic: 151,936 times 2 bytes is 303,872 bytes per token in bf16 (about 304 GB per million tokens); a top-32 cache is 194 bytes per token (32 int32 plus 32 fp16 plus one fp16 tail), a ratio of about 1,566.
- The compute ledger that every later comparison uses: 2 N_ne per generated or scored token, 6 N_ne per trained token, with the worked instance that scoring 1,000 teacher tokens on the 1.7B model costs 2 times 1.4e9 times 1e3, about 2.8e12 FLOPs, and training the 0.6B student on the same tokens 6 times 0.44e9 times 1e3, about 2.64e12.
- One sentence each: teachers behind an API return text only, so sequence-level distillation is the only option there; mismatched tokenizers forbid logit matching, which the exercise takes up with a vocabulary-agnostic sorted-probability loss.
**Derivation:** The chain rule for sequence divergences: D_KL(P||Q) equals the sum over positions of the expected per-position KL under teacher prefixes, with the reverse version under student prefixes (`eq_lm_kd_chain`), and the bias of top-k truncation. Smallest case: a two-symbol vocabulary with sequences of length 2, teacher P(AA) 0.7 and P(BB) 0.3, and a factorized student with per-position parameter a. The forward optimum is a equal to 0.7, which puts mass 2 times 0.7 times 0.3, that is 0.42, on AB and BA that the teacher never emits; the reverse KL is finite only at a in {0, 1}, with values 0.357 nats at a equal to 1 and 1.204 nats at a equal to 0, the two numbers of `sec_mdl-fwd-vs-rev-kl`. The top-k bias case of the exercises: P (0.5, 0.3, 0.2), Q (0.3, 0.5, 0.2), k equal to 2, where the renormalized loss is 0.25 ln(5/3), 0.128 nats, against a full KL of 0.2 ln(5/3), 0.102 nats.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: at matched student tokens, does training on the teacher's distribution beat training on the teacher's samples, and how much of the distribution must be stored?
2. Model and data: student Qwen3-0.6B-Base with a rank-64 LoRA on all linear layers; teacher Qwen3-1.7B in non-thinking mode (temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20), loaded only in the scoring cell that builds the top-32 cache and in the evaluation cell, never in the training cell. 2,000 GSM8K-train prompts plus 1,000 `chain` prompts; two epochs over the same sample file so tokens are identical across arms; sequence length 512; AdamW with a constant rate after warm-up, chosen once on the SFT-gold arm from {5e-5, 1e-4, 2e-4} by validation loss and reused.
3. Arms: SFT on the human solutions, SFT on teacher samples (sequence-level), forward KL on top-32 logits, reverse KL on top-32, JSD with alpha 0.5 on top-32; full-vocabulary forward KL only on a T2 host (`full_ft=True`).
4. Checks: `d2l.kd_loss` equals `F.kl_div(..., log_target=True)` to 1e-6; the forward-KL gradient at kappa 1 equals q minus p to 1e-6; JSD at alpha 1e-3 divided by alpha is within 1% of forward KL and at alpha 1 minus 1e-3 within 1% of reverse KL; the toy direction cell reproduces 0.42, 0.3567 and 1.2040 within 1e-3 and 1e-4; the top-k bias cell on a Zipf-like vocabulary of 1,000 shows the tail-bucket KL nondecreasing in k and at most the full KL to 1e-9, with the averaged sampled gradient within 3 Monte Carlo standard errors of the full gradient.
5. Claim that survives noise: with three seeds, distribution arms beat the sample arm at matched tokens if the paired interval excludes zero and seed ranges do not overlap; the ranking among divergences on teacher prefixes is reported as "not resolved" unless the same test passes. Accuracy with intervals on GSM8K test (greedy, 1,319, flagged public), `test_unseen_templates` and `test_harder` (500 each), teacher-forced held-out loss, a student-sample reverse-KL estimate, pass@8, and the ledger.
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.sft_train` with a custom `loss_fn`, `d2l.sft_collate`, `d2l.render_chat`, `d2l.LoRALinear`, `d2l.pass_at_k`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`, `d2l.load_hf`.
7. T1 is the full configuration (cached teacher, LoRA student); the T2 host adds the full-vocabulary arm.
**Figures:** `fig_lm_kd_modes` (the toy four-sequence densities with the forward and reverse fits, and the top-32 arms' answer histograms beside pass@8); `fig_lm_kd_topk` (fraction of the full forward KL captured against k in {1, ..., 128}, tail-bucket against renormalized, storage on a second axis) (plot); `fig_lm_kd_cost` (accuracy against all-in FLOPs per arm) (plot); `fig_lm_kd_tokenizer` (plot, from the measure exercise: the fraction of Qwen3 vocabulary strings present in the Qwen3.5 vocabulary). Tables `tab_lm_kd_design`, `tab_lm_kd_cost`, `tab_lm_kd_results`.
**Restate / forward:** `subsec_mdl-distillation` (soft targets with temperature and the kappa-squared gradient factor, restated in one paragraph, temperature renamed kappa); `sec_mdl-fwd-vs-rev-kl` (the two numbers 0.357 and 1.204 nats are a cross-check, not a derivation); `eq_seq_factorization` and `tab_rl_notation` (owner `sec_mdp`) for the response score and the policy notation; `sec_scaling-laws` (2N and 6N FLOPs per token). Forward: none.
**Exercises:** 7. Derive: the top-k bias on the three-token case and the smallest k that keeps the tail-bucket gap under 1% on the committed cache; the kappa-squared factor's effect on gradient norm. Measure: a temperature sweep of the teacher's sampling against student accuracy at fixed tokens; the fraction of Qwen3 vocabulary strings present in the Qwen3.5 vocabulary (`fig_lm_kd_tokenizer`). Check: `F.kl_div` argument order. Open: distillation across tokenizers with `d2l.uld_loss` from a Qwen3.5-2B teacher.
**Writer notes:**
- Pitfalls that break the section silently: `F.kl_div`'s argument order gives reverse KL when the writer expects forward; padded embedding rows and unused special tokens leak mass unless logits are masked to the tokenizer length before the softmax; a temperature applied to the teacher but not the student; comparing arms at equal steps instead of equal tokens, or ignoring the teacher's generation cost; treating renormalized top-k as unbiased truncation; greedy teacher outputs are low-diversity, so the sampling temperature decides how much of P the student sees.
- Template mismatch is the first thing to test: Qwen3's non-thinking template inserts an empty `<think></think>`; `d2l_chatml_v1` does not. Store teacher samples as text and re-render both sides with `d2l.render_chat`; a cell asserts that the first 20 tokens of teacher and student renderings agree.
- Reference implementation and tolerance: `d2l.kd_loss` against `F.kl_div` to 1e-6 (fp32, chunked over the vocabulary with `chunk=4096`); TRL's `GKDTrainer` loss function (`generalized_jsd_loss`, name to verify in the pinned release) as the production oracle in one cell; if the API drifts, compare final losses of a one-step run and mark "verify in the pinned release".
- Do not re-teach: the kappa-squared derivation (`subsec_mdl-distillation`), the KL-direction numbers (`sec_mdl-fwd-vs-rev-kl`); the divergences are a table of uses, not derivations.
- Library additions: `d2l.nonembedding_params(config) -> int` (within 3% of 0.44B, 1.4B, 3.6B, 6.95B for the Qwen3 ladder), `d2l.ComputeLedger` (`.add_generate`, `.add_score`, `.add_train`, `.flops()`, `.tokens(kind)`, `.table()`, `.to_jsonl`), `d2l.make_problems`, `d2l.kd_loss(student_logits, teacher_logits, mask, kind='fkl', alpha=0.5, kappa=1.0, chunk=4096)`, `d2l.topk_compress(logits, k=32) -> (idx, logp, tail)`, `d2l.kd_topk_loss(student_logits, idx, logp, tail, mask, mode='tail_bucket')`, `d2l.uld_loss`. `make_problems` is deliberately distinct from 8.4's `d2l.ArithmeticTasks` (flat source); do not merge them. Determinism and train-test disjointness of (template, numbers) pairs are unit-tested.
- Hardware fallbacks: if the T1 cache does not fit, drop to k equal to 16 or 1,000 prompts and print the cache size; if the pinned Transformers cannot load the Qwen3.5-2B tokenizer, use the committed text-only samples and skip the live comparison.
- Settle at authoring: the GSM8K contamination warning threshold (print a warning if GSM8K accuracy exceeds `test_seen_templates` by a margin set after the first measurement); whether `sft_collate` carries the teacher tensors or the arms wrap batches in a generator. Detail: blueprint ch09 §9.1 (derivations D1 and D2, the test list, risks a to f).

### 9.2 On-Policy Distillation · T2
**Idea:** Scoring the student's own samples with the teacher turns distillation into reinforcement learning with a dense reward and no critic, and trains the student on the states it actually visits.
**Opening:** The 9.1 student goes wrong at token 40 of a solution and never recovers, and the teacher's samples never show the way back, because the teacher never made that mistake. The concrete example is `fig_lm_opd_position_kl`: the per-position reverse KL of the student's own samples to the teacher, flat and then jumping at the first bad token. The teacher is exactly the expert that DAgger asks for. The open question: how much cheaper is this than reinforcement learning with a verifier, and what does it copy that a verifier would not?
**Teaches:**
- The on-policy objective: sample from the student, score each token by the teacher's log-probability minus the student's, a dense per-token reward r_t with no critic; the objective is `eq_kl_objective` with beta equal to 1 and reference equal to the student, whose optimum is the teacher.
- The two estimators: the return-to-go form (unbiased for the sequence reverse-KL gradient) and the discount-zero per-token form (unbiased only with the visited-state distribution held fixed); the difference is the state-distribution term, measured on the toy (cosine about 0.98, relative difference about 0.3).
- `tab_lm_opd_prefix`: who generates the prefixes and who labels the tokens, for SFT, sequence-level KD, forward KL on teacher prefixes, GKD with mixing lambda, on-policy distillation, GRPO and self-distillation with privileged context (OPSD), each a one-line relative.
- The cost ledger against RL: one sample per prompt against K equal to 8, teacher scoring as prefill (compute-bound) against student decode (memory-bound), and why the two orderings can disagree.
**Derivation:** DAgger with a soft expert. With R(x, y) equal to log P minus log pi_ref (`eq_dpo_reward` at beta 1): D_KL(Q||P) equals D_KL(Q||pi_ref) minus E_Q R, so minimizing the sequence reverse KL is the KL-regularized objective; the optimum is pi_ref e^R, which is P; R decomposes per token; the gradient is minus the expectation of the score times the return-to-go. The compounding bound: on-policy distillation minimizes under the student's state distribution (condition (ii) of `subsec_il_error_bounds`), offline distillation minimizes D_KL(P||Q) (condition (i)); for a terminal reward in [0, 1] the regret is bounded by total variation, at most sqrt(D_KL(P||Q)/2) by Pinsker, and by the sum of per-step variations by the hybrid argument. Smallest case: a tabular student and teacher with vocabulary 3 and length 3 (13 prefixes, 27 sequences, seed 0): the identity holds to 1e-10 for a random reference, gradient descent reaches the teacher within total variation 1e-6, and finite differences match the enumerated return-to-go gradient to 1e-8.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: at matched generated tokens, how do offline distillation, on-policy distillation and GRPO compare on unseen templates and harder problems, and does the ranking survive an all-in FLOP count?
2. Model and data: T2 student Qwen3-1.7B-Base with a rank-16 LoRA on all linear layers (17,432,576 adapter parameters), teacher Qwen3-8B in non-thinking mode; every arm starts from S0, a one-epoch SFT of the student on 500 teacher samples that teaches the `#### <integer>` format (committed as `lm-opd-student-sft0`). The `chain` train split is streamed; evaluation on 500 problems each of `test_unseen_templates`, `test_harder` and GSM8K test (public). Rollouts at temperature 1.0 with responses of at most 512 tokens; evaluation greedy; eight evenly spaced evaluations over a generated-token budget calibrated so that the GRPO arm takes about one hour on one A100 (value to be measured); three seeds per arm; AdamW at 1e-4.
3. Arms: offline (teacher top-32 forward KL with 9.1's `kd_topk_loss`); on-policy distillation (one sample per prompt, 64 prompts per step, `OnPolicyDistiller(mode='sampled')`); GRPO (K equal to 8, 16 prompts per step, `d2l.grpo_train`); OPSD (one sample per prompt, `teacher_context='privileged'`).
4. Checks: the `opd-kl-identity` and `opd-gradient-check` cells above; `d2l.token_logprobs` against `F.cross_entropy(reduction='none')` to 1e-6; trainer log-probabilities of 32 sampled responses against the sampler's within a staff tolerance; `d2l.opd_loss(mode='full')` against TRL's `GKDTrainer` at beta 1 on identical logits to 1e-5 in fp32.
5. Claim that survives noise: on-policy distillation reaches the offline arm's accuracy at fewer generated tokens, stated only if the paired interval excludes zero for at least two of three seeds and the seed ranges do not overlap; otherwise "unresolved". Per evaluation: accuracy on the three splits, mean length, per-token reverse KL to the teacher, unparsable fraction, generated tokens, teacher tokens, FLOPs and wall-clock.
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.grpo_train`, `d2l.verify_math`, `d2l.sample_responses`, `d2l.sync_weights`, `d2l.token_logprobs`, `d2l.kd_topk_loss`, `d2l.ComputeLedger`, `d2l.make_problems`, `d2l.sft_train`, `d2l.add_lora`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`.
7. T1 reduction (`scale='t1'`): student Qwen3-0.6B-Base with LoRA, teacher Qwen3-1.7B, GRPO 12 steps, on-policy distillation 40 steps, 100 problems per split, then every plot rebuilt from the committed T2 logs. Hosts the mini-assignment.
**Figures:** `fig_lm_opd_toy` (the tabular toy: offline against online reverse and forward KL over 20 seeds); `fig_lm_opd_position_kl` (per-position reverse KL of student samples, first-bad-token threshold at log 1e-3) (plot); `fig_lm_opd_tokens` (accuracy against generated tokens, four arms) (plot), with `fig_lm_opd_flops` and `fig_lm_opd_kl` as companion panels. Tables `tab_lm_opd_prefix`, `tab_lm_opd_cost` (tokens to reach 80% of the best arm's final accuracy), `tab_lm_opd_estimators`.
**Restate / forward:** `subsec_il_dagger` and `subsec_il_error_bounds` (DAgger and the epsilon T against epsilon T-squared proposition, framed in one paragraph, not re-proved); 9.1's divergence table and ledger; `eq_kl_objective`, `eq_kl_optimum`, `eq_dpo_reward` and `subsec_kl_direction` from `sec_regularized`; `sec_baselines` (the zero-mean lemma and reward-to-go); `eq_ppo_clip` for the optional clipped ratio. Forward: none.
**Exercises:** 7. Derive: the DAgger bound for a soft expert and when the quadratic term returns (one deviation loses all remaining reward); the optimum for general beta, Q* proportional to pi_ref^(1 minus 1/beta) P^(1/beta). Measure: teacher size against student gain (teacher Qwen3-4B against Qwen3-8B); the direction of the truncation bias on rewards (responses cut at 256 tokens). Check: the two estimators on the toy. Open: on-policy distillation as the last stage after RL, and the OPSD arm as a cautionary baseline if it is null.
**Writer notes:**
- The claim "removes the compounding error" is too strong for a soft teacher and must not be written; the quadratic term belongs to the model in which one deviation irrecoverably loses the remaining reward (blueprint ch09 §9.2, D2 step 6). Say which condition each method satisfies and show the bound.
- The toy comparison confounds sample diversity with training direction; report both directions of KL and claim only the paired count (online lower reverse KL in 16 of 20 seeds in the author's run; re-measure).
- Stale rollouts are partly off-policy and need the ratio rho_t or a refresh; the sampled-token reverse KL is unbiased but high-variance (the full-distribution mode removes sampling noise at the cost of teacher logits); truncated responses give no end-of-sequence reward and must be counted; on-policy distillation copies the teacher's errors, so verifier accuracy is reported, never KL alone; equal steps are not equal work (64 against 128 samples per step).
- Privileged context (OPSD): the student prompt must never contain the hint (`d2l.privileged_prompt` asserts it); evaluation is question-only; the teacher may copy the answer and reward shortcuts, which the text names. The OPSD arm may be null; it then becomes the cautionary example and the baseline of the open exercise.

If `grpo_train` cannot start from a LoRA-wrapped S0, a 40-line GRPO loop from `d2l.group_advantages` replaces it.

### 9.3 Training Reasoning Models · T3 (T2 reduced)
**Idea:** A reasoning model is made by cold-start supervised fine-tuning on traces, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and distillation, and each stage changes something different and measurable.
**Opening:** After RL on checkable arithmetic (8.4) the reader's base model writes longer traces and its accuracy rises; after SFT on a stronger model's traces the `<think>` format appears at once. The concrete example is two responses to the same problem from the two checkpoints, with their lengths and `d2l.behavior_stats` marker counts beside them. The open question: which of the two generalizes to templates the training never showed, at the same compute?
**Teaches:**
- The pipeline and its stages (`tab_lm_reason_pipelines`): cold-start SFT on a few thousand verified traces, RL with verifiable rewards and a format reward, rejection-sampling SFT, distillation into smaller models; what each stage's data and signal are, as stated by the sources.
- RL from a base model and the behaviours that appear (length, format, reflection markers, pass@1) against what pass@k at large k tests; the signal argument: a group of K binary rewards carries a nonzero advantage only when mixed, with probability 1 minus p^K minus (1 minus p)^K (for K equal to 8: 0.149 at p 0.02, 0.337 at 0.05, 0.832 at 0.2, 0.992 at 0.5), so a base model near zero gives all-zero groups.
- Rejection-sampling SFT as REINFORCE without a baseline (fine-tuning on correct samples has expected gradient equal to the policy gradient); GRPO differs by the group-mean subtraction (negative evidence), the division by the standard deviation and the (K minus 1)/K shrinkage.
- Prolonged RL and its plateau; reference resets; what changes with each stage (`tab_lm_reason_changes`: base, SFT, RL, SFT then RL, RFT).
**Derivation:** none in the sense of a new result; the signal probability and the RFT identity above are stated with their check cell: 200,000 simulated groups for p in {0.02, 0.05, 0.2, 0.5} and K in {4, 8, 16} within 3 standard errors, and the four-prompt verifier toy of `sec_rl_sequences` where the exact RFT gradient equals the exact policy gradient to 1e-12 and the GRPO-centered update equals (K minus 1)/K times it at K equal to 2.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: at matched compute, does SFT on teacher traces or RL from the base generalize better to unseen templates, and which stage buys pass@1 against pass@64?
2. Model and data: student Qwen3-1.7B-Base at T3, Qwen3-0.6B-Base at the T2 reduction (three seeds); trace teacher Qwen3.5-4B in thinking mode (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, never greedy), text-only, about 4,000 verified traces (up to four per problem) re-rendered through `d2l_chatml_v1`; the `chain` train split streamed with prompts never repeated; evaluation every C/8 FLOPs on 500 problems per split; responses of at most 1,024 student tokens (2,048 for the teacher); AdamW, bf16 weights with fp32 optimizer state.
3. Arms: SFT on traces (two epochs, learning rate 1e-5; teacher tokens counted in the all-in ledger); RL from base (verifier plus 0.1 times `d2l.format_reward`, GRPO with K 8, 8.4's configuration, plain-text prompt without a chat template); SFT then RL (500 traces, one epoch, then RL, budget split 10/90 by FLOPs). At the T2 reduction only: rejection-sampling SFT (two rounds) and a reference-reset variant (every C/4). The RL arm is extended threefold on its own GPU pair (prolonged RL, no reset) and re-evaluated at pass@64 on the harder slice.
4. ### 9.4 Verifiers and Process Supervision · T2
**Idea:** A step-level scorer sees what an outcome scorer cannot, the first wrong step, and pays for it in labels that are only as good as the generator that produced them.
**Opening:** Two candidate solutions reach the same wrong answer by different routes; an outcome scorer rates them alike, while a step scorer finds the first wrong step in each. The concrete example is one `chain` problem with two candidates split into `Step k:` lines, with Monte Carlo step labels under them. The open question: who pays for the labels, and does a scorer trained on one generator's mistakes still work on another's?
**Teaches:**
- Outcome against process reward models (`tab_lm_verifier_kinds`): what each reads, what each is trained on, and what each can localize.
- Monte Carlo step labels: K rollouts from each prefix; the soft label is the fraction correct with variance V(1 minus V)/K, the hard label (any rollout correct) is optimistic with mean 1 minus (1 minus V)^K (at K 8: 0.337 at V 0.05, 0.942 at V 0.3); labeling cost is K L (S minus 1)/2 tokens, about 21 times the solution's own cost at S 6 and K 8.
- Credit assignment: the value martingale V(s_j) equals the expected next value, the increments Delta_j are step advantages with zero cross-correlation, Var(R) equals the sum of their second moments, and local credit has the same expected gradient as the outcome weight; the variance ordering is not general and is measured, not asserted.
- Generative verifiers that critique before a verdict (one worked paragraph with a zero-shot instance) and calibration across generators: a scorer trained on pi under-estimates a stronger generator and over-estimates a weaker one (the direction is a prediction, tested in the notebook); AUROC and ECE defined in one short paragraph each.
**Derivation:** The variance of a Monte Carlo step label against rollouts per step, and the martingale identities. Smallest case: a chain of four independent steps each correct with probability 0.8 and R equal to their product, enumerated over 16 outcomes: the martingale and variance identities hold to 1e-12 (Var(R) 0.2418), the outcome weight, the value baseline and the local credit all have the same mean 0.0819 at every step, and the ORM-to-local variance ratios are 1.53, 1.12, 0.84, 0.64 across the four steps (re-measure; the evidence for "not ordered"); one million Monte Carlo labels at V in {0.05, 0.3} and K in {4, 8, 16} agree with the formulas within 3 standard errors.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: on the same candidate pools, does step-level reranking beat outcome reranking, per labeled solution and per FLOP, and does the gain survive a change of generator?
2. Model and data: scorer backbone Qwen3-0.6B with a rank-32 LoRA and a scoring head (`d2l.ProcessScorer`, built on the pattern of 8.1's `d2l.RewardModel`, reading several positions); training solutions from Qwen3-1.7B in non-thinking mode on GSM8K train and `chain` train (1:1), four solutions per problem, n_train in {500, 2,000, 8,000} problems; labels ORM, PRM-hard and PRM-soft at K 8; one epoch, learning rate 1e-4, three seeds. Evaluation pools of 16 samples per problem from each of three generators (Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B, 4B) on 500 problems per test split.
3. Reranking n in {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} with `d2l.select_by_score` (200 trials); baselines random, majority (from 9.5) and the oracle pass@n; three PRM aggregations (minimum, product, last); cost as labeling FLOPs plus 6N training plus 2N inference per candidate.
4. Checks: the `verifier-credit` cell above; a stub engine reproduces 2,000 labelings within 3 standard errors; the causal check that an earlier step's score does not depend on later tokens (1e-5 in fp32); `d2l.ece` of 20,000 calibrated draws is below 0.02; `d2l.auroc` equals the brute-force pair count; `select_by_score` with a perfect scorer equals 1 minus C(m minus c, n)/C(m, n) against `d2l.pass_at_k` to 1e-9.
5. Claim that survives noise: the process scorer's gain at best-of-16 on the training generator and its drop on the other two, stated only if the paired interval (common random seed across scorers) excludes zero and the sign agrees in all three seeds; the ORM may win per FLOP and the notebook is allowed to find so. Reported: best-of-n accuracy, AUROC, ECE and reliability diagrams per generator.
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.score_choices`, `d2l.pass_at_k`, `d2l.extract_answer`, `d2l.verify_math`, `d2l.sample_responses`, `d2l.add_lora`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`, `d2l.ComputeLedger`.

### 9.5 Parallel Test-Time Compute · T1
**Idea:** More samples help until they are correlated; the majority saturates at the fraction of problems the model gets right more often than not, while coverage keeps climbing as a power law that no deployable selector reaches.
**Opening:** The reader samples 16 answers to a problem and takes the majority, and accuracy rises; at 256 samples it stops rising while pass@256 keeps climbing. The concrete example is one `chain` problem with its 16 answers grouped into equivalence classes, the majority wrong by one vote. The open question: why does the vote stop paying, and would one longer trace have been the better purchase?
**Teaches:**
- Self-consistency (majority over answer equivalence classes), best-of-n with a scorer (9.4's tables), weighted voting; the oracle pass@n as a diagnostic that is never deployable; every discarded sample and every verifier token charged.
- Majority accuracy for independent samples: the binomial tail for one wrong class, the limit (1 if p exceeds the largest wrong class, 0 otherwise, a tie split among modal classes), the Chernoff bound with exponent log(2 sqrt(p(1 minus p))) in the binary case, and a case where voting reduces accuracy (p 0.3 against a wrong class at 0.5).
- Correlated samples: per-problem success rates p_i drawn from a Beta(a, b); the majority's limit is Pr[p_i above 1/2]; the variance of the empirical rate carries the factor 1 plus (N minus 1) rho with rho equal to 1/(a plus b plus 1), so the effective sample count tends to a plus b plus 1.
- Coverage and the plateau: pass@N under the Beta model is a power law with exponent a in the uncovered fraction; an imperfect binary verifier (accept correct with alpha, wrong with beta) caps selection at alpha p/(alpha p plus beta(1 minus p)), 0.794 at (0.9, 0.1, 0.3); the KL cost of best-of-n, log N minus (N minus 1)/N, is an upper bound.
- Accuracy against generated tokens as the frontier, with wall-clock reported beside it.
**Derivation:** Majority accuracy for N independent samples at accuracy p (N 3 gives 3p-squared minus 2p-cubed) and its erosion under a shared error mode. Smallest cases (`tts-majority`): binary p 0.6 at N 1, 3, 5, 9, 15 gives 0.6, 0.648, 0.6826, 0.7334, 0.7869; p 0.4 against two wrong classes at 0.3 gives 0.4, 0.424, 0.447, 0.4887, 0.5341; p 0.3 against (0.5, 0.1, 0.1) falls 0.3, 0.282, 0.2738, 0.2362, 0.1871; the bound dominates the exact error for all N up to 33 and its slope between N 257 and 513 at p 0.6 is within 10% of log(2 sqrt(0.24)). Correlation (`tts-correlation`): Beta(2, 1) gives independence 0.6667, 0.7407, 0.8552, 0.9765, 1.0 at N 1, 3, 9, 33, 129 against the Beta-binomial 0.6667, 0.7000, 0.7273, 0.7429, 0.7481 and the limit 0.75. Coverage (`tts-coverage`): Beta(0.3, 2) gives exact coverage 0.1304, 0.4415, 0.7084, 0.8532 at N 1, 10, 100, 1,000 and the asymptotic form agrees within 1e-3 from N 100.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: how does accuracy scale with generated tokens for majority vote, scorer reranking and the oracle, and where does each saturate?
2. Model and data: the committed pools `lm-tts-pools-v1` (Parquet) from Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B and 4B in non-thinking mode (temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, top-k 20, at most 1,024 new tokens) and Qwen3-1.7B in thinking mode (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, min-p 0, at most 6,144 new tokens, N at most 16); the 0.6B generator is 9.3's T2-reduced checkpoint with pools up to N 256 (the larger generators stop at 64); problems are `chain` unseen and harder (500 each, clean), a seeded 500-problem subset of GSM8K test, MATH-500 and AIME 2024 plus 2025 (60 problems, thinking only), the last three flagged public.
3. Methods: single sample, majority, weighted by ORM, best-of-n by ORM, best-of-n by PRM-minimum, best-of-n by a zero-shot generative verifier, oracle; n in {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256} where the pool allows, 200 random subsets without replacement with a shared RNG so comparisons are paired.
4. Checks: the three derivation cells above; `d2l.maj_accuracy_indep` against the closed form to 1e-10; one million Monte Carlo draws within 3 standard errors; `d2l.fit_beta_mle` on N at most 16 predicts coverage at N 64 within the bootstrap interval (reported pass or fail); the real-pool comparison of three predictions (single-rate independence, per-problem independence fitted on held-out samples 33 to 64 and voted on samples 1 to 32, and the measured curve).

7. T1 is the full configuration: CPU analysis of the committed pools plus a live mini-run of Qwen3-0.6B at N 16 on 100 MATH-500 problems (at most 768 new tokens, no scorer resident); pool generation is one T2 job outside the notebook (`gen_pools.py`, committed with `%%writefile`).

### 9.6 Sequential and Adaptive Test-Time Compute · T2 (T1 reduced)
**Idea:** A reasoning budget is a dial, set by an effort level at inference or by a length penalty at training, and the right setting is a frontier of accuracy against tokens, by difficulty, not a point.
**Opening:** DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at low effort answers a `chain` problem in a few hundred tokens and at high effort in a few thousand, and on the easy problems the answers agree. The concrete example is one easy and one hard problem at the three effort levels with their token counts and correctness. The open question: when is the long trace paying for anything, and can a model be trained to stop earlier without losing the hard problems? The closing points to a tool call in the middle of a trace.
**Teaches:**
- Effort levels as the deployed form of budget forcing: the API's `reasoning` field (a named level or a reasoning-token budget) on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, whose release encodes effort numerically in the prompt; gpt-oss's three levels set in the system prompt and Qwen3.8's `reasoning_effort` with `preserve_thinking` (earlier reasoning kept across turns) as two other deployed forms; budget forcing itself (truncate the thinking block at B tokens, or extend it by stripping the end-of-thinking marker and appending a wait token up to m times) as the mechanism underneath.
- Adaptive allocation by difficulty: the marginal gain of one more sample, p_i(1 minus p_i)^n, is decreasing, so greedy allocation is optimal for a fixed total; small budgets fund the easiest problems first and nothing goes to p near zero; the practical rule uses a difficulty signal (agreement among four pilot samples, or their mean ORM score) fitted on validation and frozen before the test set, with the pilot tokens charged to every problem; a vote-lead stopping rule as the sequential form.
- Overthinking: the first-correct-position of a trace and its tail fraction; length penalties in RL (R minus mu l) where mu is the exchange rate between accuracy and tokens, the slope of the frontier; a penalty on wrong answers rewards guessing, so the shipped schemes gate the penalty by correctness; the KL-regularized optimum tilts the policy by e^(minus mu l/beta).
- Many samples from a small model against one answer from a larger one at equal FLOPs and at equal wall-clock (the size ladder 0.6B to 8B on the clean splits): the answer depends on difficulty and on the memory-bound decode of `sec_perf_model`.
- One sentence: interleaved thinking (a tool result inside the trace) is the bridge to 10.3.
**Derivation:** Allocation as a knapsack over problems: with a_i(n) equal to 1 minus (1 minus p_i)^n, the separable concave objective is maximized by spending where the marginal accuracy per token is highest; the continuous solution funds the set {p_i above lambda} with n_i equal to ln(lambda/p_i)/ln(1 minus p_i), and a uniform budget is optimal only when the p_i are equal. Smallest case: p equal to (0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8) with a budget of 10 samples, where exhaustive search equals the greedy heap to 1e-12; 300 problems with p_i from Beta(0.5, 1) and a budget of 600 give greedy coverage 0.532 against 0.474 for two samples each (re-measure, seeded). The length-penalty case: with a_tau(l) equal to 1 minus e^(minus l/tau) and mu 0.004, the optimum l-star is tau ln(1/(mu tau)) for mu tau below 1 and zero otherwise, so tau in {10, 30, 100, 300} gives 32, 64, 92 and 0 tokens with accuracies 0.959, 0.882, 0.601 and 0: problems harder than 1/mu are abandoned. The vote-lead rule at p_A 0.8, p_B 0.2 and lead 3 errs with probability 0.0154 and stops after 4.85 samples on average.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: how do accuracy and tokens move with the effort dial by difficulty, and does a length penalty in training shift the frontier the dial traces?
2. T1 arm (the reduced configuration): the effort dial is DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 through 1.7's `d2l.ChatAPI` at three effort settings on `chain` unseen and harder (500 each) and MATH-500 (public), with reasoning tokens, latency and correctness per item, recorded once (about 4,500 calls, `max_tokens` 16,384; see "Paid API calls") and replayed at T0 from `lm-effort-api-v1`; the committed thinking traces of Qwen3-1.7B (`lm-tts-budget-v1`: traces up to 6,144 thinking tokens with offsets, forced-answer completions at B in {256, 512, 1,024, 2,048, 4,096} and m in {0, 1, 2, 4} extensions) for the budget sweep; the allocation policy fitted on the 500-problem validation split and evaluated once on the 500-problem test split (`lm-alloc-policy-v1`, frozen); a live budget-forcing demonstration on 20 problems.
3. T2 arm: a length-penalized continuation of 8.4's GRPO checkpoint (`lm-grpo-qwen3-1p7b-base`) with `d2l.length_reward(scheme='kimi')` for S steps (S set from 8.4's ledger so one arm costs a stated fraction of 8.4's training FLOPs), against a control continued for the same S steps without the penalty and against truncating the baseline with `d2l.budget_force` at B in {64, ..., 1,024}; a shortest-of-8 SFT arm and a concision self-distillation arm (the teacher is the same weights under `d2l.concise_prompt`, through 9.2's `OnPolicyDistiller`) are optional second measurements on committed logs.
4. Checks: the `alloc-greedy`, `vote-lead` and `effic-penalty` cells above; `d2l.budget_force` on a stub engine emits exactly B thinking tokens when bound and at most B with two wait insertions; `d2l.length_reward` reproduces the paper's example (group lengths 100, 200, 300 give 0.5, 0, minus 0.5 for correct and 0, 0, minus 0.5 for wrong) and is permutation-invariant; the null test (a policy fitted on shuffled validation labels is no better than the best fixed configuration in at least 90% of 50 seeds); `d2l.match_budget` within 2%.
5. Claim that survives noise: tokens rise with effort on every item while accuracy rises on hard items only, with paired intervals per item; the fitted policy beats the best fixed configuration at the same average cost on the test split, evaluated once per frozen policy, with five repeated validation splits reporting sign agreement; for the T2 arm, the penalized frontier dominates the truncated baseline on easy and medium strata and loses on the harder stratum, stated only if the matched-budget paired interval excludes zero and the T2 difference exceeds twice the T1 seed spread.
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.load_tts_pool`, `d2l.answer_classes`, `d2l.majority_vote`, `d2l.accuracy_vs_cost` (9.5), `d2l.ProcessScorer` scores (9.4), `d2l.behavior_stats`, `d2l.eval_families`, `d2l.compute_matched_grid` (9.3), `d2l.grpo_train`, `d2l.verify_math` (8.4), `d2l.OnPolicyDistiller` (9.2), `d2l.Benchmark` for tokens per second, `d2l.ChatAPI` and `d2l.chat_batch` (1.7) for the effort dial, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`.
7. The T1 reduction for the T2 arm (`scale='t1'`): the Qwen3-0.6B GRPO checkpoint (`lm-grpo-qwen3-0p6b`) with a LoRA continuation of 30 steps, 100 problems per stratum, three seeds (the yardstick for the T2 single seed); plots rebuilt from the committed T2 logs (`lm-effic-logs-v1`).
**Figures:** `fig_lm_seq_budget` (accuracy and tokens against effort level and against forced budget, by difficulty stratum) (plot); `fig_lm_effic_frontier` (accuracy against tokens for the dial, the truncated baseline and the penalized arm, dominated points hollow, strata as panels) (plot); `fig_lm_seq_alloc_toy` (the greedy allocation on four problems, with the oracle dashed and labeled "needs correctness, not deployable"). Tables `tab_lm_seq_policy`, `tab_lm_seq_speed`, `tab_lm_effic_summary`.
**Restate / forward:** 9.5's frontier and pools; 8.4's reward and trainer; 1.7's effort cell (tokens and latency only; accuracy against effort lives here); `sec_perf_model` and `sec_kv-cache` (FLOP-matched is not time-matched); `eq_kl_objective` and `eq_kl_optimum` from `sec_regularized` for the tilted optimum; `sec_mdl-constrained-optimization-duality` for mu as a multiplier; `subsec_rl_sequences_hacking` (a length reward on wrong answers is a loophole). Forward: 10.3 (interleaved thinking).
**Exercises:** 9. Derive: the knapsack allocation and when a uniform budget is optimal (the Jensen second derivative n(1 minus p)^(n minus 2)((n plus 1)p minus 2)); the vote-lead error and stopping time at p_A 0.7, p_B 0.2, lead 2 (0.0755 and about 3.40); the abandoned-difficulty threshold at mu 0.004 (tau at least 250) and the longest funded trace 1/(e mu); the break-even query count Q-star equal to C_train/(2 N_ne Delta l), 1.19e5 queries at C_train 1e17, N_ne 1.4e9 and 300 tokens saved (arithmetic, not data). Measure: budget forcing against the effort dial on the same items; a flip-rate analysis of extension (answers that change from right to wrong and back); the size ladder at equal wall-clock. Check: the null test. Open: overthinking detection from the trace alone, without the gold answer.
**Writer notes:**
- Unlike the blueprint, budget forcing, allocation and efficient reasoning are one section ordered effort levels first, adaptive allocation second, length penalties third; no single named efficient-reasoning method is taught in prose; CRISP, L1 and Kimi k1.5 appear in Sources only as the current exemplars; the T2 notebook has two trained arms (control and penalized) with the shortest-of-8 SFT and concision arms as optional cells on committed logs.
- The effort dial runs behind an API: pin DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and one provider exactly as 1.7 does, and record the served id and provider per response. Count reasoning tokens from `usage` (they sit inside completion tokens and inside `max_tokens`, so a truncated trace is a missing answer, counted separately). The first-correct position and the overthinking statistics need the reasoning text: confirm at authoring that the pinned provider returns it, and otherwise compute them on the Qwen3-1.7B traces only. Latency through an API includes queueing, so the cost axis is tokens and latency is reported, not fitted. Confirm whether the release's numeric effort passes through the router; if only named levels do, use low, medium and high. The dial and the T2 arm are different models, so their frontiers are compared stratum by stratum, never read as one model's curve.
- Budget forcing shifts the distribution: check for repeated n-gram loops after an extension; a truncated trace followed by a forced answer may still be empty, so count missing answers separately and charge the forced-answer prompt. Extension may not help a model that was not trained for it (s1's result is on a fine-tuned 32B model); a null result is then taught through the flip-rate exercise.
- Evaluate a frozen policy once (`d2l.evaluate_policy` raises on reuse unless `force_reuse=True`, logged); the quiet version of test-set reuse is evaluating several variants on the test split, so use more validation splits instead. Charge the pilot samples that compute the difficulty signal to every problem. The `difficulty` field of `make_problems` is an oracle-like signal, reported but never selected by the fit.
- Length penalties: a linear penalty on all answers rewards short wrong answers; `scheme='kimi'` and `scheme='correct_only'` gate by correctness; identical lengths in a group give reward 0.5 for all (guard). Measure length in tokens, never characters. Report accuracy on fixed-weight strata with non-attempts as failures; a single penalty weight is a product decision, so the deliverable is the frontier. Control for the extra training steps with the continued baseline. The 8.4 checkpoint may already be short; then the gain is small and the notebook says so, or the editor adds 9.3's SFT-then-RL checkpoint as a second baseline (editor's call).
- The first-correct position depends on the extractor and on `Step` segmentation; the hand test fixes `chain` only; for free-form math report extractor agreement on 20 traces.
- Library additions: `d2l.budget_force(engine, prompts, budget, extend=0, wait='Wait,', stop_note=None, answer_tokens=256, ledger=None)`, `d2l.vote_lead_stop(classes_stream, lead, min_n=2, max_n=64)`, `d2l.greedy_allocate(gain_fn, p, budget)`, `d2l.AllocationPolicy` (`.assign`, `.to_json`, `.from_json`, immutable after `freeze()`), `d2l.fit_allocation(val, configs, signal, n_bins, lam_grid, cost_cap=None)` (asserts no test id in `val`), `d2l.evaluate_policy(policy, test, charge_signal=True, n_boot=10000)`, `d2l.length_reward(correct, lengths, group_ids, scheme='kimi', mu=1.0, l_max=None)`, `d2l.first_correct_position`, `d2l.overthinking_stats`, `d2l.pareto_front(points, x='tokens', y='acc')` (10.5 builds `d2l.agent_pareto` on it), `d2l.match_budget`, `d2l.stratified_frontier`, `d2l.amortized_breakeven(c_train_flops, tokens_saved_per_query, n_ne)`, `d2l.concise_prompt`. The GRPO reward closure passes `group_ids` derived from prompt-major order (`idx // cfg.K`). ## Chapter 10 Agents and Tool Use

**Label:** `chap_lm_agents` (5 sections, T0 to T3; no Further Reading notebook).
**Hook:** The reader has prompted a model, fine-tuned it and trained it with a verifier; a model that only emits text can be asked a question, while a model that emits actions can be given a job. This chapter turns the models of Chapters 1 to 9 into agents: systems that call a tool, read what comes back, run code and keep going over many turns.
**Route:** How does a model ask for a tool, and how is the asking measured (10.1)? How is an output kept parseable without changing what the model would have said (10.2)? What makes an agent loop succeed: the model, the interface it is given, or the context it keeps (10.3)? How is an agent trained when part of every trajectory was written by the environment (10.4)? How is an agent judged for reliability and cost, and attacked through what it reads (10.5)?
**Out of scope:** Computer-use and multimodal agents (screens, images) belong to the Image Models part. RL algorithms, verifiers and rollout systems are Chapter 8 (`sec_lm_reward_models`, 8.4, 8.5); 10.4 adds only the multi-turn mask and the environment. Index construction and the single-turn RAG baseline are Chapter 2 (`sec_lm_retrieval`, `sec_lm_rag`). Chat templates and special tokens are 1.3 (`sec_lm_prompting`); 10.1 adds only the `tools` field. Prefix caching for served agents is 13.4; KV compression is 12.6 and 12.7 (pointers only).
**Writer notes:**
- *Running models.* Qwen3-1.7B (tool calling, search agent at T3, pass^k on function calls) and Qwen3-0.6B (constrained decoding at T0, the T1 search agent); Qwen3.5-4B as the agent of 10.3 and 10.5 (Table 5; the blueprint used Qwen3-4B, which stays the fallback under the pilot rule: the smallest model whose base configuration solves at least 20% of the ten development tasks); Qwen3.5-2B as the second tool-call format in 10.1. Qwen3-8B synthesizes the search questions of 10.4 at T2. All Apache-2.0; revisions are pinned in the notebooks (blueprint ch10 lists the commit hashes read on 28 October 2026).
- *Two tool-call formats.* Qwen3 renders calls as JSON inside `<tool_call>` and tool results as a user turn with `<tool_response>` blocks; Qwen3.5 renders `<function=name>` with `<parameter=key>` lines. The two are not interchangeable (the wrong parser silently returns no calls) and `tab_lm_tool_formats` sets them side by side. Qwen3's non-thinking template inserts an empty think block at the last assistant position only, so re-rendering a history changes earlier tokens (not prefix-stable); Qwen3.5's non-thinking template is prefix-stable. This one fact shapes 10.1's SFT sample construction, 10.3's token accounting, 10.4's append-only rollouts and 13.4's cache reuse; the `tool-calling-prefix-stability` cell re-runs the check with the pinned tokenizers and the prose quotes its output.
- *Shared artifacts.* The book corpus of 2.4 (`d2l.book_corpus`, `d2l.BookRetriever`) is the retrieval tool of 10.1, the environment of 10.4 and the corpus 10.5 poisons; `d2l.book_qa` (2.5) supplies the single-turn RAG baseline. - Anthropic, [Writing effective tools for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents): the three rules for tool descriptions (name by action, say when not to use, return what the next step needs) used in 10.1 and 10.3.
- Anthropic, [Equipping agents with Agent Skills](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills) and the [Agent Skills standard](https://agentskills.io/) (specification linked from the page): the `SKILL.md` folder format and progressive disclosure that 10.3 teaches and 10.5 attacks.
- Lilian Weng, [LLM Powered Autonomous Agents](https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2023-06-23-agent/): the planning, memory and tool-use taxonomy; the memory taxonomy of 10.3's external-memory paragraph.
- Chip Huyen, [Agents](https://huyenchip.com/2025/01/07/agents.html): planning, tool selection and failure modes; the failure taxonomy of 10.3.
- Qwen, [Function Calling](https://qwen.readthedocs.io/en/latest/framework/function_call.html): the model-specific template and parser conventions of 10.1.
- Courses: [Stanford CS224N, Winter 2026](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/) (agents, tool use and RAG lecture), [CMU 11-711, Spring 2026](https://cmu-l3.github.io/anlp-spring2026) (LM agents lecture), [Berkeley CS288, Spring 2026](https://cal-cs288.github.io/sp26) (reasoning and agents; a guest lecture on computer-use agent safety), [Princeton COS 484, Spring 2026](https://princeton-nlp.github.io/cos484) (language agents; assignment A4 on systems for LLMs and agents, the closest published analogue of A9), [CMU 11-766, Spring 2026](https://www.beri.net/learning/cmu-11-766-llm-applications-spring-2026) (tool use, assistants, multi-agent systems, harms and attacks; secondary page).

### 10.1 Tool Calling · T1
**Idea:** A tool call is a structured assistant turn in the chat template and the tool's answer is another turn, so calling a tool is text generation and its accuracy is measured like any other output.
**Opening:** The chat model of Chapter 1 multiplies a three-digit number by a two-digit number and gets it wrong, and when asked to use a calculator it writes something no program can parse. The concrete example is the opening cell: 200 seeded products, Qwen3-1.7B with and without a calculator reachable through `d2l.tool_chat`, exact-match accuracy, the prompt-token overhead of the schema, and one rendered prompt. The open question: once the call parses and the tool answers, how far should the model trust the text that comes back?
**Teaches:**
- The tool turn: a JSON schema per function rendered into the system prompt by the chat template (the `tools` argument of `apply_chat_template`), the call emitted as text inside `<tool_call>` (Qwen3) or as `<function=name>` with `<parameter=key>` lines (Qwen3.5), parsed by a parser that returns errors instead of raising, and the result returned as a tool turn; parallel calls as several blocks in one turn, dependent calls as two rounds; `tab_lm_tool_formats` with the two formats, their thinking defaults and their vocabularies.
- The error taxonomy (`tab_lm_tool_errors`): no call, spurious call, syntax, truncation, unknown tool, schema, value, wrong selection, wrong count, execution; which errors the harness returns to the model as an `Error:` tool message with one retry.
- Training data for tool use: synthetic traces kept only if they execute (three verification stages: format, execution, semantic), the trace mix (single call, parallel, dependent, abstention, error recovery); Toolformer's self-supervised insertion in one sentence and Gorilla's retrieval-aware API calling in one sentence (historical); the current signal is agentic RL (10.4) and synthetic traces at scale.
- MCP as the protocol between models and tool servers: JSON-RPC 2.0 with `initialize`, `tools/list` and `tools/call`, a 30-line server and client, the printed token cost of 20 tool descriptions; one sentence on governance: MCP was donated to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025 together with AGENTS.md and goose.
- Accuracy by name, by arguments and by execution, on a BFCL-style set with intervals clustered by function name.
**Derivation:** none as a section result; two small ones with check cells. Toolformer's filter is a thresholded weighted log-likelihood ratio: keep a call if min(L(none), L(call text)) minus L(call and result) is at least a threshold, with the extra baseline ruling out gains from the call text alone; checked on 30 seeded arithmetic sentences with Qwen3-0.6B (a correct result gives positive gain, a corrupted one negative; sign fractions with a bootstrap interval). The per-turn SFT samples equal the masked full-sequence loss exactly when the template is prefix-stable; checked in fp32 on one trace with Qwen3.5-0.8B (agreement to 1e-4 relative, token equality of the two renderings) and shown to fail for Qwen3-0.6B (token sequences differ, loss gap printed).
**Notebook:**
1. Question: does SFT on executed synthetic traces raise call accuracy on held-in tool families, and what does it do to held-out families, to BFCL categories and to the abstention rate?
2. Model and data: Qwen3-1.7B, non-thinking, greedy, at most 256 new tokens, batch 32; tools `calculator` (AST whitelist with exponent and result-size caps), `python` (10.3's sandbox) and `search_book` (2.4's retriever); 60 items per BFCL v3 category (simple, multiple, parallel, parallel-multiple, irrelevance; ids committed in `lm-bfcl-subset`, revision pinned, Apache-2.0) plus 100 held-in and 50 held-out synthetic items, about 450 in all; 2,000 to 3,000 verified traces from `d2l.make_tool_traces` over six training families, with `convert_currency`, `send_note` and every BFCL function held out (a cell asserts no training function name occurs in the subset).
3. Fine-tune: LoRA rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, all linear layers, learning rate 2e-4 cosine with 3% warm-up, one epoch, batch 16, length 768, loss on target tokens only, seeds 0 and 1; Qwen3.5-2B in its native XML format as a no-fine-tune comparison.
4. Checks: `d2l.function_to_schema` equals Transformers' `get_json_schema` on five functions; the parser round-trips 200 seeded (name, arguments) pairs in both formats (the documented counterexample: an argument containing `</tool_call>` breaks the non-greedy match); `d2l.validate_args` agrees with `jsonschema.validate` on 200 random schemas; the calculator agrees with `eval` on 1,000 seeded expressions and rejects `__import__('os')` and `9**9**9` within 10 ms; `d2l.bfcl_match` agrees with `bfcl-eval` on 200 outputs in at least 98%; `d2l.turn_samples` prompts equal `d2l.tool_chat`'s inference prompts token for token on 20 traces.
5. Claim that survives noise: held-in families gain beyond the paired-bootstrap interval (cluster by function name) with the same sign for both seeds; BFCL categories and held-out families are reported with no direction asserted, and the base model is re-run once to expose bf16 batch nondeterminism (a few item flips are expected). Metrics: call accuracy, format-valid rate, error counts, rounds and tokens per item, repair rate after one retry.
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.generate`, `d2l.BookRetriever.search` (a `Hit` NamedTuple with `chunk_id, score, rank, text, heading_path, scores`), `d2l.sft_train`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`, `d2l.EvalResult`.
7. T1 is the full configuration; if over budget cut traces to 2,000 and BFCL items to 40 per category.
**Figures:** `fig_lm_tool_turn` (the annotated Qwen3 rendering of a tool turn: schema in the system prompt, call block, result as a user turn); `fig_lm_tc_accuracy` (grouped bars by category: base, with LoRA for both seeds, Qwen3.5-2B, 95% intervals) (plot); `fig_lm_tc_mcp` (sequence diagram of `initialize`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`). Tables `tab_lm_tool_formats`, `tab_lm_tool_errors`, `tab_lm_tc_trace_stats`.
**Restate / forward:** `subsec_il_sft` (SFT as behaviour cloning, one sentence) and `subsec_il_error_bounds` (compounding error over turns, one sentence); `sec_rl_sequences` (the exercise on tool outputs in the trajectory, which 10.4 takes up); `sec_decoding` (sampling is unchanged). Forward: 10.2 (guaranteed parsing).
**Exercises:** 7. Derive: why a format needs a schema and not only a grammar; the min() in Toolformer's filter; parallel calls as one turn against dependent calls as two rounds (turn counts). Measure: distractor tools (irrelevance accuracy as the tool list grows); rewriting one tool description by the three rules; `enable_thinking=True` on the same items. Check: fix a prefix-unstable template by hand and re-run the stability cell. Open: an MCP server for the book corpus, called by Qwen3-8B with paraphrased queries.
**Writer notes:**
- The model has no tool API, only a text convention; the schema's token cost is paid every turn, and a tool that returns 50 KB is a context bug. Results come back as user turns, so result text can be mistaken for instructions (10.5 owns the attack).
- The wrong parser silently returns no calls; `tab_lm_tool_formats` and `d2l.parse_tool_calls(fmt=...)` make the choice explicit. BFCL names contain dots and types like `dict`, `float`, `tuple`; convert to JSON Schema (`object`, `number`, `array`).
- Narrow tool fine-tuning can raise the spurious-call rate on irrelevance items (over-calling); report `E_SPURIOUS` next to accuracy. Greedy decoding hides sampling variance, not batch nondeterminism.
- Reference implementations: Transformers `get_json_schema` and, where it exists in the pinned release, `tokenizer.parse_response` (skip with a printed note otherwise); vLLM's `--enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser hermes` for Qwen3 as the production parser, counting how many of the 450 generations it reads differently; `bfcl-eval` for scoring. Do not copy BFCL leaderboard numbers; the subset scores are not comparable (sampling, prompt format, AST-only).
- MCP: pin the specification revision (2026-07-28 resolved on 28 October 2026) and the `mcp` package major version; the from-scratch server and client are the fallback if the SDK API moved. The governance sentence cites the AAIF announcement (primary); tool poisoning through descriptions is one sentence here and 10.5's subject.
- Library additions (signatures): `d2l.parse_tool_calls(text, fmt='qwen3', schemas=None) -> (text, list[ToolCall])`; `d2l.ToolRegistry` with `.add(fn)`, `.schemas`, `.execute(call) -> str` (validates, runs, truncates to 2,000 characters, never raises), `.log`; `d2l.tool_chat(model, tokenizer, messages, registry, fmt='qwen3', max_rounds=4, enable_thinking=False, **sampling)`; `d2l.turn_samples(messages, tools, tokenizer, fmt)` (also 10.4's oracle); `d2l.load_bfcl(category, n=None, seed=0, revision=...)`; `d2l.make_tool_traces(n, seed, families=...)`. The BFCL v3 revision may be superseded by v4 (agentic categories); state that the v3 single-turn files are used and leave multi-turn to 10.5.
- Settle at authoring: whether the production cell uses `peft` or `d2l.add_lora`; the blueprint says do not depend on `d2l.LoRALinear`'s constructor. Detail: blueprint ch10 §10.1.
**Sources:**
- Papers: [Toolformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.04761) (self-supervised insertion; the filter of the derivation); [Gorilla](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15334) (retrieval-aware API calling; the origin of BFCL); [ToolACE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00920) (verified synthetic function-calling data with complexity grading; the model for the trace generator); [Qwen3 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09388) (tool use and the thinking switch).
- Code and documentation: [Tool use in chat templates](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/chat_extras) (the `tools` argument and `get_json_schema`); [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) (the specification); [Qwen Function Calling](https://qwen.readthedocs.io/en/latest/framework/function_call.html) (parser conventions); [Gorilla repository](https://github.com/ShishirPatil/gorilla) (`bfcl-eval`); [BFCL leaderboard](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/leaderboard.html) and [BFCL v3 multi-turn post](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/13_bfcl_v3_multi_turn.html) (categories and AST scoring); Anthropic, [Donating the Model Context Protocol and establishing the Agentic AI Foundation](https://www.anthropic.com/news/donating-the-model-context-protocol-and-establishing-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation) (the governance sentence).
