### 10.2 Structured Outputs and Constrained Decoding · T0
**Idea:** A grammar over characters becomes an automaton over tokens, and masking the logits with it guarantees a parseable string while changing the distribution in a way that can be computed exactly.
**Opening:** Some of 10.1's calls fail to parse: 100 unconstrained samples at temperature 0.7 from Qwen3-0.6B on the calculator prompt, with the parse-failure and schema-violation rates printed (a minority, not zero). The reader wants a decoder that cannot emit an invalid string. The open question: what does the guarantee cost, in time and in what the model would otherwise have said?
**Teaches:**
- A JSON schema as a regular language (required keys first, optional keys as groups, a whitespace policy of none, single or any) and the regular language as a byte-level automaton built by derivatives; a token is allowed in a state if its byte string reaches a live state, and the end-of-turn token exactly when the state is final.
- Tokens that span several transitions or end mid-string: the token automaton tracks one state per token through a trie walk; non-canonical tokenizations are allowed because the automaton constrains strings, not tokenizations; logits have 151,936 columns while the tokenizer has 151,669 ids, so the padding ids are always masked.
- Masking is not conditioning: token-by-token renormalization produces p(y)/prod Z(prefix), the true conditional is p(y)/p(L), the two agree only when the product of the normalizers is constant across the language; the KL between them has a closed form and a bound T log(1/(1 minus lambda)) over T constrained steps.
- Triggered grammars (free text until `<tool_call>`), masking before temperature and top-p, jump-forward decoding in one paragraph; "valid syntax is not a correct answer" and constraining after thinking (the grammar starts when the think block closes).
**Derivation:** The token automaton from the character automaton (acceptance is preserved; with all 256 single bytes in the vocabulary no live state becomes dead), and the distribution masked sampling produces. Smallest case: the language {ax, by} with p(a) 0.5, p(b) 0.4, p(other) 0.1, p(x given a) 0.01, p(y given b) 0.9. Then p(ax) is 0.005, p(by) 0.36, p(L) 0.365, the true conditionals 0.0137 and 0.9863; the normalizers are 0.9 at the first step and 0.01 or 0.9 at the second, so masked sampling gives 0.5556 and 0.4444, a ratio of 40.56 for ax and 0.45 for by, and a KL of 1.7028 nats. The exact fix weights each token by the probability of completing the language from that prefix, which is intractable in general. The case of vocabulary {a, ab} and language {ab} is the one-token illustration of a token spanning two transitions and appears first.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: does a tokenizer-aware masker keep 10.1's call accuracy at a 100% parse rate, and what does the whitespace policy and the trigger do to accuracy, spurious calls and time?
2. Model and data: Qwen3-0.6B on CPU (Qwen3-1.7B behind `--gpu` on T1 with double the items), non-thinking, greedy; 30 items per BFCL category for simple, multiple, parallel and irrelevance from `lm-bfcl-subset` (120 items); 10.1's schemas through `d2l.tool_call_regex`.
3. Arms: unconstrained; forced call with single whitespace; triggered grammar; forced call with no whitespace.
4. Checks: the regex engine against `re.fullmatch` on 10 patterns by 200 strings; `d2l.schema_to_regex` on 8 schemas (100 valid instances match, 100 mutated fail both the regex and `d2l.validate_args`); the token automaton against `re` on decoded strings over 10 patterns by 200 random token paths, and no reachable state with an empty mask; the toy distribution cell reproduces 1.7028 nats and 200,000 samples match the masked distribution within 3 standard errors; a mask-for-mask comparison with XGrammar on 50 completions by 10 patterns (identical on ASCII patterns, every other difference explained: end tokens, special tokens, partial UTF-8, whitespace); the real-model cell enumerates a finite answer set of 12 to 20 multi-token city names with `d2l.exact_masked_distribution` and reports the KL, the largest ratio and the mass on non-canonical tokenizations.
5. Claim that survives noise: schema validity is 100% for the constrained arms by construction (asserted); the forced arm calls on every irrelevance item and the triggered arm does not; accuracy effects are reported with paired intervals (cluster by function name, greedy so no sampling noise) and no direction is asserted. A 40-problem side probe compares free-form reasoning then `Answer: N`, a constrained `{"answer": N}`, and a constrained `{"reasoning": ..., "answer": N}` (no claim unless the interval excludes zero).
6. Reused pieces: `sample_next` from `sec_decoding` with its logits step replaced, 10.1's `load_bfcl`, `bfcl_match`, `parse_tool_calls`, `validate_args`, `classify_call`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`.
7. T0 is the full configuration; no committed artifact (a mask-cache timing table is printed, not stored).
**Figures:** `fig_lm_token_automaton` (the derivative automaton of `-?(0|[1-9][0-9]*)` with token edges overlaid); `fig_lm_so_distortion` (the toy bars and the real-model scatter of masked against conditional probability on log axes) (plot); `fig_lm_so_headline` (schema validity, accuracy and spurious calls by arm; histogram of the summed log normalizers for the two whitespace policies) (plot). Tables `tab_lm_so_engines` (measured mask seconds per step), `tab_lm_so_patterns` (state counts for an integer, a five-word enum, an ISO date, a calculator call).
**Restate / forward:** `sec_decoding` (greedy, temperature, top-k, top-p and min-p are unchanged; only the logits step is replaced); `sec_text-sequence` (byte-level BPE in one paragraph; special tokens are single symbols). Forward: none.
**Exercises:** 7. Derive: when the end token is allowed (nullable states); the completion weights for the toy (0.01 and 0.9) and the exact conditional they give; the KL bound at T 20 and lambda 0.05 (about 1.03 nats, larger than ln 2). Measure: the three whitespace policies on the same items; the reasoning-order probe at n 200 on Qwen3-1.7B. Check: the token set allowed in the `calc` state. Open: strict UTF-8, `$ref` and recursion, jump-forward decoding.
**Writer notes:**
- Mask before temperature and top-p, never after. Validity holds only at a final state: a generation cut by `max_new_tokens` is a valid prefix, not a valid output (check `is_final`). Bytes at or above 0x80 are admitted freely, so output can be invalid UTF-8 (the open exercise). Decoding a partial UTF-8 token does not give its bytes; work in bytes.
- `ws='any'` can emit whitespace forever; bound it. A schema whose property order differs from the model's habit forces low-probability tokens; a grammar that cannot express "do not call" makes the model hallucinate a call (the triggered arm exists for this reason).
- Reference implementation: XGrammar (`TokenizerInfo.from_huggingface(tokenizer, vocab_size=model.config.vocab_size)`, `GrammarCompiler`, `compile_regex`, `compile_json_schema(..., any_whitespace=False)`, `GrammarMatcher`, the bitmask functions; API as of 0.1 to 0.2, verify in the pinned release); Outlines (`outlines.from_transformers`); `llguidance` only if installed; vLLM `structured_outputs` for serving. Pin versions, smoke-test the first bitmask fill, and keep the `re` oracle if the production cells break. XGrammar supports rollback, which is what speculative verification needs (12.4).
- Performance fallbacks: if the pure-Python trie walk exceeds 1 s per state, precompute visited states only, restrict the headline to 10.1's tools, and cache masks to disk keyed by pattern and tokenizer revision; if 120 items exceed 10 minutes on CPU, cut to 20 per category or require `--gpu`; cap exact enumeration at 500 paths.
- Library additions: `d2l.parse_regex(pattern) -> Node` (literals, escapes, classes, groups, alternation, repetition, the `@{<tool_call>}` token for a special symbol); `d2l.schema_to_regex(schema, ws='single')`; `d2l.tool_call_regex(tools, fmt='qwen3', max_calls=3)`; `d2l.TokenFSM(pattern, tokenizer, vocab_size, trigger=None)` with `.start`, `.mask(state)`, `.step(state, token_id)`, `.is_final(state)`, `.n_states`, `.stats`; `d2l.constrained_generate(model, tokenizer, prompt_ids, fsm, max_new_tokens, temperature=0.0, top_p=1.0, seed=0)` (KV-cached, per-step log Z recorded); `d2l.enumerate_paths`, `d2l.exact_masked_distribution`. The XML format of Qwen3.5 is left to an exercise. Detail: blueprint ch10 §10.2.
**Sources:**
- Papers: [Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09702) (Outlines; the index design); [XGrammar](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15100) (pushdown automaton and token-mask caching); [Grammar-Aligned Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.21047) (exactly the derivation's distortion and an approximate fix); [Guiding LLMs The Right Way](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.06988) (subword misalignment, minimal invasiveness); [Let Me Speak Freely?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02442) (format restriction and reasoning; the side probe); [SGLang](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104) (compressed automaton and jump-forward decoding in a serving runtime).
- Code and documentation: [outlines](https://github.com/dottxt-ai/outlines) and its [documentation](https://dottxt-ai.github.io/outlines/latest/); [XGrammar](https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar) and its [documentation](https://xgrammar.mlc.ai/docs/); [vLLM structured outputs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/structured_outputs/); [llguidance](https://github.com/guidance-ai/llguidance) and [guidance](https://github.com/guidance-ai/guidance).
- Courses, tutorials and blogs: [CMU 11-711, Spring 2026](https://cmu-l3.github.io/anlp-spring2026) (decoding algorithms lecture, constrained decoding); [Hugging Face Agents Course](https://huggingface.co/learn/agents-course/unit0/introduction) (structured tool arguments in practice).

### 10.3 Agent Loops and Harnesses · T1
**Idea:** An agent is a loop of observe, think and act whose success depends as much on the interface it is given and the context it keeps as on the model inside it.
**Opening:** On a repair task that needs five commands in a row, 10.1's model redoes a step it has already finished, because the output of that step scrolled out of a context it never managed. The concrete example is the opening cell: a 12-line scripted agent that applies the gold patch succeeds, and the live model over three seeds prints outcome, steps, summed prompt tokens and generated tokens, with the summed prompt tokens exceeding the final context length by a large factor. The open question: when the agent fails, is it the model's failure or the harness's?
**Teaches:**
- The loop: the model emits an action, the harness executes it in a sandbox and returns an observation, the episode ends on submit, a step limit, a context overflow or a format limit; `tab_lm_al_notation` maps the loop's objects to `tab_rl_notation` (prompt, agent turns, observations, trajectory, policy, reward as the hidden-test outcome).
- Code as the action space and the agent-computer interface: a bash-only interface, an interface with file viewing and editing commands (SWE-agent's ACI), and CodeAct (a Python program as the action); observations formatted to at most 2,000 characters (head and tail) with the exit code.
- Long horizons: token cost with and without prefix caching (the quadratic sum against the linear one), truncation, observation masking (keep the last k observations verbatim), compaction (ask the model for a summary at half the budget), file memory and subagents (described, exercised); interleaved thinking, a tool call inside the reasoning trace, as 9.6's bridge arrives here.
- Agent Skills: a `SKILL.md` folder with name and description loaded at startup, the full instructions loaded only when a task matches, bundled scripts loaded on execution; progressive disclosure as a context policy for procedural knowledge, with the token cost of each stage measured on the repair tasks.
- A failure taxonomy (`tab_lm_al_failures`: format, action loop, context overflow, navigation, edit failure, wrong fix, regression, tampering, no submit) with hand-labeling agreement on 30 failed episodes; cost and latency accounting per episode.
**Derivation:** Token cost over an episode of T steps with initial context c0, generated a_s and observed o_s tokens per step: without caching P equals T c0 plus the sum over s of (T minus s)(a_s plus o_s); with caching P equals c0 plus the sum of (a_s plus o_s); at constant u per step these are T c0 plus u T(T minus 1)/2 against c0 plus u(T minus 1). Smallest case: c0 800, 12 steps, 300 tokens each, giving 29,400 against 4,100. When compaction pays: replacing H history tokens by a summary of S tokens costing phi S saves tokens only for the remaining steps R above phi S/(H minus S) without caching, or (phi S plus c0 plus S)/(H minus S) with it; masking costs no generated tokens so its break-even is near zero. Check cells recompute the identity from logged lengths (exact for the full policy) and simulate the break-even for T 5 to 40 and phi in {1, 4} (within one step of the formula).
**Notebook:**
1. Question: interface or context policy: which moves success and cost more for a 4B agent on 30 repair tasks under a small context budget?
2. Model and data: Qwen3.5-4B (text-only, non-thinking, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, at most 512 new tokens per step; Qwen3-4B as the fallback by the pilot rule), the book-authored `repair30` (ten Python modules of 40 to 80 lines, three injected bugs each, 4 visible and 4 to 8 hidden pytest tests; success is every fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass hidden test passing with no tampering) and `dev10` for calibration; `max_steps` 15; `max_ctx_tokens` chosen on `dev10` from {3,072, 4,096, 6,144, 8,192} as the smallest value at which the base configuration overflows in 15 to 40% of episodes, written into the notebook before the test run.
3. Arms: ACI with full context, with observation masking (k 3) and with compaction, plus bash-only with full context; seeds 0 and 1, with a pre-registered rule adding seed 2 for all four cells only if a claimed contrast has an interval including zero while its point estimate exceeds the between-seed difference; 240 episodes (360 at most), run offline with vLLM (`run_grid.py`, committed) and analyzed from `lm-agent-runs-ablation`. A skills arm (ACI plus a build-and-test skill) is a fifth cell only if the budget allows; otherwise the skill's token cost is measured on `dev10` and the arm is the open exercise.
4. Checks: `Sandbox.selftest()` prints CONTAINED or ESCAPED for ten threats (infinite loop, memory bomb, fork bomb, disk fill, many files, outbound connection, read and write outside the workdir, secrets in the environment, signals to other processes) and asserts agreement with `capabilities()`; the grader passes 30 of 30 gold patches, 0 of 30 unpatched, and flags tampering; a scripted oracle policy solves 30 of 30 under all three interfaces and a random-edit policy 0 of 30; policy unit tests (system prompt and first user message preserved; at most k observations verbatim after masking; compaction leaves the last two steps; prompts within budget or `ctx_overflow`, never silent truncation); replay determinism; the token identity.
5. ### 10.4 Training Agents with Reinforcement Learning · T3 (T1 reduced)
**Idea:** In a multi-turn episode only the agent's tokens are actions, the environment's tokens are transitions, and the loss mask is what makes the policy gradient correct.
**Opening:** The 10.3 agent's episode interleaves its own tokens with tool outputs it never produced; feed the whole transcript to 8.4's trainer and it learns to predict, and then to invent, the observations. The concrete example is the opening cell: 10.1's loop with `search_book` on 100 development questions, Qwen3-1.7B zero-shot, with exact match, mean searches and the fraction without a final answer, next to the single-turn RAG baseline. The open question: how is reward given for a late failure that an early search caused?
**Teaches:**
- The episode as an MDP with tool outputs as transitions: the trajectory probability factorizes into policy terms and environment terms, the environment terms do not depend on theta, so the gradient sums the score only over agent tokens; an unmasked loss adds a term that is nonzero whenever the reward correlates with the observation, and a baseline that depends on the observation is biased.
- Trajectory-level against turn-level rewards (reward-to-go with a history-dependent baseline; earlier rewards drop out of later turns); clipping and group advantages applied at masked positions only; the three aggregations (token mean, sequence mean, constant divisor) and what each rewards.
- Environments as code: a search environment over the book corpus with append-only prompts (token-in, token-out, special-token parsing off so a retrieved passage cannot forge a turn boundary), throughput as the bottleneck (environment idle fraction, search latency against a sandboxed `pytest`), and asynchronous rollouts with a staleness cap in one paragraph (8.5 owns the systems).
- Search and software agents as the shipped forms (Search-R1, SWE-RL), task and environment synthesis at scale (the question-synthesis recipe here; Kimi K2's agentic data synthesis as the pointer), and reward hacking in agentic settings (editing the test, listing several answers for a lenient verifier).
**Derivation:** The multi-turn policy gradient with its mask (`eq_lm_arl_mt_gradient`): the gradient of the expected reward is the expectation of (R minus b) times the sum over agent tokens of the score function, with no observation term; the masked clipped loss divides by the count of masked tokens. Smallest case: a two-turn toy with a softmax over three queries, a stochastic observation in {0, 1} with fixed environment probabilities, a softmax answer conditioned on the observation, and reward 1 when the answer matches f(query, observation), with a block of parameters that gives the model its own distribution over observations; enumerating all (query, observation, answer) triples, the masked estimator's expectation equals the exact gradient to 1e-12 and the unmasked estimator differs by a printed nonzero norm. On a two-layer random Qwen3 configuration in fp32, the masked-loss gradient on the concatenated three-turn trajectory equals the sum of per-turn gradients from separate forward passes within 1e-5 relative, and adding environment positions to the mask changes it by more than 1e-3.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: does GRPO with outcome rewards and masked environment tokens beat prompting with the same tool and single-turn RAG with the same retriever, and does it learn to search more than once on two-hop questions?
2. Model and data: Qwen3-1.7B at T3 (Qwen3-0.6B at T1), non-thinking; the environment `d2l.SearchEnv(retriever, item, max_turns=4, k=3, obs_tokens=200)` over 2.4's retriever; `lm-book-search-qa` (at least 3,000 train, 300 dev, 300 test after filtering; 60% one-hop chunks and 40% two-hop pairs linked by `:numref:` or a shared heading; questions and short answers written by Qwen3-8B verbatim from the gold chunks; filters for verbatim answers, closed-book solvability, retrievability in the top 10 and near-duplicates; a 100-item manual audit with its error rate; split by source section); 2.5's `d2l.book_qa(split='test')` as the test set.
3. Training at T3: 64 prompts per step with K 8 (512 trajectories), at most 256 new tokens per turn, temperature 1.0, AdamW at 1e-6 constant with a 10-step warm-up, gradient clip 1.0, epsilon 0.2, beta 0 (0.001 as an exercise), token-mean aggregation, one update per rollout batch, as many steps as fit the 2-hour cap (about 100), dev evaluation every 10 steps (greedy, 300 questions), FSDP2 trainer beside a vLLM replica; dynamic sampling (8.4) if more than half the groups are degenerate. Final test for four conditions: closed-book, prompted agent, single-turn RAG, RL agent.
4. Checks: the tabular and transformer cells above; the mask sums to the sampled-token count with observation positions at 0; `d2l.masked_pg_loss` reduces to the plain GRPO token loss with an all-ones mask and to minus A times the sum of log-probabilities at large clip; `d2l.group_advantages` is zero-mean within groups and zero for degenerate groups; a passage containing a literal `<|im_end|>` yields no special-token id; determinism at temperature 0; the retokenization check (fraction of rollouts whose decode-then-encode ids differ from the sampled ids; trainer against engine log-probability gap per token).
5. Claim that survives noise: the RL agent beats prompting beyond the paired interval over test questions (cluster by source section) and by more than the three-seed T1 spread in relative terms; a single T3 run is otherwise reported as one run. Logged: reward, dev exact match, mean searches, fraction without a final answer, length, clip fraction, KL to the initial policy, mean log-probability of observation tokens (the drift monitor the derivation predicts).
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.turn_samples`, `d2l.parse_tool_calls`, `d2l.ToolRegistry`, `d2l.search_book` (10.1), `d2l.Sandbox` (10.3), `d2l.group_advantages`, `d2l.sample_responses` (8.4), `d2l.sync_weights` (8.5), `d2l.fsdp_wrap` (6.2), `d2l.BookRetriever`, `d2l.book_qa`, `d2l.gold_chunk_ids` (2.4, 2.5), `d2l.pass_at_k`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`.

- The two silent breakages: re-rendering the history changes Qwen3's earlier tokens, so trajectories are concatenated from sampled ids (token-in, token-out; the observation format is fixed text with special-token parsing off); and trainer against engine log-probabilities differ, so decide which is "old" and measure the gap (a truncated importance correction from 8.5 only if the gap is large). - Sequence-mean aggregation rewards shorter responses and under-penalizes long failures; it shows up as the number of searches. A strict outcome reward on a weak model gives mostly zero-advantage groups; check the degenerate fraction before blaming the optimizer. Single-run reward curves are not evidence; the T1 envelope is.

### 10.5 Evaluating and Securing Agents · T1
**Idea:** An agent is judged by reliability over repeated trials and by cost, not by its best run, and it is attacked through what it reads, so a defence is measured by attack success and by what it costs in utility.
**Opening:** The 10.3 agent solves six tasks in ten once; a user who runs it every day wants the same task solved every time. The concrete example is the opening cell on the committed tau-bench airline trajectories: pass@1 0.42, pass^4 0.20, pass@4 0.72, with the histogram of per-task successes among four trials (14 tasks at 0, 12 at 1, 10 at 2, 4 at 3, 10 at 4). The open question: what defence against an attacker who writes into a web page lasts longer than the next template?
**Teaches:**
- pass^k against pass@k: both from per-task success rates, the unbiased estimators from n trials, the mirror between them, and the two regimes (reliable-but-imperfect tasks, where pass^k falls far faster than pass@k rises, against heterogeneous tasks, where the Beta-binomial fit shows power laws in k with exponents set by the mass near 1 and near 0); the time-horizon statistic (the task length at 50% success) as the second reliability number, with its 80% variant.
- Variance across tasks and trials: the between-task term is divided by the number of tasks, not by tasks times trials, so the naive binomial interval is too narrow by up to the trial count; task-cluster bootstrap, nested bootstrap, and for a fixed budget one trial per task minimizes the variance of pass@1 while pass^k needs n at least k.
- Cost-normalized scores (prompt, cached, generated tokens, tool and model seconds, a price supplied, never hard-coded), the frontier of success against cost, and the retry argument: a cheap agent retried r times beats an expensive one unless the expensive one's rate exceeds 1 minus (1 minus p)^r, which needs a perfect verifier.
- Harness sensitivity, reproducible environments and leakage: a benchmark lifecycle paragraph with Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Pro and future-commit leakage as dated examples, and the validity checklist (task validity, outcome validity, reporting); names, licences, counts and tiers in the data file `data/lm_benchmarks.json` (table `tab_lm_ae_benchmarks`); the one-page evaluation card `tab_lm_ae_card` as the deliverable of every agent report.
- Indirect prompt injection through tool outputs, retrieved pages and tool descriptions, and a malicious `SKILL.md` as a supply-chain attack: the threat model (the attacker controls content the agent reads, not the prompt or the weights), two goals (exfiltration of a canary planted as a private note; answer hijack to a fixed string), ten template families, three defences measured (spotlighting with delimiters or data marking, a least-privilege tool gate derived from the task, both), and instruction hierarchy, plan-then-execute and capability-based designs described.
**Derivation:** pass^k as the mean over tasks of p_i^k and pass@k as the mean of 1 minus (1 minus p_i)^k, with the unbiased forms C(c, k)/C(n, k) and 1 minus C(n minus c, k)/C(n, k). Smallest case: two tasks at 0.9 and 0.5 give pass^5 near 0.31 and pass@5 near 0.98; the committed airline file (mean 0.42) gives the other regime, where pass@k rises more than pass^k falls over k at most 4. Under p drawn from Beta(alpha, beta), E[p^k] is the product of (alpha plus j)/(alpha plus beta plus j) and decays like k to the minus beta. The variance identity: Var of the mean equals sigma_t squared over N plus E[p_i(1 minus p_i)] over N n, against the naive mu(1 minus mu)/(N n). Check cells enumerate all k-subsets at n 6 (1e-12), simulate 200,000 draws from Beta(2, 1) at k 4 (1/3), fit the airline file (alpha about 0.65, beta about 0.85 on a 0.05 grid; predicted pass^k 0.433, 0.286, 0.217, 0.176 against the recomputed 0.420, 0.273, 0.220, 0.200), and measure interval coverage over 2,000 simulated experiments (N 50, n 4) for the naive, cluster and nested bootstraps.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: how much does one defence cut attack success, and at what cost in utility, on the same agent whose reliability is first measured with pass^k?
2. Reliability arm: the best cell of 10.3's grid (Qwen3.5-4B, ACI, chosen policy) on `repair30` with 8 trials per task at temperature 0.7 (240 episodes, committed) and Qwen3-1.7B on the BFCL single-turn subset with 8 trials (in the notebook, about 10 minutes), with the tau-bench trajectories as the reference; pass@1, pass@k and pass^k for k in {1, 2, 4, 8} with cluster-bootstrap intervals, the Beta fit, the variance components, mean and 95th-percentile latency and tokens. A five-trial live sizing is the floor when the budget is short (k at most 4).
3. Security arm: Qwen3.5-4B with `search_book` and a mock `send_note` over the poisoned book corpus on development questions of `lm-book-search-qa`; interactive cells with 100 episodes per arm for no defence and spotlighting; the offline grid of 50 questions by 20 variants (ten templates by two goals; a live subset of 60 attacks is run live) by four defences, about 4,000 episodes, committed. Injection is appended to the question's gold chunk (retrieval-aligned poisoning); delivery rate is reported, since an attack never retrieved measures nothing. A malicious-skill arm plants the injection in a `SKILL.md` that the task matches.
4. Checks: `d2l.agent_report` reproduces the four README pass^k values on each tau-bench file to 1e-3; `d2l.pass_pow_k` and `d2l.pass_at_k` against enumeration; the spotlighting round trip; `d2l.ToolPolicy` blocks `send_note` for QA and allows `search_book`; the `attack_success` truth table (achieved, attempted but blocked, no attempt); the poisoned chunk reaches the top 3 for at least 95% of 20 questions.
5. Claim that survives noise: the gate reduces exfiltration success to zero by construction and leaves answer hijack unchanged; spotlighting reduces attack success by an amount to be measured, with paired intervals on (question, variant) clustered by question, and every defence's utility cost is reported on the clean corpus and under attack; with one sample per episode the within-episode noise is not separately estimated, and the text says so. Attack success without defence is reported as a lower bound (static templates; adaptive attackers do better).
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.pass_at_k` (1.4), `d2l.paired_bootstrap`, `d2l.EvalResult` (1.5), `d2l.pareto_front` (9.6), `d2l.load_bfcl`, `d2l.bfcl_match`, `d2l.tool_chat`, `d2l.ToolRegistry`, `d2l.search_book` (10.1), `d2l.Episode`, `d2l.run_batch`, `d2l.Sandbox` (`capabilities()` gates the exfiltration cells), `d2l.load_repair30`, `d2l.grade_repair`, `d2l.cost_report` (10.3), the 10.4 agent as an optional arm, `d2l.BookRetriever`.
7. T1 is the configuration: the reliability analysis of committed trajectories is T0; the BFCL run and the interactive injection cells run live; T2 extensions behind `--tier t2` (tau2-bench airline with Qwen3-8B as agent and user simulator; a 30-task SWE-bench Verified subset with `mini-swe-agent` and Qwen3-30B-A3B on a T2 pair; BFCL multi-turn) are separate tables.
**Figures:** `fig_lm_injection_paths` (user, agent, tools, retrieved content, skill file, the attacker's path and the two gates); `fig_lm_ae_passk` (pass@k and pass^k against k for the three sources with the Beta-binomial fit dashed and an inset of the homogeneous case) (plot); `fig_lm_ae_asr` (attack success by defence and goal; template-by-defence heatmap; attack success against utility under attack) (plot). - Changes over the blueprint: benchmark names live in the data file `data/lm_benchmarks.json` (Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Pro and METR's time horizon are dated examples in the lifecycle paragraph; WebArena and tau2-bench stay as rows); the time horizon joins pass^k as the second reliability statistic; the malicious `SKILL.md` arm sits next to injection (counts of malicious skills on community hubs are secondary and are not quoted); the agent is Qwen3.5-4B. A single trial per task reports pass@1 only, and "reliable" needs n at least k; never mix pass@k with a verifier (a search budget) and pass^k in one headline.
- Statistics pitfalls: treating trials as independent shrinks intervals; resample tasks. A benchmark you tune on is no longer a test (keep the frozen subset). A cost without its token convention and its price source is not a number. Leaderboard numbers are not comparable across harnesses, user simulators and judges.
- Security scope: the gate stops tool-call attacks by construction and does nothing for content attacks (confused deputy against data corruption); zero observed injections is not safety; the allow-list is only as good as the task-derived policy; answer-hijack success is string match and misses semantic hijacks. Shell-capable agents on injected content refuse to run without `net_blocked`; a host without namespaces runs only the search-agent arm. Tool descriptions are prompt text (MCP tool poisoning): pin, review, show to the user, diff between sessions; a `SKILL.md` is the same surface with a folder of scripts behind it.

Injection results for small models may sit near 0 or 1; report as measured and add harder templates rather than changing the model.

## Chapter 11 Model Compression

**Label:** `chap_lm_compression` (6 sections plus a Further Reading notebook; every section is T1, the Further Reading notebook is T0).
**Hook:** In 7.5 the reader stored a frozen model in four bits so that a fine-tuning run would fit, and the model ran no faster. A served model has to be fast, its activations enter the arithmetic, and it is judged on held-out quality at a stated speed. This chapter builds, one mechanism at a time, the methods that compress a trained model for that purpose, and checks each against brute force, an exact identity, or a paired interval.
**Route:** What does quantization speed up, and what does it only shrink (11.1)? Why do a few activation channels break an eight-bit grid, and how does a rescaling move the difficulty into the weights (11.2)? Why is rounding a layer's weights a least-squares problem, and what does solving it column by column recover (11.3)? Why does a random rotation turn outliers into ordinary coordinates, and what does that make possible at four bits (11.4)? What does training through the quantizer recover that calibration cannot, and in which formats do models now ship (11.5)? When does removing weights remove work (11.6)?
**Out of scope:** Number formats are owned by `sec_numerics` and `sec_hardware` (block formats and their layouts; `tab_gpu_specs`). The quantizers themselves (absmax, blockwise, NF4) are owned by 7.5 and restated in 11.1. The KV cache is compressed in 12.6 and 12.7, not here. Kernels that read packed weights are measured here through torchao and Marlin; writing such a kernel is 12.1 and 12.2. Running a quantized model on a CPU or a laptop is 12.8. Which quantized checkpoint to download and how to pin it is `sec_software_ecosystem`.
**Writer notes:** The chapter runs on Qwen3-1.7B through Transformers for kernels and benchmarks, on the Qwen3-0.6B checkpoint loaded into the book's own code (`d2l.load_qwen3`, 1.2) wherever a method rewrites weights in place (rotations in 11.4, quantization-aware training in 11.5), and on Qwen3-0.6B, 4B and 8B only for the fixed-memory sweep of 11.1. Calibration data is the committed `lm-c11-calib-fineweb-128x2048` array (128 sequences of 2,048 Qwen3 token ids from FineWeb-Edu, seed 0); evaluation text is WikiText-2 (test split) in non-overlapping 2,048-token windows, so that perplexity differences are paired over windows and bootstrapped with `d2l.paired_bootstrap` (1.5). The chapter's shared artifact is `data/compression_report.jsonl`: one row per compressed checkpoint written by `d2l.compression_row` (11.1) and appended by every later section, with the fields listed in blueprint ch11 "Running examples"; 11.6 builds the chapter's closing table `tab_lm_comp_all` from it. 11.1 exports the helpers every later section imports (`d2l.fake_quant`, `d2l.pack_int4`, `d2l.effective_bits`, `d2l.replace_linears`, `d2l.W8A8Linear`, `d2l.window_nll`, `d2l.calib_tokens`, `d2l.decode_tps`, `d2l.compression_row`); 11.3's `d2l.gptq_quantize` is reused by 11.4 (rotate, then quantize), 11.5 (the post-training comparator) and 11.6 (SparseGPT is the same sweep with a zero grid). Every result is labelled "native", "real kernel, emulated format" or "simulated (fake quantization)", and no speed is ever claimed from a simulated result; the hardware table in blueprint ch11 "Compute plan" (what runs natively on A100, Ada and Blackwell) is reproduced once in 11.1 as `tab_lm_q_hw`. The chapter hosts the optional mini-assignment `sec_lm_a11_mini` (compress Qwen3-1.7B to a byte budget, report packed bytes with `d2l.effective_bits`, perplexity within a stated band of BF16 with its paired interval, a layer-output match within `1e-3` relative error against the student's own fake-quantized reference, and a one-page decision for batch 1 on Ada versus batch 64 on A100); with 12.8 in place the assignment gains an optional part that deploys the compressed checkpoint on a CPU through llama.cpp and reports decode tokens per second against the host's measured memory bandwidth. Cross-chapter consistency: 7.5 owns the quantizers and the `d2l.QTensor` type (`codes, scales, zeros, block_size, shape, bits`; `q.scales`, never `absmax`); 4.3 owns the block-scaling error of MXFP4 and NVFP4 and 11.5 restates it; `sec_custom_layer` owns the straight-through estimator; 12.1 consumes the int4 packing convention of 11.1 (`pack_int4`, group 128, bf16 scale and zero, 4.25 bits per weight) and 12.8 consumes the GGUF block layouts of 11.1. Cross-references to the hardware chapter use its second-pass numbering (5.3 for the decode step-time model `d2l.ServingModel`). Pitfalls common to the chapter: fake quantization is never faster; "4-bit" files are rarely 4 bits per parameter (scales, zero points, the head and the embedding stay in 16 bits); perplexities are comparable only at the same tokenizer, window size and context; calibrating on the evaluation text inflates every gain; torchao's configuration API changes between releases, so the notebook pins the version and gates every library row with a try/except that marks the row `n/a`.
**Teaching sources:**
- [MIT 6.5940 TinyML and Efficient AI Computing](https://hanlab.mit.edu/courses/2026-fall-65940): the lecture sequence quantization, pruning, distillation, and the labs that implement linear and k-means quantization from scratch before inspecting them; the chapter follows this ordering (11.1 to 11.6).
- Maarten Grootendorst, [A Visual Guide to Quantization](https://newsletter.maartengrootendorst.com/p/a-visual-guide-to-quantization): the visual vocabulary (absmax versus zero point, outliers, calibration) behind the figures of 11.1 and 11.2; redraw, do not copy.
- [EMNLP 2025 tutorial on efficient inference for LLMs](https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-tutorials.1/): the taxonomy used to check that 11.1 to 11.6 cover the post-training, training-aware and pruning branches.
- Alex Smola, [Efficiency in LLMs](https://alex.smola.org/posts/45-mlss-efficiency/): the memory-traffic framing and the progression from lossless coding to weight compression (11.1, 11.6, Further Reading).
- [torchao](https://github.com/pytorch/ao) and its [documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/ao/stable/index.html): the production API for weight-only and weight-and-activation quantization, quantization-aware training and sparsity (11.1, 11.5, 11.6).
- [llm-compressor](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor) and [NVIDIA Model Optimizer](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Model-Optimizer): calibration and deployment workflows for serving stacks (SmoothQuant and AWQ recipes in 11.2, GPTQ settings in 11.3, NVFP4 and pruning in 11.5 and 11.6); read for their defaults, not run on the T1 path.
- [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) and the [GGUF specification](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md): the block formats of 11.1 and the deployment target of 12.8.
**Further Reading:** `sec_lm_compression_fr`, the entry at the end of this chapter: codebooks and lattices (QuIP#, AQLM), lossless exponent coding (DFloat11, ZipNN), structured pruning with distillation at scale (Minitron), the k-bit inference scaling laws, quantization-aware training recipes at scale (LLM-QAT, ParetoQ), ternary models trained with the quantizer in the loop (BitNet b1.58).

### 11.1 Quantization for Inference · T1
**Idea:** Decode time tracks the bytes read per token, so weight-only quantization speeds up decode, while quantizing activations as well is what speeds up prefill and large batches.
**Opening:** The reader has 7.5's four-bit model and the fact from `sec_hardware` that single-stream decode is bound by weight bytes over bandwidth. The opening cell loads Qwen3-1.7B in BF16, prints its measured decode tokens per second next to the bound computed from its byte count, then applies 7.5's four-bit round trip to every linear layer and prints perplexity (fine) and tokens per second (unchanged within noise), because the dequantized weights are stored in BF16 again. The question the section answers is what has to change for the smaller file to become a faster model, and the closing question is why eight-bit activations, which should help prefill, hurt accuracy in a way eight-bit weights do not.
**Teaches:**
- What changes from fine-tuning to inference: memory traffic and arithmetic rate instead of capacity, activations as well as weights, calibrated final weights judged on held-out quality and speed; one recap paragraph of 7.5's absmax, blockwise and NF4 quantizers with the table `tab_lm_q_vs_qlora`.
- Granularity and effective bits: per-tensor, per-channel, per-group scales for weights and per-token scales for activations; symmetric against asymmetric grids; range clipping; `b_eff = b + (b_s + b_z)/g`, with the formats of this chapter in `tab_lm_q_effbits` (INT4 at group 128 is 4.125 bits; GGUF Q4_0 is 4.5 and Q4_K is 4.5; MXFP4 is 4.25; NVFP4 is 4.5 plus one float per tensor).
- Weight-only against weight-and-activation quantization and the kernels that make each fast: dequantize inside the matrix multiply (tinygemm, Marlin) against an integer or FP8 matrix multiply with scaling in the epilogue; why a per-input-channel activation scale cannot be applied in an integer epilogue, which is the problem 11.2 solves.
- A roofline for one quantized layer: the batch at which a weight-only format stops helping, and why W8A8 is flat in the batch and helps prefill rather than small-batch decode.
- GGUF block formats as a two-level scheme (super-blocks with sub-scales), checked against the bytes of a real tensor, and why a `Q4_K_M` file mixes types.
- Bits against parameters at a fixed memory budget: at four gigabytes of weights, is Qwen3-1.7B in BF16, Qwen3-4B in INT8 or Qwen3-8B in INT4 the better model?
**Derivation:** Speed of a quantized linear layer. With weight bytes per parameter `w_f`, activation bytes `a_f` and peak rate `π_f` of the unit a format uses, `t_f(B) ≥ max((w_f mn + a_f B(m + n))/β, 2Bmn/π_f)`; weight-only formats gain up to `16/b_eff` at small batch and lose the gain by `B* = π w_f/(2β)`; W8A8 gains the integer-to-float rate ratio at every batch. Smallest case: one 2048 by 6144 layer of Qwen3-1.7B at `B = 1` and `B = 256` with `tab_gpu_specs` numbers, then the whole model: the tied head and embedding stay in 16 bits, so quantizing the blocks alone caps the decode speedup below the bytes ratio (the arithmetic of 12.1's byte accounting, previewed in one line).
**Notebook:**
1. The question: does decode speed follow weight bytes once a real kernel reads the packed format? Model Qwen3-1.7B; calibration from `d2l.calib_tokens`; evaluation on WikiText-2 windows and `d2l.EvalSuite(['arc_challenge', 'hellaswag', 'arc_easy', 'piqa'], n=500, seed=0)`.
2. Measure the copy bandwidth and the INT8-to-BF16 rate ratio on the host GPU first and use them, not datasheet values, in every model overlay.
3. Part A, one layer: the two MLP shapes of Qwen3-1.7B at `B` from 1 to 512 for BF16, INT8 weight-only, INT4 group 128 (tinygemm), INT8 W8A8 (dynamic per-token) and FP8 W8A8 (native on Ada; skipped on A100 with the reason printed); seven interleaved repetitions.
4. Part B, the model: BF16; INT8 weight-only; INT4 weight-only at groups 32, 64, 128, 256 (round-to-nearest, torchao kernels); W8A8 INT and FP8; perplexity with paired intervals over windows, task scores with paired intervals, prefill tokens per second at 2,048 tokens, decode tokens per second at batch 1 with `d2l.decode_tps` (CUDA graphs on), peak memory, `b_eff`, percent of the decode bound; one `d2l.compression_row` per configuration.
5. The GGUF check: reference Q8_0 and Q4_0 quantizers (ten lines each) against one tensor of `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF` read with `gguf.GGUFReader`, and the block sizes asserted against the `gguf` package's size table.
6. The fixed-memory sweep: Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B, 4B and 8B at BF16, INT8 and INT4 group 128 on one plane of weight gigabytes against perplexity (the 8B is quantized on load from host memory, since its BF16 weights do not fit a 15 GiB slot).
7. Claims that survive noise: within a format family, decode tokens per second are ordered by bytes per token, within about 10% of the byte ratio and never above the recomputed bound; the weight-only speedup decays past the measured `B*`; INT8 weight-only is indistinguishable from BF16 in perplexity by the paired interval; adjacent group sizes are called different only if their paired interval excludes zero. At a fixed byte budget the larger model in fewer bits wins or ties on this family (to be measured; stated as measured).
8. Reused pieces: `d2l.quantize_blockwise`, `d2l.quantize_nf4`, `d2l.dequantize`, `d2l.QTensor` (7.5); `d2l.Benchmark` (`sec_perf_model`); `d2l.load_hf` (1.1); `d2l.EvalSuite`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap` (1.5); `d2l.ServingModel` (5.3) for the batch at which the layer turns compute-bound.
**Figures:** `fig_lm_q_granularity` (one weight row quantized per tensor, per channel, group 128 and group 32, drawn as error histograms, plus one activation row per token against per tensor); `fig_lm_q_layer_speed` (plot: speedup against batch for each format with the derivation's dashed curves and the `B*` ticks); `fig_lm_q_pareto` (plot: perplexity against weight gigabytes for four sizes and three formats, with the four-gigabyte line).
**Restate / forward:** `eq_hw_decode_bound` (decode tokens per second are at most bandwidth over bytes read per token); `subsec_hw-two-workloads` (prefill is compute-bound, decode is bandwidth-bound); `sec_memory_precision` (halving the bytes wins twice, in capacity and in traffic); 7.5's quantizers in one paragraph; `subsec_comp-overhead` (CUDA-graph replay for the decode loop, used through `d2l.decode_tps`). Forward: 11.2.
**Exercises:** 6 to 8. Check: predict the batch-1 decode ceiling of an 8B model in BF16, W8A16 and W4A16 at group 64 on a 3.35 TB/s GPU, then with a 20 GB KV cache read per step. Derive: `B*_f = π w_f/(2β)` for a weight-only format and the batch at which W4A16's advantage over W8A8 vanishes; the int32 overflow bound for int8 products. Measure: predict, before running, the batch at which the INT4 kernel loses to BF16 on the host GPU, then sweep to `B = 2048` and explain the gap by the dequantization overhead. Measure: quantize `lm_head` to INT8 and INT4 and report the decode and perplexity change with paired intervals. Open: pick a memory budget and find the best Qwen3 checkpoint, format and group size on WikiText-2 and one task, with a half-page decision memo that names what was not measured.
**Writer notes:** The notebook's first lesson is that an accuracy simulation is not a speedup; keep the opening cell's "unchanged tokens per second" visible and do not tune it away. Measured bandwidth and rate ratio replace datasheet numbers in every overlay (the datasheet ridge is not exact). Decode must be timed with CUDA graphs; eager timing hides the byte ratio at batch 1 (`subsec_comp-overhead`). Blocks of `d2l.quantize_blockwise` run over the row-major flattened tensor, so a block size dividing `d_in` equals a group along the input dimension; assert `d_in % block_size == 0`. `torch._int_mm` has shape restrictions (a minimum row count and multiples of eight) to be verified against the pinned version; the decode path pads or falls back and the timing says which. FP8 W8A8 is skipped on A100 by design (no FP8 tensor cores; storage plus dequantization only). Quantizing the head and embedding hurts quality disproportionately and saves less than the body; the standard choice skips `lm_head` and the embedding, and the notebook says so once. The pre-quantized Hub checkpoints (`Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-FP8`, `Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-GPTQ-Int8`, `Qwen/Qwen3-8B-AWQ`, `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-AWQ`) are existence checks only, each wrapped in a try/except and marked `n/a` if the pinned package set cannot run it. Reference implementation and tolerance: the reference `fake_quant` round trip against torchao's dequantized weights (exact equality of codes, scales within float tolerance); `pack_int4` and `unpack_int4` exact. The GGUF byte counts (Q4_0 18 bytes per 32, Q8_0 34 per 32, Q4_K 144 per 256, Q6_K 210 per 256) are asserted against the `gguf` package table rather than typed into prose. Do not re-teach: formats (`sec_numerics`), the decode bound's derivation (`sec_hardware`), the quantizers (7.5). Library additions: the exports listed in the chapter notes, all `#@save`; the artifact `data/compression_report.jsonl`. Hardware fallback: if decode graph capture fails for a quantized tensor subclass, report the layer microbenchmark and an eager decode with the overhead stated. Blueprint ch11 11.1 has the derivation steps (D1, D2 integer epilogue), the normative export signatures and the GGUF layout check; the fixed-memory frontier cites the k-bit scaling laws for the direction and says what one family and one metric do not show. The 8B row stays: it needs at least 20 GB of host memory to quantize on load (confirm on the build host at authoring); if the host cannot do it, drop the row rather than claim a whole 24 GB card.
**Sources:**
- Papers: [Quantization and Training of Neural Networks for Efficient Integer-Arithmetic-Only Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.05877) (the affine scheme and the integer matrix multiply with a fixed-point epilogue); [The case for 4-bit precision: k-bit Inference Scaling Laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09720) (bits against parameters at a fixed total; the direction of the fixed-memory sweep); [MARLIN: Mixed-Precision Auto-Regressive Parallel Inference on Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11743) (why a packed four-bit format needs its own kernel and how far the batch can grow before the gain decays); ["Give Me BF16 or Give Me Death"? Accuracy-Performance Trade-Offs in LLM Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02355) (what FP8, INT8 and INT4 cost on one model family, the calibration point for Part B's directions).
- Code and documentation: [torchao](https://github.com/pytorch/ao) and [its documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/ao/stable/index.html) (the kernels and configurations of Part A and B); [Marlin](https://github.com/IST-DASLab/marlin) (the optional fused int4 row); [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) and the [GGUF specification](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md) (the block layouts of step 5); the [llama.cpp quantize tool README](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/quantize/README.md) (the type mix behind `Q4_K_M`); [llm-compressor](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor) (the production counterpart, read only).

### 11.2 Activation Outliers and Equivalent Rescaling · T1
**Idea:** A few activation channels carry most of the range, and because the product `a_j w_j` is unchanged by scaling one factor up and the other down, the range can be moved from activations into weights before either is quantized.
**Opening:** The reader has 11.1's finding that eight-bit weights are free and eight-bit activations with a per-tensor scale are not. The opening cell runs Qwen3-1.7B at W8A16, then at W8A8 with one static activation scale per tensor, and prints the perplexity gap, followed by the largest and the median per-channel absolute maximum at one `down_proj` input and their ratio. The question is why a per-tensor scale fails for activations when it works for weights, and the closing question is whether the difficulty can be removed instead of moved.
**Teaches:**
- Where outliers live: a channel survey over the four linear-layer input sites (`qkv`, `o`, `gate` and `up`, `down`) across layers, with streaming statistics (`absmax`, root mean square, the fraction of tokens with a large entry per channel); channel outliers against token-specific massive activations and why the per-token against per-channel distinction decides which scale granularity can absorb them.
- LLM.int8()'s mixed decomposition: outlier columns kept in 16 bits, the rest in INT8, exact in float; an accuracy tool whose two-kernel structure is not a speed recipe.
- The rescaling identity `X Wᵀ = (X diag(s)⁻¹)(W diag(s))ᵀ` and SmoothQuant's balancing choice `s_j = a_j^α / w_j^(1−α)`; where `1/s` and `s` can be fused (into the preceding RMSNorm weight `γ` or into the producing linear layer) and where they cannot (a SiLU does not commute with a scale; a value projection shared by a GQA group must be scaled per group).
- AWQ as the weight-only relative: the same identity, with `s` chosen by a grid search on activation statistics to protect salient weight channels at three and four bits; no gradients, a calibration set, and a clipping search.
- Why the gain depends on granularity: per-token dynamic scales already absorb token-level magnitude, so SmoothQuant helps most for per-tensor static scales; smaller weight groups already isolate outliers, so AWQ helps most at per-channel.
**Derivation:** The rescaling identity and the balancing choice. For every `s` the product of the per-tensor activation range and the per-tensor weight range is at least `max_j a_j w_j`; `α = 1/2` makes every channel's two ranges equal to `√(a_j w_j)` and attains the bound. Smallest case: two channels with `(a, w) = (64, 1)` and `(1, 1)`, where an INT8 per-tensor grid on the unscaled activations wastes six bits on the second channel, and the balanced scaling gives both factors the range 8. The AWQ error term for one group with one salient channel is derived in an exercise.
**Notebook:**
1. The question: how much of the W8A8 and W4 loss do rescaling and calibration recover, and does the answer depend on the scale granularity? Qwen3-1.7B BF16; the 11.1 calibration array; WikiText-2 windows and the 11.1 task suite.
2. One statistics pass with forward hooks (`d2l.collect_input_stats`), committed as `lm-c11-act-stats-qwen3-1p7b`; the sorted channel ranges per site and layer are the first figure.
3. The exactness check before any quantization: fuse the scales (`d2l.apply_smoothing`) and compare logits in float64 against the unscaled model; this cell must pass before any perplexity is reported.
4. W8A8 arms with INT8 per-channel weights: activations per-tensor static, per-tensor dynamic, per-token dynamic; methods round-to-nearest, SmoothQuant at `α` in {0.5, 0.75}, LLM.int8()-style decomposition as the reference. W4A16 arms at per-channel and group 128: round-to-nearest, AWQ with a 20-point grid, AWQ with clipping. Fake quantization throughout (simulated; no speed claimed), with the INT8 per-token path cross-checked once against the real `d2l.W8A8Linear`.
5. The `α` grid is searched on 64 calibration sequences and scored on the other 64; the calibration draw is repeated with seed 1 for the main rows.
6. Claims that survive noise: an ordering between two methods is stated only if it holds in both calibration draws and the paired interval over windows excludes zero; the per-tensor static gap closes most, the per-token gap least (direction from the derivation; magnitude measured); AWQ's gain over round-to-nearest is larger at per-channel than at group 128 (direction; measured). Qwen3's QK-norm and RMSNorm layout may put the outliers at different sites from the papers' models, which is why the survey comes first and is reported as found.
7. Reused pieces: `d2l.fake_quant`, `d2l.W8A8Linear`, `d2l.replace_linears`, `d2l.window_nll`, `d2l.calib_tokens`, `d2l.compression_row` (11.1); `d2l.paired_bootstrap` (1.5).

Forward: 11.4.

Check: with per-token INT8 activations, which tokens lose precision when one massive activation appears. Derive: the lower bound on the product of per-tensor ranges and that `α = 1/2` attains it. ### 11.3 Reconstruction-Based Quantization · T1
**Idea:** Rounding a layer's weights is a least-squares problem whose Hessian is the input covariance, and rounding one column at a time while compensating the rest with that Hessian loses far less than rounding all at once.
**Opening:** The reader has 11.2's calibrated grids and knows that round-to-nearest at three bits is much worse than at four. The opening cell takes a row of six weights with a known input covariance, rounds it to a 2-bit grid three ways (nearest, one column at a time with compensation, and exhaustive search over all grid points) and prints the three reconstruction losses: the compensated rounding is far below nearest and close to the exhaustive optimum. The question is where the compensation comes from and whether it scales to a 6,144-column layer, and the closing question is whether a better local loss is a better model.
**Teaches:**
- The layer-wise objective `‖X Wᵀ − X Ŵᵀ‖²` with `H = XᵀX` shared by every output row, its conditioning (`κ(XᵀX) = κ(X)²`), rank deficiency when calibration tokens are fewer than input channels, and damping as a ridge that pulls the solution toward nearest rounding.
- The Optimal Brain Surgeon step: fixing one weight to a grid point costs `Δ²/[H_F⁻¹]_qq` and the remaining free weights move along a column of `H_F⁻¹`; the Schur-complement update that removes the fixed index.
- GPTQ's three changes: a fixed column order so one Cholesky factor of `H⁻¹` supplies every update, lazy block updates that turn rank-one updates into matrix products, and the dampening constant; act-order as the one-difference variant and what it does to kernel layouts.
- Calibration as part of the method: size, domain and the "true sequential" propagation of quantization through the block; the random-token control.
- The local loss as a proxy: per-layer loss ratios predict perplexity only loosely; the single-site swap that tests which layers matter.
**Derivation:** The Optimal Brain Surgeon update from a quadratic with one equality constraint (Lagrangian, closed form), then the GPTQ column sweep: with the columns processed in a fixed order the needed entries of the successive inverses are the rows of one upper Cholesky factor of `H⁻¹`, so a single factorization replaces a sequence of inverses. Smallest case: the 2 by 2 weight row against every grid point, drawn with the loss ellipse of `H`.
**Notebook:**
1. The question: how much of the round-to-nearest gap does Hessian compensation recover at four and three bits, and how does the answer depend on calibration? Qwen3-1.7B; the 11.1 calibration array; WikiText-2 and a held-out FineWeb-Edu slice; the 11.1 task suite.
2. Check against brute force: `d2l.gptq_quantize` against `d2l.brute_force_quantize` on rows of six to eight weights with random positive-definite `H` (the greedy sweep is not optimal; the gap on tiny rows is shown, not hidden).
3. Quantize the model block by block with Hessians collected from the already-quantized prefix (`d2l.quantize_model_gptq`, order `q,k,v`, `o`, `gate,up`, `down`), at W4 group 128, W3 group 128 and W4 per-channel, with round-to-nearest and AWQ (11.2) as baselines; log per-linear proxy losses for both.
4. The calibration ablation at W4 group 128: sizes 4 to 512 sequences by three domains (FineWeb-Edu, WikiText-2 train, random tokens); damping 0 to 0.1 at 16 sequences to expose rank deficiency; the eigenvalue spectrum of `H` at two sites.
5. The sensitivity study: swap one site type at a time from nearest to GPTQ and record the perplexity change.
6. Claims that survive noise: GPTQ below round-to-nearest at three bits by the paired interval in both calibration draws (seeds 0 and 1); the gain grows as the grid coarsens; more calibration helps and saturates; same-domain calibration helps most and random tokens are worst (directions from the papers; magnitudes measured); the proxy-loss ranking of sites is compared with the single-site swap and reported even if they disagree.
7. Artifacts: the packed checkpoint `lm-c11-qwen3-1p7b-gptq-w4g128` (reused by 12.1 as a quantized target), the per-layer loss table, rows in the report.
8. Reused pieces: 11.1's helpers; `d2l.awq_search` (11.2) for the baseline; `d2l.QTensor` (7.5) to wrap codes, scales and zeros so `d2l.dequantize` reproduces the dequantized weight.
**Figures:** `fig_lm_gptq_toy` (the six-weight row: nearest, compensated and exhaustive points on the loss ellipse of `H` for two coordinates); (plot) proxy-loss ratio GPTQ over nearest by layer and linear type; (plot) perplexity against calibration size by domain with the paired interval against nearest.
**Restate / forward:** `sec_mdl-numerical-stability-conditioning` (`eq_mdl-opt-kappa-squared`: squaring a matrix squares its condition number, which is why `H` is ill-conditioned and damping is needed); `subsec_mdl-psd` (a positive definite matrix has a Cholesky factorization); `sec_mdl-svd-low-rank` (the rank of `H` is at most the number of calibration tokens). Forward: 11.6.
**Exercises:** 6 to 8. Check: why every row of a layer shares one Hessian and one Cholesky factor. Check: the maximum rank of `H` for a 6,144-channel input calibrated on 4,096 tokens and what GPTQ does on the null space. Derive: the Schur-complement downdate from the block-inverse formula. Derive: that lazy blocks of size `B` cut the weight-matrix reads from `d_in` to `d_in/B` at unchanged arithmetic and raise the update's arithmetic intensity from about 1 to about `B`. Measure: the proxy-loss ratio against the activation energy `Σ_j H_jj` per layer, with and without act-order. Measure: calibration size in {1, 2, 4, 16} sequences against damping, predicting from the rank argument where damping takes over. Open: calibration for mixture-of-experts layers, where each expert sees a fraction of the tokens (Qwen3-30B-A3B or gpt-oss-20b).
**Writer notes:** Accumulate `H` in float32 from BF16 inputs with a running normalization (`d2l.accumulate_hessian`); BF16 accumulation overflows or loses the small eigenvalues. Collecting `H` from the unquantized model's activations (`sequential=False`) is a legal variant with a different, usually worse, result; the notebook runs the sequential variant and names the other. Act-order with groups breaks the contiguous-group layout fast kernels expect unless static groups or a `g_idx` are supported; say so where the packed checkpoint is written. Zero "pruned" entries explicitly after a sweep (rounding leaves `1e-18`). The per-column loop is slow in eager PyTorch (6,144 iterations for `down_proj`): lazy blocks of 128 keep it within budget; fall back to `torch.compile` on the inner loop or to the `FAST` flag (first 8 blocks) with the full result committed. The largest Hessian (`down_proj`, 6144 squared, 151 MB in float32) fits; keep it on the host and move it for the Cholesky if 10 GiB is exceeded. Reference implementation and tolerance: brute force on rows of at most eight weights (exact comparison of losses; GPTQ's loss must be at most that of nearest rounding and is allowed to exceed the exhaustive optimum); optionally the IST-DASLab `gptq` reference line by line as the convention oracle (symmetric against asymmetric grids, zero-point rounding, group-scale rule); the published `Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-GPTQ-Int8` configuration is read only for its settings table `tab_lm_gptq_defaults`. The WikiText-2 train against test ablation is an in-domain effect, not generalization; say so. Do not re-teach: conditioning, Cholesky, 11.2's rescaling. Library additions: `d2l.accumulate_hessian`, `d2l.gptq_quantize`, `d2l.quantize_model_gptq`, `d2l.obs_step`, `d2l.brute_force_quantize`; artifact `lm-c11-qwen3-1p7b-gptq-w4g128`. Blueprint ch11 11.3 has derivations D1 (OBS) and D2 (the Cholesky sweep) with numbered steps and the check cells, the export signatures, the calibration-ablation design and the exercise sketches. The packed checkpoint (about 1.1 GB) is committed only if the storage budget allows, since 12.1 can regenerate it in under 15 minutes; otherwise the notebook regenerates it.
**Sources:**
- Papers: [GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323) (the algorithm: arbitrary order, lazy batch updates, the Cholesky reformulation, and its ablations); [Optimal Brain Compression: A Framework for Accurate Post-Training Quantization and Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.11580) (the exact OBS-based quantizer and pruner that GPTQ approximates); [Second order derivatives for network pruning: Optimal Brain Surgeon](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/1992/hash/303ed4c69846ab36c2904d3ba8573050-Abstract.html) (the original update, cited for the derivation); [SparseGPT: Massive Language Models Can Be Accurately Pruned in One-Shot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.00774) (the same machinery with a zero grid; 11.6 builds on it).
- Code and documentation: the [GPTQ reference repository](https://github.com/IST-DASLab/gptq) (Hessian accumulation and the block loop, the line-by-line oracle); [GPTQModel](https://github.com/ModelCloud/GPTQModel) and [llm-compressor](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor) (production defaults for damping, act-order, static groups and true-sequential quantization).
- Courses, tutorials and blogs: [MIT 6.5940](https://hanlab.mit.edu/courses/2026-fall-65940) (post-training quantization lectures); [CMU 11-868 LLM Systems](https://llmsystem.github.io/llmsystem2026spring/) (its quantization and GPTQ lecture); Smola, [Efficiency in LLMs](https://alex.smola.org/posts/45-mlss-efficiency/) (weight compression as a reconstruction problem).

### 11.4 Rotations and Incoherence · T1
**Idea:** An outlier is a property of the coordinate system, and a random orthogonal rotation folded into the weights spreads every vector so evenly that four-bit activations become workable.
**Opening:** The reader has 11.2's rescalings, which make eight-bit activations work and still leave four-bit activations far from the model. The opening cell takes one residual-stream vector of Qwen3-1.7B, prints its maximum over its root mean square (near the worst case `√d` when one channel dominates), applies a random sign flip followed by a Hadamard transform, and prints the ratio again (a small constant). The question is why rotating helps when scaling did not, and why the network does not notice the rotation; the closing question is how random the rotation should be.
**Teaches:**
- Hadamard matrices (Sylvester for `2^k`, the order-12 construction for `12·2^k`) and the fast transform in `O(d log d)`; incoherence as a small maximum-over-norm ratio; which Qwen3 widths admit which orders.
- Computational invariance: the residual stream can be rotated by any orthogonal `R` if every writer (embedding, every block's output projections) is multiplied by `R` and every reader by `Rᵀ`, provided the RMSNorm scale `γ` is first folded into the following linear layers; the four rotation sites of QuaRot (residual, inside attention, inside the MLP before the down projection, and the KV cache) and which are free (fused offline) and which run online.
- Why randomness is needed: a fixed Hadamard has adversarial inputs (the all-ones vector); random signs give a sub-Gaussian spread.
- The effect on grids: rotated activations quantize well per token at four bits; weights were already roughly Gaussian and gain less; interaction with group sizes of 16 to 32 (block formats of 11.5).
- Learned rotations as the one-difference relative (SpinQuant: optimize `R` on the Stiefel manifold against the fake-quantized loss) and the variance across random rotations that motivates them; codebooks and lattices named in one sentence with a pointer to the Further Reading notebook.
**Derivation:** The concentration bound. For a unit vector `x` and `R = H D/√d` with random signs `D`, each coordinate of `Rx` is a signed sum with sub-Gaussian proxy `1/d`, so `max_j |(Rx)_j| ≤ √(2 log(2d/δ)/d)` with probability at least `1 − δ`, while the root mean square is `1/√d`; the ratio is `O(√log d)` against the worst case `√d` before rotation. Smallest case: `(8, 0, 0, 0)` under a 4-point Hadamard with and without signs. Second derivation, short: that folding `γ` and rotating readers and writers leaves the function unchanged (the RMSNorm without mean subtraction commutes with an orthogonal map after its scale is removed).
**Notebook:**
1. The question: how much of the four-bit activation loss does a rotation recover, and how much depends on which rotation? Qwen3-1.7B as a `d2l.GPT` (hidden 2048 and MLP 6144 admit Hadamard orders); Qwen3-0.6B for the exactness checks.
2. Exactness first: `d2l.rotate_gpt` with quantization off must reproduce the logits of the unrotated model to float tolerance for every seed, including the untied head; a forgotten matrix gives plausible but wrong logits.
3. The spread statistics: the maximum-over-RMS ratio per site and layer before and after rotation on 16 calibration sequences, against the derivation's bound.
4. Arms with simulated quantization through `d2l.SimQuantLinear` (11.2): weights 16 or 4 bits, activations 8, 6 and 4 bits per token; rotations none, SmoothQuant at `α = 0.5` (11.2's baseline), the residual rotation only, residual plus attention plus MLP rotations at three seeds, a dense Haar-random residual rotation, and rotation followed by GPTQ W4 (11.3) for one seed if time allows.
5. A small learned-rotation toy (`d2l.learn_rotation`, Cayley parametrization, 200 steps) on one layer, as the bridge to SpinQuant.
6. Claims that survive noise: at W4A4 the rotated model's perplexity is below the unrotated one by more than both the paired interval and the across-seed range; most of the gain is in the residual and down-projection rotations (direction; measured); A8 is unchanged by rotation within the interval. A small model may stay well above BF16 at W4A4 even after rotation, and that is reported as the result, with W4A8 and W6A6 as the practical points.
7. Reused pieces: `d2l.fake_quant`, `d2l.window_nll`, `d2l.calib_tokens`, `d2l.compression_row` (11.1); `d2l.SimQuantLinear`, `d2l.apply_smoothing` (11.2); `d2l.gptq_quantize` (11.3); `d2l.load_qwen3` (1.2).
**Figures:** `fig_lm_rot_spread` (one vector before and after a random Hadamard: coordinates sorted by magnitude, with the `√d` and `√log d` levels); `fig_lm_rot_sites` (the residual stream with the four rotation sites, writers and readers marked, `γ` folded); (plot) perplexity against activation bits for unrotated, rescaled and rotated at W16 and W4.
**Restate / forward:** `sec_mdl-geometry-linear-algebraic-ops` (orthogonal maps preserve norms and inner products); `sec_mdl-concentration-generalization` (`eq_mdl-subgaussian`: a signed sum of bounded terms is sub-Gaussian; the maximum of `d` such sums is `O(√log d)`); `sec_transformer-block` (RMSNorm without mean subtraction and its scale `γ`); 11.2's rescaling as the comparison. Forward: 11.5 (block formats and their group sizes).
**Exercises:** 6 to 8. Check: why `γ` must be folded before the residual rotation and which parameters become untied. Check: which rotations fuse offline and why the one before the down projection cannot (the SiLU product is not linear in any weight). Derive: that the all-ones vector attains the worst ratio under a fixed Hadamard and that random signs remove the adversary. Derive: the rate-distortion gap of a scalar grid against a Gaussian source (about 0.25 bits) and what a lattice can recover of it (the one codebook exercise that remains). Measure: twenty random rotations on one layer, the layer-output error of A4 against the seed, predicted coefficient of variation against the measured one, then the best and worst seed on full-model perplexity. Measure: weights only at W3 per channel with and without the residual rotation, predicting from the derivation that weights gain less. Open: SpinQuant-style learning of the residual rotation on Qwen3-0.6B against the best of twenty random Hadamards at W4A4, with the compute spent.
**Writer notes:** The rotation is exact only if every reader and writer of the residual stream is transformed: the embedding, the head (untied first), every `W_q, W_k, W_v` and `W_g, W_1` as readers, every `W_o` and `W_2` as writers, and the folded `γ` of both norms; the exactness cell runs before anything else and bisects by layer with 1.2's matcher on failure. Online rotations need a kernel (`d2l.OnlineHadamard` before `W_2`); say that "free" applies to the fused ones only. Hadamard orders: Qwen3-0.6B and 1.7B widths are `2^k` or `12·2^k`; Qwen3-4B's 2560 and 9728 would need orders 20 and 76, which is why 4B is not used here (an exercise handles general widths); Qwen3-8B's widths work and are a T2-sized extension. With group sizes of 16 to 32 (11.5's block formats) a full-width rotation mixes across groups; use group-sized rotations there and say why. The KV-cache rotation site is named and left to 12.6 (keys are rotated after RoPE there). Reference implementations: the invariance test is the oracle; QuaRot and SpinQuant code are optional comparisons behind try/except (their licences are checked before any vendoring). Do not re-teach: orthogonality, sub-Gaussian tails, 11.2's identity. Library additions: `d2l.hadamard`, `d2l.fast_hadamard`, `d2l.random_hadamard`, `d2l.max_rms`, `d2l.OnlineHadamard`, `d2l.rotate_gpt`, `d2l.learn_rotation`; the committed rotation seeds (sign vectors) and the per-site spread table. Blueprint ch11 11.4 has the concentration derivation D1 with numbered steps, the invariance derivation D2 with the folding order, the export signatures, the Hadamard-order table and the exercise sketches; its `d2l.kmeans_vq` export and the codebook subsection move to the Further Reading notebook. Time: about seventeen evaluations of a simulated model; cut the A8 and A6 rows to 80 windows if over budget.
**Sources:**
- Papers: [QuaRot: Outlier-Free 4-Bit Inference in Rotated LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00456) (computational invariance and the four rotation sites); [SpinQuant: LLM quantization with learned rotations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16406) (learned rotations and the variance across random ones); [QuIP: 2-Bit Quantization of Large Language Models With Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13304) (incoherence processing, the bound the derivation follows); [QuIP#: Even Better LLM Quantization with Hadamard Incoherence and Lattice Codebooks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04396) (the Hadamard construction and, for the Further Reading notebook, lattice codebooks).
