## Chapter 13 Serving Systems

**Label:** `chap_lm_serving` (9 sections; T1 to T3, every T3 section has a T2-pair live reduction and a T1 path on committed logs).
**Hook:** The reader has 12.1's decoder, which answers one request near the bandwidth bound. A service never sees one request: it sees an arrival process, a mix of prompt and output lengths, a latency contract, and a hundred users who are each waiting. This chapter builds the mechanisms inside a serving engine, each with an invariant a test can check and a measurement against a reference server, from the contract a service makes to the layouts that spread one model over a node.
**Route:** What does a server promise, and where does the latency curve turn up (13.1)? How does scheduling per iteration keep the GPU full while a long prompt does not stall everyone else (13.2)? How does cache memory stop fragmenting, so the batch is bounded by real tokens (13.3)? When may two requests share a prefix's cache, and which workloads share most (13.4)? Under overload, whom does the server serve, drop or pause (13.5)? Where does a cache live when it outgrows one GPU, and how does a request find its prefix among replicas (13.6)? How are a dense and a mixture model cut across the GPUs of one node (13.7)? Why are prefill and decode given separate pools, and what does moving the cache between them cost (13.8)? How are many fine-tuned variants served from one base model (13.9)?
**Out of scope:** Running vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp or Ollama as a user, their flags, the client contract and the engine landscape stay in `sec_model_serving` (`subsec_model-serving-contract`, `subsec_model-serving-local`, `tab_serving_workloads`); this chapter links them and measures against them. Rental prices and cost per instance-hour are `sec_cloud_instances`; the cost-per-token arithmetic and the throughput-interactivity frontier are the hardware chapter's (5.3 and 5.8) and are restated here. Training parallelism is Chapter 6; this chapter revisits tensor and expert parallelism for decode only. Kernels are Chapter 12. Rollout engines inside reinforcement-learning training are 8.5; 13.4 and 13.8 restate what serving gives them.
**Writer notes:** The engine of 13.1 to 13.6 and 13.9 is built around Qwen3-0.6B in the book's own code through 12.1's `d2l.FastGenerator` (slots, `pos` and `kv_len`, the `KVCache` protocol, `forward` with per-row positions); 13.2 adds `d2l.RaggedLM` (a flat-token forward over the same slots and weights), 13.3 replaces the slot store by `d2l.PagedKV`, 13.4 adds `d2l.RadixCache`, 13.5 adds policies to `d2l.ContinuousScheduler`, 13.6 adds a host tier, and nothing changes the model code. Qwen3-30B-A3B is the node-scale model of 13.7 and 13.8 (61 GB in BF16, which does not fit one 40 GB A100, so the smallest feasible tensor-parallel degree is 2); Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-0.6B are the T2-pair stand-ins. Reference servers are vLLM and SGLang at pinned versions in separate virtual environments (their torch pins differ from each other and from the book's), reached only over HTTP through `d2l.OpenAIServer`; `LIVE_VLLM=False` replays committed curves. Every latency-throughput experiment reports a full curve over at least six offered loads that bracket saturation, with at least three arrival seeds, and pairs two systems on the same seed and requests; nothing is claimed from a single operating point. Traces: the Azure LLM inference traces of 2023 and 2024 (CC-BY), BurstGPT (licence read from its repository before any excerpt is committed), the Mooncake FAST'25 traces (conversation, tool-and-agent, synthetic; with block hash ids that 13.4 and 13.6 use), and ShareGPT token lengths only; prompts are seeded windows of the book corpus tokenized with the Qwen3 tokenizer so token counts are exact. The step-time model is `d2l.ServeStepModel` (13.2; fitted `P_eff`, `β_eff`, `t_ovh`), distinct from the hardware chapter's analytic `d2l.ServingModel`; `d2l.SimExecutor` plugs it into the same scheduler so every policy can be swept on a CPU and validated at three live loads with a stated error. The chapter hosts assignment A10 (`sec_lm_a10`, in 13.3): an inference engine with paged KV, continuous batching, a prefix cache and optional speculative decoding, graded on allocator invariants, exact logits, batch invariance under 12.3's `det_mode`, hit-rate equality with an oracle, and throughput and tail-latency targets on a fixed trace; its hooks come from 12.1 to 12.4 and its parts map to 13.2, 13.3, 13.4 and 13.5. Owners of shared names changed from the blueprints: `d2l.det_mode` is 12.3's; `d2l.ReplicaRouter` and `d2l.kv_transfer_time` are 13.6's; `d2l.ClusterSim`, `d2l.ServePool` and `d2l.handoff_kv` are 13.8's; `d2l.tp_ep_traffic`, `d2l.moe_routing_stats`, `d2l.expected_distinct_experts` and `d2l.MoEServeStepModel` are 13.7's; `d2l.swap_blocks`, `d2l.VirtualTokenCounter` are 13.5's; `d2l.TieredKV` is 13.6's. Cross-references to the hardware and parallelism chapters use their second-pass numbering (5.3 step-time model, 5.4 memory and storage tiers, 5.5 and 5.6 link costs, 5.6 rack domains, 5.8 cost per token, 6.3 tensor parallelism, 6.6 expert parallelism). Pitfalls common to the chapter: averages hide the tail (percentiles with intervals, always); closed-loop clients never overload a server (open loop, intended send times, no coordinated omission); engines differ in streaming granularity and `ignore_eos` handling, so output lengths must be forced equal before tokens per second are compared; prefix caching is on by default in vLLM V1 and must be off wherever prompts are meant not to repeat; the first requests pay graph capture and autotuning (warm-up discarded and counted).

### 13.1 Workloads and Service Objectives · T1
**Idea:** A serving system is judged by how many requests per second it serves within a latency contract, and a queueing model predicts where the latency curve turns up long before the GPU is busy.
**Opening:** The reader sends two requests to 12.1's decoder and the second one waits; with ten clients the wait dominates. The opening cell replays the same 200 requests against the same vLLM server three ways (one at a time, closed loop with 32 clients, open loop at the trace's arrival rate) and prints three different "performance numbers" for one server. The question is which number a service should promise, and the closing question is how to keep the knee away.
**Teaches:**
- What a request experiences: arrival, queue, prefill, first token, decode steps, last token; time to first token, time per output token, inter-token latency, end-to-end latency, throughput; client-observed against server-measured timestamps; service objectives as a pair of limits and goodput as the rate at which at least 90% of requests meet both (restated from `sec_model_serving`'s metrics in one paragraph).
- Workloads: arrival processes (Poisson, Gamma renewal with a coefficient of variation, trace-driven and rescaled traces that keep burstiness), prompt and output length distributions from real traces (conversation against code against agent), the prefill-to-decode token ratio as the number that decides which mechanism matters; open against closed loop and coordinated omission.
- A load generator: open-loop asynchronous replay with intended send times, streaming timestamps per token, the null server that bounds client overhead, and a cross-check against the engines' own benchmark tools.
- Little's law and the first queueing model: the mean wait of a single server, the batch server's formation wait and completion barrier, and a load-dependent birth-death model of iteration-level batching whose capacity grows with the batch until the ridge.
- Energy and cost per token: the GPU's power during the sweep, joules per output token falling with load until the knee, and the cost per million tokens restated from the hardware chapter with a link to `sec_cloud_instances`; one paragraph on exported graphs (a compiled step is what an engine replays; `torch.export`, ONNX and TensorRT-LLM as the export path), which pays comp-perf/further-reading.md:202.
**Derivation:** Little's law `L = λ W` (exact, assumption-free), then the Pollaczek-Khinchine mean wait `W_q = λ E[S²]/(2(1 − ρ))` from residual life, with the batch-server extension (service time the maximum of `B` exponential lengths, about `H_B E[S]`). Smallest case: `ρ = 0.8` with exponential service of mean one second gives a mean wait of four seconds, and deterministic service halves it.
**Notebook:**
1. The question: at what offered load does the 99th-percentile time to first token cross the objective, for static batching and for a reference server, and does the knee sit where the queueing model puts it? Qwen3-0.6B; the Azure 2023 conversation trace clipped to prompts of at most 2,048 and outputs of at most 128 tokens; `d2l.StaticBatchServer(batch_size=8)` over `FastGenerator` behind `d2l.serve_http`, and vLLM with prefix caching off and memory capped below 14 GiB.
2. Workload cells: the length histograms of the traces (`tab_lm_serve_traces`), counts per ten-second bin for Poisson against the Azure trace at the same mean rate with the index of dispersion, the closed-loop law `N = X(R + Z)` and a `queue_sim` demonstration of coordinated omission.
3. The queueing checks: simulated against predicted mean wait against `ρ` for exponential, deterministic and lognormal service; the birth-death model against a discrete-event simulation of iteration-level batching.
4. The sweep: saturation rate of each system from a closed-loop probe; open-loop loads at 0.2 to 1.3 times vLLM's saturation; 30 seconds of arrivals plus a drain; three seeds (three trace windows); objectives scaled from idle measurements (`slo_ttft = max(0.25 s, 5 × idle)`, `slo_tpot = 3 × idle`), also reported at half and double scale; `d2l.latency_report` per row; GPU power sampled every 100 ms during each load when `nvidia-smi` shows no other process on the GPU, else the energy column is taken from the committed artifact.
5. Claims that survive noise: both systems have a flat region and a knee near their predicted capacity (static `B/E[S_B]`; vLLM its measured maximum); static batching has the worse median time to first token at low load (formation wait) and saturates earlier by about `E[max_B n]/E[n]`; past the knee throughput stays high while goodput collapses; joules per output token fall with load until the knee and rise little after (measured); per-request paired differences between the two systems at equal seed and load are stated only when the interval excludes zero and exceeds the seed spread.
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.FastGenerator` (12.1); `d2l.book_corpus` (2.4) for prompt text; `d2l.paired_bootstrap` (1.5); `d2l.ServingModel` and the cost-per-token arithmetic (hardware chapter).
**Figures:** `fig_lm_serve_timeline` (one request's phases and a batch of overlapping requests, client against server clocks); (plot) 50th and 99th percentile time to first token against offered load for both systems with predicted knees, the achieved-throughput against tail-latency curve, and goodput against offered load; (plot) joules per output token against offered load.
**Restate / forward:** `sec_model_serving` (`tab_serving_workloads`, the metric definitions, the client contract; linked, not absorbed); `subsec_kv-cache-prefill-decode` (prefill sets time to first token, decode sets time per token); `eq_hw_decode_bound` (the idle time per token the objectives scale from); the hardware chapter's cost per million tokens and `sec_cloud_instances` (prices). Forward: 13.2.
**Exercises:** 6 to 8. Check: a release doubles throughput and doubles tail latency at the same load; two mechanisms consistent with both and the measurement that separates them. Check: 64 closed-loop clients, zero think time, 2,000 output tokens per second, 200-token outputs: the mean latency, again at 32 clients, and what an open-loop client at 12 requests per second sees. Derive: residual life `E[S²]/(2E[S])` by renewal reward and that deterministic service halves the exponential wait. Derive: the flat region of the load-dependent model and the load at which the batch limit is hit 1% of the time. Measure: Gamma arrivals at coefficients of variation 0.5 to 4 at the same mean, predicting the tail ordering from Kingman's approximation. Measure: stall the server for two seconds mid-run and compare open-loop against naive closed-loop tail latency. Open: for the code and conversation traces, search the engine's batch limit and token budget for the best goodput at a fixed objective and say whether the setting transfers.
**Writer notes:** Percentiles with intervals, never means. Time from the intended send time (coordinated omission). Set the engines' stream interval to one token and say so; force `ignore_eos` and a minimum length so output lengths equal the trace. Discard and count warm-up requests. Keep vLLM's prefix cache off in 13.1 and 13.2 (synthetic windows must not repeat). Pin the client and server to different cores and bound client overhead with the null server. The exported-graphs paragraph names the path and stops; usage is `sec_model_serving`. ### 13.2 Continuous Batching and Chunked Prefill · T1
**Idea:** Scheduling per iteration admits and retires requests between decode steps so that no slot waits for the longest output, and chunked prefill under a token budget lets prompts ride on memory-bound decode steps without stalling them.
**Opening:** The reader runs 13.1's static batch of eight on mixed-length requests and the opening cell prints the slot utilization (useful token-steps over `B` times steps), then adds one long prompt mid-run and prints the largest gap between consecutive tokens that the other seven requests saw. The question is how to fill slots as they free and how to take a long prompt without a stall, and the closing question is what the engine does between two GPU steps.
**Teaches:**
- Iteration-level scheduling: schedule per step rather than per request; run the non-attention operators on flattened tokens because only attention needs to know which token belongs to which sequence; the slot-utilization statement `U_static = mean n / E[max n]` (`1/H_B` for exponential lengths).
- The ragged forward: positions, not lengths, drive the rotary embedding; `seq_ids` and positions index the cache writes; attention over a padded gather with the mask `key_idx ≤ q_pos`; two attention calls per layer (decode rows at `q_len = 1`, prefill chunks padded to the longest); exactness of a chunk against full causal attention.
- The scheduler's step in four moves (decodes first, continue running prefills, admit while budget and cache room remain, otherwise defer), with the invariants asserted every step; the three policies (static, prefill-first, chunked) as a handful of lines in one loop.
- The token budget: the free chunk `c_free ≈ P/β − n_dec` of prefill tokens that a memory-bound decode step absorbs at no cost; the stall rate of unchunked prefill; the budget that holds inter-token latency under a limit.
- Between two steps: sampling, detokenization, structured-output masks (the grammar automaton of 10.2 restated in one sentence: a mask per step from the grammar state), scheduling itself; why this CPU work sits on the critical path of a small model and how engines overlap it with the GPU step (asynchronous scheduling, a masks-ahead computation); the engine's deterministic mode as 12.3's `det_mode` applied to the ragged step.
**Derivation:** The free chunk and the stall rate. A decode step with `n_dec` rows is memory-bound with time `(W + n_dec L k_KV)/β`; adding `c` prefill tokens adds compute `2N(n_dec + c)/P`, so the step stays flat while `c ≤ P/β − n_dec` (about 150 tokens on an RTX 4090 with `n_dec = 16`); unchunked, a prompt of `n` tokens stalls every running row for `t_p(n)`, and at arrival rate `λ` the fraction of time in stalls is `λ t_p`, which exceeds 1% at `λ = 0.01/t_p`. Smallest case: rows of 10, 20, 40 and 80 output tokens under static batching leave 53% of slot-steps idle.
**Notebook:**
1. The question: on one trace, what do continuous batching and chunked prefill do to throughput, tail time to first token and tail inter-token latency, and does a fitted step model predict it? Qwen3-0.6B, `d2l.RaggedLM` over 12.1's slots, the clipped Azure conversation trace, `max_num_seqs = 32`, a slot store of 32 slots of 2,560 tokens.
2. Exactness: `RaggedLM` logits against the full-sequence forward at every position for chunk sizes 1, 7, 64 and 512 and for a mixed step of two decode rows and one chunk (float32, TF32 off, `atol = rtol = 1e-4`); in BF16 the maximum logit difference and top-1 agreement are reported without a threshold, which sets up the deterministic-mode cell.
3. The step-time sweep: `n_dec` in {1, 8, 32} by chunk size 0 to 1,024; the knee against `c_free`; `d2l.ServeStepModel` fitted by non-negative least squares on about 280 measured steps with 20% held out and the median and 90th-percentile relative error reported.
4. The golden-schedule test: the same 60-request trace through the live executor with a virtual clock and through `d2l.SimExecutor`; batch compositions per step must be identical.
5. The sweep: static (`B = 8`), prefill-first (budget 2,048), chunked at budgets 64, 256 and 1,024; twelve loads from 0.2 to 1.4 times each policy's saturation in the simulator (five seeds), three live loads per policy (three seeds), vLLM at matching `--max-num-batched-tokens` from the committed artifact or live; one profiled steady-state window with the GPU-busy fraction and the five largest kernels.
6. The deterministic cell: under `d2l.det_mode` (12.3) the engine's logits at every generated position are bitwise equal to its own batch-1 run across policies, chunk sizes and co-batched requests, or the first differing operation is named; tokens per second in both modes.
7. Claims that survive noise: above the stall rate, prefill-first has a higher tail inter-token latency than chunked at a budget near `c_free`, by about the stall time of a typical prompt; chunked's tail time to first token is within the seed spread of prefill-first except for the longest prompts; step time is flat in the budget up to about `c_free` and grows beyond it; static saturates earlier by about `E[max]/E[mean]`; the from-scratch engine trails vLLM and the profile attributes the gap mostly to GPU idle time between kernels, not kernel time; the simulator's live-against-simulated error is stated per load, and any live point outside the seed band widened by 15% is flagged.
8. Reused pieces: `d2l.ServeRequest`, `d2l.replay`, `d2l.latency_report`, `d2l.goodput`, `d2l.StaticBatchServer`, `d2l.load_trace` (13.1); `d2l.FastGenerator` slots and `KVCache` (12.1); `d2l.det_mode` (12.3); `d2l.chip_specs` and `d2l.ServingModel` (hardware chapter) as the fit's starting point; `d2l.paired_bootstrap` (1.5).
**Figures:** `fig_lm_cb_timeline` (a slot-against-time diagram for static, prefill-first and chunked on the same eight requests, drawn from a scheduler log); (plot) step time against chunk size with the fitted model and the predicted knee; (plot) tail time to first token, tail inter-token latency, tokens per second and goodput against offered load for the policies and vLLM, simulator bands with live markers.
**Restate / forward:** `sec_model_serving` (`fig_tools_continuous_batching`, the toy scheduler; linked, superseded); `subsec_kv-cache-cached-forward` (the cached step and its mask; this section removes its one-token restriction with an explicit offset mask); `eq_online-softmax` (a chunk's attention over the cached prefix equals the rows of full causal attention); `eq_hw_decode_bound` and `tab_gpu_specs` (the ridge that sets the budget); 10.2's grammar mask in one sentence. Forward: 13.3.
**Exercises:** 6 to 8. Check: with a budget of 512 and 40 decoding requests, the steps a 1,500-token prompt needs and the lower bound on its time to first token, then at a budget of 64. Check: why `is_causal=True` is wrong for a chunk appended to a cache and the correct bottom-right-aligned mask. Derive: `c_free` with the cache-read and attention terms for Qwen3-0.6B at `n_dec = 16` and `L = 1,024`, and when the cache term dominates. Derive: that with `max_num_seqs ≤ budget − 1` every prompt finishes its prefill within `⌈n/(budget − max_num_seqs)⌉` steps and no decode starves. Measure: the budget sweep at 0.9 of saturation, predicting the inter-token knee from the fitted `c_free`. Measure: graphs on pure-decode steps through 12.1's `decode_step` after `warmup`, predicting from the profile how much of the gap to vLLM they close and which cause remains. Open: a structured-output arm with 10.2's grammar masks computed on the critical path against masks computed one step ahead on a second thread, with tail inter-token latency at three loads.
**Writer notes:** Padding rows of a graph bucket are slots beyond `n_active` with `pos = 0`; a hand-built step that points padding at slot 0 corrupts a live request (a bug that appears only when the batch is not full). The rotary position of a chunk's first token is `n_computed`, not 0; the chunk-size sweep catches it. Enforce `max_num_seqs < token_budget` or prefill starves. Tie sampling randomness to `(request, position)` with a per-request generator so that preemption and recompute (13.5) change timing but not outputs. "Continuous batching" is not "bigger batches"; its benefit is utilization under variable output lengths, a workload property. Never quote a chunked-prefill speedup without the two tail latencies it came with. The reference `RaggedLM` reads the cache through `view` plus a row copy per layer, so its fitted `β_eff` includes that copy; the fitted efficiency says nothing about vLLM's kernels. `RaggedLM` does not call `forward` for mixed steps (two calls would read the weights twice; one padded call would pad decode rows to the chunk); the two-call variant stays as a comparison arm in the step-time sweep. The ragged step is not graph-captured; graphs are available for pure-decode steps through 12.1 and that is an exercise. The deterministic mode is 12.3's; this section applies it and reports the cost on the ragged step, and A10 check 4 inherits 12.3's fallback (name the first diverging operation, grade token-id equality). The between-steps paragraph names the CPU work and the overlap, cites vLLM V1's asynchronous scheduling and XGrammar's mask overlap, and stops; the grammar automaton itself is 10.2's. Do not re-teach: the cached step, the cache formula, GQA, CUDA graphs, the grammar. Library additions: `d2l.StepBatch`, `d2l.KVManager` (protocol), `d2l.SlotKV`, `d2l.RaggedLM`, `d2l.ContinuousScheduler` (with `add(req, prefilled=False)` as the hook 13.8's simulator uses), `d2l.ServeStepModel`, `d2l.SimExecutor`; artifacts `lm-serving-step-model-r1`, the 13.2 rows of `lm-serving-curves-t1`, the profiler summary, the golden-schedule log. Blueprint ch13 13.2 has derivations D1 (free chunk) and D2 (stall rate), the scheduler's four moves with invariants, the fitted model's formula (`eq_lm_cb_step_time`) and the exercise sketches; its 13.2.6 (admission) and 13.2.7 (batch invariance) are covered by 13.5 and 12.3.

### 13.3 Paged KV Memory · T1
**Idea:** Fixed-size blocks located through a per-sequence table waste at most one block per sequence and never fragment, so the number of concurrent requests is bounded by the tokens they hold rather than the tokens they might hold.
**Opening:** The reader runs 13.2's engine with a fixed 8 GiB pool at a load above the slot store's saturation. The opening cell prints the number of slots (29 at 2,560 tokens each), the mean live length, the fraction of reserved cache that holds tokens, and the throughput: most of the reserved cache is empty and the batch is capped by slots. The question is how to reserve only what a sequence has, and the closing question is what two sequences that start the same way should share.
**Teaches:**
- Three kinds of waste in contiguous allocation (internal, external, duplication) shown by an allocator simulation with a reservation policy, an oracle that knows final lengths, and paging; even perfect length knowledge fragments.
- Blocks and block tables: logical blocks of a sequence map to physical blocks through a table (`physical = table[pos // B]`, `offset = pos % B`); one pool tensor per layer; allocation on demand as tokens arrive; the allocator's state is a free list and a reference count.
- The allocator's invariants (a block is free or referenced, never both; references equal table entries; table lengths equal `⌈ℓ/B⌉`; a shared block is never written; freeing everything returns every block) and a randomized operation generator that checks them.
- The paged read: the block-table variant of 12.2's decode kernel against a gather-then-attention reference; the cost of the indirection; vAttention's alternative (virtual memory keeps the cache contiguous so an ordinary kernel works) as the one-difference relative.
- Block size as a design variable (waste grows with `B`, bookkeeping and gather overhead shrink, prefix-cache granularity coarsens); copy-on-write forks for parallel sampling and beam search; recurrent state of hybrid models (constant size per snapshot, so a prefix is cacheable only at saved boundaries) in one paragraph with a config-based table.
**Derivation:** Expected waste and the concurrency gain. With residues of `ℓ mod B` uniform, the waste per sequence has mean `(B − 1)/2` and variance `(B² − 1)/12`; reserving `L_max` instead wastes `L_max − ℓ`, so a fixed pool holds `G(B) = L_max/(ℓ̄ + (B − 1)/2)` times more sequences; block-table overhead is 4 bytes per block. After a fork of `n` samples from a prompt of `P = qB + r` tokens generating `T` each, copy-on-write uses `⌊P/B⌋ + n⌈(T + r)/B⌉` blocks and `n − 1` partial copies. Smallest case: 64 requests, maximum 4,096, mean 500, block 16: `G = 8.1`; a 70-token prompt, three samples of 20 tokens, `B = 16`: 10 blocks with copy-on-write against 18 without.
**Notebook:**
1. The question: how much concurrency does paging buy for the same pool, and what does the block size cost? Qwen3-0.6B, `RaggedLM` with 13.2's chunked scheduler (budget 256, `max_num_seqs = 128`), an 8 GiB pool for both stores.
2. Property tests first: the allocator's invariants under 20,000 random operations (allocate, append, fork, free, evict) at two seeds; a failing invariant stops the notebook.
3. Exactness: `d2l.paged_attention_ref` against contiguous attention (float32, `atol = 1e-5`) at `B` in {1, 4, 16}; the 12.2 paged kernel against the reference; end-to-end logits of `RaggedLM` on `PagedKV` against the full forward (`atol = rtol = 1e-4`); `FastGenerator.generate(..., sampling=None)` with a `PagedKV` installed against the slot store (float32, equal token ids).
4. The sweep: `SlotKV` at 2,560 tokens per slot against `PagedKV` at `B = 16` on the clipped Azure trace at six loads (three live seeds, five simulated); concurrency over time, useful fraction, throughput, goodput, tail latencies; vLLM from the committed artifact.
5. The block-size sweep `B` in {1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128}: measured waste per sequence against `(B − 1)/2`, gather time per layer for a 32-sequence batch, and the prefix hit rate on the Mooncake excerpt (a preview of 13.4; hits only on full blocks).
6. The fork cell: `n` in {1, 2, 4, 8} samples from one prompt with copy-on-write; blocks used against the formula and against no sharing.

### 13.4 Prefix Caching and Shared-Prefix Workloads · T1
**Idea:** Requests that begin with the same tokens at the same positions can share the blocks that store that prefix, so a prefix is computed once and the gain from caching is a property of the workload.
**Opening:** The reader runs 13.3's engine on a trace in which every request starts with the same 512-token system prompt and the opening cell counts prefill tokens recomputed: every request pays for the prompt again. The question is which requests may share a prefix and how to find it quickly, and the closing question is what happens when the shared blocks do not fit on the GPU.
**Teaches:**
- When two requests may share cache: same weights, same adapter, same tokens at the same absolute positions (keys depend on position through the rotary embedding, which a prefix satisfies by construction), same execution configuration (dtype, cache dtype, attention scheme); non-prefix reuse is not exact and is named as a pointer.
- The radix tree over page-aligned token runs: match walks from the root, insert splits nodes at page boundaries, running sequences lock their path, eviction removes unlocked leaves in least-recently-used order so a node outlives its descendants; block ownership (one reference from the tree, one per running sequence); the rules tests encode (a full-prompt hit is capped at `len − 1` because the last token's logits are needed; only full pages are cached; insertion after the step that computed the tokens, so two identical prompts admitted together do not share).
- Hash-chained blocks (vLLM) and token-level radix trees (SGLang) as the same trie at different granularity, with extra keys (adapter name, a cache salt) in the hash; cache-aware admission (order the waiting queue by matched prefix length with an aging term) against first come first served.
- The workloads that share most: multi-turn chat (the prefix grows by one turn), agents (every tool call re-sends the whole context, so hits approach the whole prompt and the cache must survive the tool's latency), parallel samples (`n` outputs per prompt, the groups of 8.5 and the best-of-`n` of Chapter 9, forked with copy-on-write), and the shared-prefix attention kernel that reads the prefix's cache once for all `n` rows.
- Predicting the hit rate: the exact oracle at unbounded capacity, Che's approximation for least-recently-used eviction, and the first-order model of the time to first token saved.
**Derivation:** Che's approximation. For items with request rates `λ_i` under least-recently-used eviction with capacity `C`, the hit probability of item `i` is about `1 − e^{−λ_i T_C}`, where `T_C` solves `Σ_i (1 − e^{−λ_i T_C}) = C`; the expected prefill saved per request is the hit length, and the time to first token falls by about `t_p(n) − t_p(n − hit)`. Smallest case: two prompts that share 512 of 1,024 tokens, where the second computes 512 tokens (plus the last one) instead of 1,024.
**Notebook:**

2. Workloads: the 16-times-downscaled Mooncake conversation excerpt (32-token pages, one block id per page; the compute ratios differ from the original and the reuse structure is preserved, stated), the Mooncake tool-and-agent excerpt, and a synthetic set with `K` in {1, 8, 64} system prompts of 512 tokens under Zipf popularity with unique suffixes from the clipped Azure prompt distribution.
3. Arms: cache off; cache on with first-come-first-served admission; cache on with longest-prefix-match admission; capacity from 10% to 100% of the pool in the simulator, three live capacity points.
4. The fork cell: `n` in {2, 4, 8} samples per prompt with copy-on-write, blocks and prefill against no sharing; and the shared-prefix attention cell: 12.2's kernel reading the prefix blocks once for `n` rows against `n` independent reads, step time at `n` in {1, 8, 32}.

Claims that survive noise: measured hit tokens equal `d2l.oracle_hit_rate` exactly at unbounded capacity (no noise); the agent trace's hit rate is far above the conversation trace's (measured; direction from the trace structure); time to first token falls by about the first-order model where hits occur; longest-prefix-match admission raises the hit rate over first-come-first-served at a measured cost in maximum wait; Che's approximation tracks the simulated hit rate against capacity for the Zipf set; the shared-prefix read scales as one prefix plus `n` suffixes, not `n` prefixes (measured against the ledger).

### 13.5 Scheduling under Overload · T1
**Idea:** When demand exceeds capacity the scheduler decides whom to serve, whom to pause and whom to refuse, and the policy, not the hardware, sets goodput and fairness.
**Opening:** The reader offers 13.2's engine 1.3 times its saturation rate and the opening cell prints a queue that grows without bound, a tail time to first token that grows with the length of the run, and a goodput of zero, while throughput is at its maximum. The question is what a server should do with work it cannot finish in time, and the closing question is where a paused request's cache should go.
**Teaches:**
- Admission control: a request that has already waited longer than its objective cannot be good, so shedding it at the head of the queue frees capacity for requests that can be; goodput against offered load with and without shedding; backpressure to the client.
- Preemption: when a running request cannot get a block, pause one; recompute (free its blocks, requeue it with its generated tokens appended) against swap (move its blocks to host memory and back); which request to pause (most recent, lowest priority, largest cache).
- Priorities and deadlines: two classes (interactive with a tight objective, batch with none), earliest deadline first with preemption of batch requests; what starvation looks like and how aging bounds it.
- Fairness across tenants: a weighted fair queue over tokens (a virtual token counter per client, serve the client with the smallest counter, charge prompt and output tokens at different rates); why a heavy tenant otherwise takes the capacity under first come first served; isolation against efficiency.
- Overload across replicas in one paragraph: migrating a running request's cache to a less loaded replica (Llumnix) as the cluster-level form of preemption, with the transfer cost of 13.6.
**Derivation:** Recompute against swap. Pausing a request with `n` cached tokens and resuming it costs `2n k_KV/β_link` by swap (out and back over the host link) and `n · 2N/P_eff` by recompute, so swap wins only if `β_link > k_KV P_eff/N`. Smallest case: Qwen3-0.6B (`k_KV` 112 KiB per token, `N` about 0.44 billion body parameters, `P_eff` 80 TFLOP/s) gives a break-even near 21 GB/s, about what a PCIe host link delivers, so recompute and swap tie for a small model; Qwen3-30B-A3B's break-even is near 6 GB/s, so swap wins. Second, short: under first come first served two tenants offering 10 and 1 requests per second to a capacity of 6 get shares in proportion to demand; the fair queue gives each tenant up to half and the remainder to whoever has demand.
**Notebook:**
1. The question: under overload, which admission, preemption and fairness policy keeps goodput and gives each tenant its share? Qwen3-0.6B on `PagedKV` (13.3) with 13.2's chunked scheduler; the clipped Azure conversation trace split into two tenants, one bursty (the code trace's arrival pattern) and one steady; loads from 0.8 to 1.6 times saturation; five simulator seeds, three live loads.
2. Policies: first come first served; shedding at the objective; earliest deadline first with two classes and preemption of the batch class; the virtual token counter across the two tenants; each with recompute or swap as the preemption mechanism.
3. The swap cell: `d2l.swap_blocks` moves a request's blocks to pinned host memory and back; measured round-trip time against prefix length 64 to 4,096 and against recompute, with the break-even from the derivation using the fitted `P_eff` of 13.2 and the hardware chapter's measured host bandwidth.
4. Metrics: goodput, shed fraction, preemption count, per-tenant share of served tokens, per-class tail time to first token, maximum wait.
5. Claims that survive noise: without shedding goodput falls to zero past the knee while throughput stays high, and with shedding it stays near capacity (measured, direction from 13.1); earliest deadline first keeps the interactive class within its objective at the batch class's expense, and aging bounds the batch class's maximum wait (measured); the fair queue holds the steady tenant's share near its weight while first come first served gives the bursty tenant most of the capacity (measured, direction from the derivation); for Qwen3-0.6B recompute and swap tie within the measurement spread, and the derivation says why.
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.ContinuousScheduler` (13.2, which gains `policy` values `'edf'` and `'vtc'` and a `preempt` argument `'recompute'` or `'swap'`), `d2l.PagedKV` (13.3), `d2l.SimExecutor` and `d2l.ServeStepModel` (13.2), `d2l.goodput` and `d2l.latency_report` (13.1), the hardware chapter's host-link measurement.
**Figures:** `fig_lm_overload_queue` (a queue under three policies: who is served, paused, refused, with the tenant and class marked); (plot) goodput against offered load for the admission policies; (plot) per-tenant share and per-class tail time to first token against offered load.
**Restate / forward:** 13.1's queueing model (the wait grows as `1/(1 − ρ)`); `subsec_hw-cpu` and the hardware chapter's tiers (host memory bandwidth and the pinned path); 13.3's blocks (what a swap moves). Forward: 13.6.

### 13.6 KV-Cache Offload, Stores and Prefix-Aware Routing · T1
**Idea:** A cache that outlives one GPU's memory becomes a store across tiers and replicas, and once it does, where a request is routed decides whether its prefix is near.
**Opening:** The reader has 13.4's prefix cache, whose hit rate falls as the GPU pool fills, and 13.5's swap, which moves blocks to host memory and back. The opening cell prints, for the Mooncake agent excerpt, the hit rate with a 2 GiB GPU pool, with 8 GiB, and with a 2 GiB pool backed by 8 GiB of host memory, next to the measured time to reload a 1,024-token prefix from host memory and the time to recompute it. The question is when reloading beats recomputing and how far a cache can be from the GPU, and the closing question is what happens when there are four replicas and a prefix is on only one of them.
**Teaches:**
- The tiers a cache can live in (GPU, pinned host memory, local NVMe, a remote store over the network) with their bandwidths and latencies restated from the hardware chapter; reload against recompute as the only question that matters; layer-wise pipelining that hides a transfer behind a prefill.
- A two-tier prefix cache: GPU blocks plus host blocks under one radix tree, with promotion on hit and demotion on eviction; the hit rate of two tiers from Che's approximation applied to the combined capacity; the expected time to first token as a mixture of GPU hits, host hits and misses.
- Compressing the cache for transfer (CacheGen: delta coding of keys and values with a quality-aware bit rate) and reusing non-prefix chunks with partial recompute (CacheBlend) as the two one-difference relatives.
- Replicas: with `R` independent caches and random routing each replica sees a thinned stream, so the hit rate equals one cache at rate `λ/R`; prefix-aware routing (hash the first page, or query a global index of cached blocks) restores the single-cache hit rate at the price of load imbalance; the trade-off, and the router that mixes locality and load (the SGLang router's cache-aware policy, Dynamo's KV-aware router, Preble).
- A global store (Mooncake Store, LMCache) that decouples placement from routing: any replica can fetch a prefix over the network, so the router balances load and the store serves locality, at the transfer cost of the first paragraph.
**Derivation:** Reload against recompute, and the two-tier hit rate. Reloading `n` tokens costs `α + n k_KV/β_link`, recomputing costs `n · 2N/P_eff`, so to first order reloading wins above `β* = k_KV P_eff/(2N)`, independent of `n`; for Qwen3-0.6B `β*` is about 10 GB/s (a PCIe host link wins, a 10 Gb/s network loses), for Qwen3-30B-A3B about 3 GB/s. The two-tier hit rate is `H(C_gpu)` on the GPU and `H(C_gpu + C_host) − H(C_gpu)` on the host, with `H` from Che's approximation (13.4), and the expected time to first token is the mixture. Smallest case: a Zipf(1) set of 64 prompts, 8 GPU and 32 host slots. Thinning: with `R` replicas and random routing, each replica's hit rate is `H` evaluated at rates `λ_i/R`, which is lower for every capacity.
**Notebook:**
1. The question: how much hit rate does a host tier add at fixed GPU bytes, and does a router that knows the prefixes recover what splitting the cache across replicas loses? 3. The sweep: GPU capacity from 0.5 to 8 GiB with and without an 8 GiB host tier; hit rate by tier, prefill tokens saved, tail time to first token at three loads; the two-tier prediction overlaid.
4. The replica cell (T0, on the committed hash lists): `R` in {1, 2, 4, 8} replicas of equal total capacity with round-robin, least-loaded, prefix-hash and cache-aware routing in `d2l.ReplicaSim` (each replica a `RadixCache` with a load counter driven by 13.2's step model); hit rate against load imbalance per policy; a pooled store as the fifth arm.

Claims that survive noise: a host tier raises the hit rate at fixed GPU bytes by about the two-tier prediction and lowers the tail time to first token where host hits replace misses (measured); reload beats recompute above the derived link bandwidth and the measured crossing in `n` reflects the link's latency (measured); splitting the cache across `R` replicas under random routing lowers the hit rate as the thinning predicts, prefix-aware routing recovers most of it at a measured imbalance, and the pooled store recovers it without the imbalance at the transfer cost (simulated on the committed lists; the live two-replica check agrees in direction).

### 13.7 Tensor and Expert Parallelism for Serving · T3 (T2 pair; T1 on committed logs)
**Idea:** For decode, tensor parallelism trades bytes per GPU for a collective's latency on every layer, and expert parallelism keeps each request's cache local while pooling the batch that the experts see, so the two layouts win in different regimes of batch and load.
**Opening:** The reader has a 30-billion-parameter mixture model whose 61 GB of weights do not fit one 40 GB GPU. The opening cell prints, from the configuration and the datasheet alone, what one 8-GPU node holds under five layouts (replicas, tensor-parallel groups of 2, 4 and 8, and data-parallel attention with the experts spread over 8): weights per GPU, cache bytes per token per GPU, total cache tokens; the first layout does not fit, the others differ by about five times in cache capacity, and the 8-way tensor split stores every KV head twice. The question is which layout serves a workload best and how to know without trying all of them, and the closing question is whether prefill and decode should share a layout at all.
**Teaches:**
- Why serving differs from training: no backward pass, no optimizer state, tiny messages (a decode step moves `b × d` activations), and an objective that is a latency percentile, so the collective's latency `α` matters as much as its bandwidth; 96 all-reduces or all-to-alls per decode step of a 48-layer model.
- Tensor parallelism for decode: two all-reduces per layer, bytes per rank and in aggregate, the KV head replication when the degree exceeds the KV heads, the inefficient expert tile when an expert's width is split eight ways, and why the degree stays inside the fast link domain.
- Expert parallelism with data-parallel attention: each rank owns requests, their cache and replicated attention weights and shares the experts; dispatch and combine as all-to-alls with destination deduplication; the pooled batch the experts see; dummy steps on idle ranks.
- The decode paradox of mixtures: at moderate batch nearly every expert is touched, so weight traffic approaches the whole model; tokens per expert against the ridge (about `ridge × E/k` tokens per step), which is why wide expert parallelism exists; load imbalance (the straggler factor) and hot-expert replication (EPLB); recorded routing on real text as the only honest input.
- Capacity per layout (weights, replicated KV heads, cache tokens) and the fitted mixture step model that predicts step time from the layout and the link table; production forms (wide EP across nodes, DeepEP kernels) as the case studies the formulas extend to.
**Derivation:** Traffic and distinct experts. Under tensor parallelism of degree `t`, each rank sends `8 d (t − 1)/t` bytes per token per layer (two ring all-reduces of `n d` elements); under expert parallelism of degree `e` with `E` experts and top-`k`, the expected number of remote destinations is `(e − 1)(1 − C(E − E/e, k)/C(E, k))`, so a token sends `2(e − 1)p × 2d` bytes per layer; a step of `n` tokens touches `E(1 − (1 − k/E)^n)` experts; the busiest of `e` ranks carries about `1 + z_e √((e − 1)/(nk))` times the mean load. Smallest case: `d = 2048`, `t = 8` gives 14,336 bytes per rank and 114,688 in aggregate; `E = 128`, `k = 8`, `e = 8` gives 4.67 remote destinations and about 38 KB per token per layer, three times less than the tensor split; `n = 16` touches 82 of 128 experts; on an A100 the experts reach the ridge at about 3,210 tokens per step.
**Notebook:**

3. Layouts swept: four replicas of 2-way tensor parallelism, one 8-way tensor group, and 8-way data-parallel attention with expert parallelism; the 4-way tensor pair started once for its capacity line and idle probes; the one-replica layout printed as infeasible. Workload: the Azure conversation trace with outputs clipped to 256; a closed-loop probe for saturation, then open-loop loads at 0.3 to 1.3 of it, 60 seconds plus drain, one repeated middle load; objectives scaled from idle probes.
4. Routing statistics recorded once with Transformers across the node (`lm-moe-routing-qwen3-30b-a3b`: top-8 expert ids per token and layer on 4,096 book-corpus and 4,096 FineWeb-Edu tokens): distinct experts per step, the straggler factor with and without replicating the hottest experts.
5. Analysis on the committed logs (T0): curves per layout, goodput per GPU at three objective scales, capacity reported by each engine against the prediction, the prediction scoring, and the mixture step model calibrated on the colocated rows.

T2 pair (two A100 with an NVLink bridge): Qwen3-1.7B as two replicas against one 2-way tensor group, four loads, the tensor penalty predicted from the bridge's all-reduce row; routing statistics of OLMoE-1B-7B recorded on one GPU for the straggler check at `E = 64`. T1: the analysis cells on the committed logs and the same OLMoE routing cell.

### 13.8 Prefill and Decode Disaggregation · T3 (T2 pair; T1 on committed logs)
**Idea:** Prefill and decode want different batch sizes, parallelism and even hardware, so giving each its own pool of GPUs removes their interference and decouples their layouts, at the price of moving the cache from one pool to the other.
**Opening:** The reader has 13.2's chunked prefill, which bounds the stall that a long prompt causes but still spends decode steps on prompt tokens, and 13.7's layouts, which were chosen for decode. The opening cell prints, for the Azure code trace (long prompts, short outputs), the fraction of each colocated step's time spent on prefill chunks and the tail time per token at a tight objective, then the same with prefill on two GPUs and decode on six. The question is what disaggregation buys and costs, and the closing question is which pool a cached prefix belongs to.
**Teaches:**
- The two arguments: interference (every prompt chunk lengthens every decode step; 13.2's stall rate in another form) and resource coupling (prefill wants compute and a high tensor degree, decode wants cache capacity and a large batch; one layout serves neither well); DistServe's pools with independent objectives, Splitwise's machines and the fast backplane, Mooncake's cache-centric scheduler.
- The costs: moving the cache (`α + n k_KV/β_link`), hidden by layer-wise pipelining when the link is fast against the per-token prefill compute; pool imbalance and integer granularity on 8 GPUs; weights stored twice, which shrinks the decode pool's cache; lost prefix locality unless the router restores it (13.6).
- The transfer path: GPU to GPU over NVLink or RDMA with a transfer library (NIXL, Mooncake's Transfer Engine) against host-staged copies; the connector in an engine; what a request's hand-off looks like in the scheduler (`add(req, prefilled=True)`).
- A fluid model of capacity: colocated steady state with `b` decode rows and `b n_in/m` prefill tokens per step against a prefill pool at the utilization its objective allows and a decode pool limited by cache or by the time-per-token objective; the two limits (compute-bound at the objective, where disaggregation cannot beat colocation; a tight time-per-token objective, where it does).
- The ratio of prefill to decode GPUs from a trace (prompt and output lengths set it), and what changes for reasoning workloads with long outputs (the decode pool grows) and agent workloads with repeated prefixes (the prefill pool shrinks when the cache hits).
**Derivation:** Exposed transfer and the fluid model. With `L` layers, pipelining layer `l`'s transfer behind layer `l + 1`'s prefill gives an exposed time of `τ_x + max(0, T_x − T_pre)` with `τ_x = T_x/L`; the transfer is hidden (apart from `τ_x`) when `β_link ≥ k_KV P_eff/(2N)` (13.6's bound restated, now per request). Colocated capacity is `λ_col = b*/(m t_s(b*, b* n_in/m))` at the largest feasible `b*`; disaggregated capacity is `min(n_p ρ_max/τ_p, n_d b_d/(m t_dec(b_d)))` over integer splits `n_p + n_d = 8`, with goodput per GPU `λ/8`. Smallest case: a 4,096-token prompt of Qwen3-30B-A3B is 403 MB of cache and prefills in about 0.14 s at half the A100's peak; NVLink moves it in under a millisecond, a 100 Gb/s network in 32 ms (hidden), a 10 Gb/s network in 0.32 s (exposed by about 0.18 s).
**Notebook:**
1. The question: where is the crossover between colocated and disaggregated serving in prompt-to-output ratio and objective tightness, and does the fluid model predict it? T3: the node of 13.7, vLLM with NIXL transfer over the node's links; colocated four replicas of 2-way tensor parallelism against 1 prefill and 3 decode, 2 and 2, 3 and 1 (all 2-way groups); workloads Azure conversation and Azure code; loads at 0.5 to 1.3 of saturation, 60 seconds plus drain; objectives from idle probes; goodput recomputed offline at three objective scales.

### 13.9 Serving Many Adapters · T1
**Idea:** Fine-tuned variants that share a base model can share one batch, because only a low-rank term depends on the request, and the cost of serving many adapters is bytes per distinct adapter, not arithmetic.
**Opening:** The reader has eight adapters from Chapter 7 on one base model and the opening cell prints the memory of eight full copies of Qwen3-0.6B, the memory of one base plus eight adapters, and the decode throughput of an engine that serves one adapter at a time by merging and unmerging as requests interleave: the adapters fit with room to spare, and the serial engine's throughput falls with the number of adapters in flight. The question is how many adapters one batch can carry and what it costs, and the closing question is whether a prefix computed under one adapter is worth anything to another.
**Teaches:**
- Why adapters share a batch: `y = x Wᵀ + s (x A_aᵀ) B_aᵀ`, with the base term identical for every token and the low-rank term per request; merged serving (free per token, one adapter per replica) against unmerged serving (an extra `r(d_in + d_out)` weights per distinct adapter in the step); which regime a traffic mix wants.
- Three ways to compute the batched term: grouped by adapter (two small matrix products per adapter segment; reads each adapter once), gathered per token (one launch, reads an adapter per token), and dense-masked (all resident adapters, two dense products); the production kernels (SGMV, BGMV, the engine's own) as fused forms of the first two.
- Adapters in the engine: an adapter id per token in the step batch, a pool of resident adapters as a cache with least-recently-used eviction and pinning for running requests, admission that waits for a slot, prefetch; Che's approximation (13.4) for the pool's hit rate; load stalls of 20 MB adapters against 350 MB ones.
- Cache correctness: any adapter changes every later layer's keys and values, so the prefix cache key includes the adapter (13.4's `key_prefix`), and a cache without it returns wrong activations, not stale ones; unified paging of adapter weights and cache blocks in one pool.
- Routing between models and cascades in one paragraph (a cheap model answers and escalates on a confidence signal; a router picks the model before generating), with the oracle bound and the random-mixing line stated and the evaluation left to an exercise.
**Derivation:** Bytes of heterogeneous batching. For one projection with `T` tokens, `A_dist` distinct adapters of rank `r` and `N` resident adapters, grouped batching reads `2 A_dist r (d_in + d_out)` bytes against the base's `2 d_in d_out`, per-token gathering reads `2 T r (d_in + d_out)`, dense masking `2 N r (d_in + d_out)`; over Qwen3-0.6B's seven projections at `r = 16` the grouped overhead is `0.0229 A_dist` of the base bytes, so grouped batching doubles decode bytes at about 44 distinct adapters, while serial merging costs about `A_dist` weight passes and loses for every `A_dist ≥ 2`. Smallest case: `T = 32`, `A_dist = 4`, `N = 16` ranked by bytes and launches.
**Notebook:**
1. The question: how does decode step time grow with the number of distinct adapters in a batch, and does the batched engine hold its goodput where the serial one loses it? Qwen3-0.6B through `RaggedLM` with `d2l.attach_adapters`; rank-16 adapters on all seven projections (random for timing, the trained rank-8 adapter `lm-lora-r1-demo` of 7.4 zero-padded to 16 for correctness); a pool of 16 slots over 64 adapters in host memory.
2. Correctness: each mode equals the merged-weight output for each adapter's tokens (float32, `atol = rtol = 1e-5`), equals PEFT for one adapter, and equals the base for tokens with adapter id `−1`; a prefix cached under adapter `a` hits for `a`, misses for `b`, and a cache without the key returns wrong tokens (shown once).
3. The microbenchmark: step time at `T = 32` for `A_dist` in {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32} under grouped, gathered, dense-masked, base-only and serial merge; the fitted slope against the ideal 0.0229 per adapter.
4. The curves: the 13.2 scheduler with adapters assigned by Zipf popularity over 64 adapters on the clipped Azure trace, six loads, three engines (base-only, batched, serial merge); the pool's hit rate against slots with Che's curve; simulator sweeps with the fitted overhead and three live loads.
5. Claims that survive noise: grouped step time grows about linearly in `A_dist` with a slope near the ideal bytes times a measured inefficiency; gathering costs a constant proportional to `T` even at one adapter; dense masking costs a constant in the resident count; serial merging scales as `A_dist` (measured); under Zipf popularity the batched engine's goodput stays near the base-only engine's across the load range while the serial engine's saturation falls with the number of distinct adapters (measured); the pool's hit rate follows Che's approximation within a few points and load stalls are negligible for 20 MB adapters (measured; 350 MB adapters at rank 64 on an 8B base are arithmetic in a table).
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.LoRALinear`, `d2l.add_lora` (7.4); `d2l.RaggedLM`, `d2l.StepBatch.adapter_ids`, `d2l.ContinuousScheduler`, `d2l.ServeStepModel`, `d2l.SimExecutor` (13.2); `d2l.RadixCache(key_prefix=...)`, `d2l.che_hit_rate` (13.4); `d2l.replay`, `d2l.latency_report` (13.1); the hardware chapter's host-to-device bandwidth for load times.
**Figures:** `fig_lm_lora_batch` (one step's tokens grouped by adapter, the shared base product and the per-adapter low-rank products); (plot) decode step time relative to base-only against distinct adapters for the four modes with the ideal-bytes line; (plot) goodput against offered load for the three engines, and pool hit rate against slots with Che's curve.
**Restate / forward:** 7.4's adapter (`lora_A [r, d_in]`, `lora_B [d_out, r]`, scaling, merge and unmerge; not re-taught); `sec_mdl-svd-low-rank` (low-rank updates, one sentence); `eq_hw_decode_bound` (why extra bytes, not extra arithmetic, set the cost at decode); 13.4's cache keys and Che. Forward: none.
**Exercises:** 6 to 8. Check: the size of a rank-64 adapter on all projections of Qwen3-8B and its load time at 25 and 5 GB/s. Check: rank the three modes by bytes and launches for `T = 32`, `A_dist = 4`, `N = 16`. Derive: the break-even number of adapters for serial merging against grouped batching, and why merging one dominant adapter into a separate pass never pays at decode. Derive: the padded-rank overhead when ranks {8, 16, 32, 64} share a batch at `r_max`. Measure: rank heterogeneity by padding against grouping by rank. Measure: prefetching the next `k` waiting requests' adapters on a second stream against tail time to first token at a 70% pool hit rate, predicted from the miss rate and load time first. Open: routing between models and cascades: for Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B and 4B on a verifiable task, draw accuracy against mean cost per query for a confidence router and a learned router against the random-mixing line and the oracle bound `p_S + min(δ, q)`, with paired intervals over items, and say when a cascade beats the strong model alone at lower cost.
**Writer notes:** Unmerged adapters are not free: at decode the cost is bytes per distinct adapter, and a per-token gather multiplies it by the batch. Merging is right when one adapter dominates a replica's traffic; batching is right for a long tail; the break-even is a traffic statistic, not a model property. Sharing a prefix cache across adapters returns wrong activations; adapter identity belongs in the key. Padding to `r_max` makes every adapter pay the largest rank's bytes; grouped kernels that handle ranks per adapter avoid it. The reference grouped mode is launch-bound for large `A_dist` and may look worse than dense masking for small pools; say so and name the fused kernel as the remedy rather than tuning the reference. If `lm-lora-r1-demo` is unavailable, train three one-epoch adapters (about two minutes each) for correctness and use random adapters for timing. Routing and cascades are the open exercise here, with the derivation of the random line and the oracle bound stated in the text in three sentences; the committed per-item outputs of Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B and 4B on GSM8K (`lm-cascade-items`, generated with `d2l.generate(..., return_logprobs=True)` and scored with `d2l.extract_answer`) support it without a live run. vLLM's adapter serving (`--enable-lora`, `--max-loras`, `--max-lora-rank`) is the production comparison at the pinned version. Do not re-teach: the adapter, merging (7.9), the allocator. Library additions: `d2l.multi_lora_linear(x, W, A_stack, B_stack, adapter_ids, scale, mode)`, `d2l.AdapterPool`, `d2l.attach_adapters`, `d2l.detach_adapters`, `d2l.cascade_curve` and `d2l.pgr` (for the exercise); artifacts `lm-multilora-timing`, `lm-cascade-items`. Blueprint ch13 13.5 has derivations D1 (bytes), D2 (the pool as a cache) and D3 (cascade cost and accuracy), the three modes' contracts, the production-flag list and the exercise sketches.
**Sources:**
- Papers: [S-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03285) (unified paging, heterogeneous batching, adapter-aware tensor parallelism); [Punica: Multi-Tenant LoRA Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.18547) (the segmented gather-matrix-vector kernel and multi-tenant scheduling); [RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18665) (routers and their cost metrics, for the exercise); [FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176) (cascades, for the exercise).
- Code and documentation: [S-LoRA](https://github.com/S-LoRA/S-LoRA) and [Punica](https://github.com/punica-ai/punica) (the reference systems and kernels); vLLM, [LoRA Adapters](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/lora.html) (adapter serving in a production engine); [RouteLLM](https://github.com/lm-sys/RouteLLM) (a router framework, for the exercise).
- Courses, tutorials and blogs: [CMU 11-868](https://llmsystem.github.io/llmsystem2026spring/) (its LoRA and QLoRA lecture next to serving); Thinking Machines, [LoRA Without Regret](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/lora/) (what adapters can and cannot capture, cited from 7.4); [Inside vLLM](https://blog.vllm.ai/2025/09/05/anatomy-of-vllm.html) (where adapters enter the engine loop).
## Chapter 14 Advanced Architectures

**Label:** `chap_lm_architectures` (7 sections plus a Further Reading notebook, T0 to T3).
**Hook:** The reader has the transformer of Advanced (RoPE, GQA, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, a mixture of experts, sliding windows and sinks, DeltaNet and hybrid stacks) and a configuration file from 1.1 with fields that match none of it: a latent rank, an indexer that keeps 512 of a million keys, a layer type called `linear_attention`, an `hc_mult` of 4, an embedding table with 384 million rows. This chapter teaches those fields, one design axis per section, and for each change asks what it saves, what it costs, and which training and serving setup makes the trade worthwhile.
**Route:** What does a configuration file determine, and how is a technical report read against it (14.1)? How sparse should a model be, and how is the router co-designed with the network (14.2)? How is the cache shrunk in training rather than after it (14.3)? Where does a softmax head put the mass it does not need, and what do sinks, gates, windows and partial positions each trade (14.4)? Can a model learn which blocks of its context to read (14.5)? What does a released hybrid cost to serve (14.6)? Why does depth dilute a layer's contribution, and what restores it (14.7)?
**Out of scope:** The transformer block, MoE basics (routing, balancing with and without a loss, fine-grained and shared experts), the KV cache with its windows and sinks, RoPE and its extensions, and the SSM, DeltaNet and hybrid layers are Advanced (`sec_transformer-block`, `sec_moe`, `sec_kv-cache`, `sec_positional-information`, `chap_modern_rnn`); this chapter restates each in one sentence with its label and never re-derives it. Multimodal encoders and vision towers are the Image Models part (the loaders here skip them by name prefix). The release calendar, byte-level patching, diffusion language models, depth-aggregation variants, zero-computation experts, test-time training and the capstone checklist live in the Further Reading notebook, which is refreshed each edition. Inference-time KV compression is 12.6 and 12.7; drafting heads are 12.5; expert parallelism is 6.6; the decode-step model is 5.3.
**Writer notes:**
- *The one chapter that reads technical reports in depth.* Every model fact in the chapter is read from a `config.json`, a safetensors header, the Hub API or a report, with the field or section named; numbers that sources dispute (Kimi K3's active parameters) are never printed in prose and appear only as configuration-derived table entries. Freshness lives in two places: the data file behind 14.1's table (`lm-arch-registry`, `lm-arch-configs`, `lm-arch-expected`) and the Further Reading notebook. The maintenance manual (row procedure, the four-condition rule for a new section, the per-edition refresh checklist) is blueprint ch14 "How to extend this chapter" and is summarized in one paragraph at the end of 14.1.

- *Assignment.* The chapter hosts the capstone (`sec_lm_capstone`, "design under a budget"), hosted by the Further Reading notebook; it stands alone on 14.1's `d2l.config_stats` and 5.3's decode model: a design that satisfies a scenario's parameter, memory, latency and training-FLOP constraints with hand-derived claims checked to 0.5% (exact for cache bytes of GQA, MLA and GDN layers), one measured baseline on a released small model (peak memory within 15% and decode tokens per second within 25% of prediction, or a profile that localizes the gap), one rejected design with a pre-registered rule and at least three seeds or a paired interval, and a dossier. Scenario B (a small private assistant on one 16 GB GPU, the floor; this plan's 16 GB overrides the blueprint's 24 GB) is the T1 path; scenarios A and C use the 8x A100 80 GB analytic row.
- *Compute notes.* T0 for 14.1 (about 5 minutes on CPU after a one-time download; offline thereafter); T1 for 14.3, 14.5 and the loading half of 14.6 (at most 12 GiB); T2 for 14.2 (a sweep of 17 runs capped at about 8 minutes each by a token budget, about 3 hours, plus 20 minutes of routing on a T2 pair holding Qwen3-30B-A3B at about 30.5 GB per GPU), 14.4 (6 runs at about 30 minutes, about 3.5 hours) and 14.7 (up to 16 runs at about 8 minutes, 2.5 to 3.5 hours), each at most 34 GiB with a T1 reduction at width 256 and 6 or 12 blocks; T3 once per release for 14.6 (about 16 GPU-hours, at most 36 GiB per GPU). Training variants share the reference model's recipe and WSD schedule (`subsec_scheduler-branching`) so comparisons are within-notebook only.
- *Noise discipline.* A difference below two standard deviations of the baseline's seed spread is a tie, and ties are the expected outcome of most small-scale architecture comparisons (the 14.4 and 14.7 notebooks say so); paired bootstrap over evaluation sequences or documents; stability claims need a pre-registered divergence criterion (14.7). No conclusion is drawn from a 0.02-nat difference.
