Two different things are called "gated": the attention output gate of 14.4 (Qwen3.5's doubled `q_proj`) and the decay and write gates of the DeltaNet layer in 14.6; name both every time. `tab_modern-recipe` in `sec_scaling-laws` links here as the canonical data source after this chapter lands (book-side edit). The label `tab_hy-recipe` that the blueprint cites does not exist (`sec_hybrids` has the attention-fraction cache arithmetic and `fig_hy-cache` only; the released-hybrid survey is in `chap_modern_rnn`'s Further Reading); cite `sec_hybrids` and `fig_hy-cache`. Systems sections are cited by their second-pass numbers (5.3 decode model, 6.6 expert parallelism, 12.5 drafters, 12.6 and 12.7 KV compression, 13.4 prefix caching).
**Teaching sources:**
- Sebastian Raschka, [The Big LLM Architecture Comparison](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/the-big-llm-architecture-comparison) and [From GPT-2 to gpt-oss](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/from-gpt-2-to-gpt-oss-analyzing-the): the "what changed relative to the previous model" framing behind 14.1's `axis_notes`, and the walk through sliding windows, learned sinks, MoE and MXFP4 in one model (14.4); the pages predate 2026 releases, so they are templates for rows, not sources of facts.
- [Smol Training Playbook](https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceTB/smol-training-playbook): small-scale architecture ablations and how to decide which to run; the noise-check discipline of 14.4 and 14.7 and the capstone's experiment matrix.
- [How to Scale Your Model](https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/): the derive-then-measure style of analytic cost models; its attention and MoE arithmetic is translated into `config_stats` and the 14.3 and 14.5 decode-intensity derivations, without its JAX code.
- Hugging Face, [Mixture of Experts Explained](https://huggingface.co/blog/moe): the vocabulary and the router and capacity picture of 14.2.
- Songlin Yang, [DeltaNet Explained](https://sustcsonglin.github.io/blog/2024/deltanet-1/) and [flash-linear-attention](https://github.com/fla-org/flash-linear-attention): the WY and UT derivation and the Triton kernels behind 14.6's chunked form; `fla` is also the optional fast path there.
- [Ultra-Scale Playbook](https://huggingface.co/spaces/nanotron/ultrascale-playbook) and Andrej Karpathy's [nanochat](https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat): budget reasoning and a complete small-model recipe; the capstone's companions.
- The Transformers modeling files as executable ground truth for every row: [`modeling_qwen3_5.py`](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/models/qwen3_5/modeling_qwen3_5.py), [`modeling_deepseek_v3.py`](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/models/deepseek_v3/modeling_deepseek_v3.py), [`modeling_gpt_oss.py`](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py), [`modeling_qwen3_moe.py`](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/models/qwen3_moe/modeling_qwen3_moe.py); the oracles of 14.2 to 14.6.
- Courses: [Stanford CS336, Spring 2026](https://cs336.stanford.edu/) (architectures and hyperparameters, attention alternatives and MoE lectures; the scaling assignment as the style model for 14.2's fit and the capstone's pre-registration), [CMU 11-711, Spring 2026](https://cmu-l3.github.io/anlp-spring2026) (MoE and scaling-sequence-length lectures), [CMU 11-868, Spring 2026](https://llmsystem.github.io/llmsystem2026spring/) (MoE and attention-sink lectures from the systems side), [Berkeley CS288, Spring 2026](https://cal-cs288.github.io/sp26) (advanced architectures lecture).
**Further Reading:** `sec_lm_architectures_fr`: the open-weight release calendar, byte-level patching, diffusion language models, depth aggregation, zero-computation experts, test-time training and memory layers, and the design-under-a-budget checklist that hosts the capstone (entry below).

### 14.1 Architecture Configurations · T0
**Idea:** A configuration file determines a model's parameters, active compute and cache bytes per token, and a technical report is read against those derived numbers rather than taken on its word.
**Opening:** The configuration files of Qwen3-0.6B and Gemma 4 E2B do not yield their cards' parameter counts from the obvious fields, and the opening cell shows why: flattening the Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash configurations gives 26 keys against 87, and one repository carries three "parameter counts" (a 552B backbone in the report, 763,205,315,794 elements in the safetensors index, and the 12 L d-squared count), none of which agree, each right for a different question. The open question: what does a report leave out, and how would the reader notice?
**Teaches:**
- The design axes, one per later section (`tab_lm_arch_axes`): token mixing (`layer_types`, `full_attention_interval`, `sliding_window`, `index_topk`, `compress_ratios`; 14.4 to 14.6), KV layout (`num_key_value_heads`, `kv_lora_rank`, `kv_source_layer_ids`; 14.3), feed-forward (`num_experts`, `num_experts_per_tok`, `moe_intermediate_size`, `routed_expert_hidden_size`, `scoring_func`, `n_group` and `topk_group`; 14.2), lookup memory (`engram_*`, `ngram_*`, `ple_*`; 14.2, an axis distinct from MoE), residual paths and norms (`hc_mult`, `hc_count`, `mhc`, `attn_res_block_size`, QK-norm; 14.7), positions (`rope_theta`, `partial_rotary_factor`, `rope_scaling`, NoPE layers; 14.4), output heads (`num_nextn_predict_layers`, `mtp_*`, `dspark_*`; 12.5), tokenization and numerics (`vocab_size`, tied embeddings, `quantization_config`, `expert_dtype`; 3.6, 4.3, Chapter 11).
- The table: `tab_modern-recipe` of `sec_scaling-laws` made data, extended to 2024 to 2026 and to MoE, MLA, sparse-attention, hybrid and lookup layers, regenerated from pinned configuration files, with one row per model and one column per axis (release date, family, total and active parameters, active fraction, layers, attention mix, cache bytes per token, state bytes, expert count, top-k and shared count, score function, dense-prefix layers, position scheme, residual scheme, shipped heads, weight dtype); the four small multiples of `fig_lm_arch_axes_timeline` are read for moves, not trends.
- Reading a report with a schema (`tab_lm_arch_schema`): architecture fields tagged disclosed, in-config or inferred; training (tokens, stages, optimizer, precision); systems (parallelism, hardware, MFU if disclosed); claims with their evidence type (ablation, final-model-only, none), baseline and budget; reconciliation of report against configuration, recorded in `axis_notes`.
- DeepSeek's line of releases as configuration diffs (`tab_lm_arch_deepseek`, built by a ten-line key-diff printer): V2 adds MLA; V3 adds sigmoid scoring with bias-controlled balancing, a multi-token-prediction head and block-scaled fp8; V3.2 adds the indexer fields; V4 (April 2026) adds `compress_ratios`, `hc_mult` 4 (mHC) and `num_hash_layers`, a single KV head of width 512, and a 1M-token context; V4.1-Flash adds cross-layer KV and index reuse, Engram tables and the drafting module. The honest statement: V4 and V4.1 each change several axes.
**Derivation:** Total parameters, active parameters per token, FLOPs per token (affine in context) and cache bytes per token from the configuration fields, for dense GQA (with gate, QK-norm, biases and sinks), MLA (with a query LoRA), gated DeltaNet, KDA, MoE and latent MoE layers (`eq_lm_arch_params`, `eq_lm_arch_flops`, `eq_lm_arch_cache`). Smallest case: Qwen3-0.6B against its safetensors index, exact to the parameter, and the Qwen3-8B row (8,190,735,360 elements; 147,456 cache bytes per token in bf16). Worked residuals: gpt-oss-20b and -120b differ from their headers by 768 and 4,608, the router biases (24 by 32 and 36 by 128); DeepSeek-V3's 671.0B backbone against 684.5B in the index is the 13.5B MTP module; Qwen3.5-2B splits into a text backbone of 1,881,825,088, a vision tower of 331,416,576 and an MTP head of 60,828,160. The report reconstruction: V4.1-Flash's stated 890 bytes of global KV per token follows from 2.5 cache entries per token (three ratio-2 encoder layers and one ratio-1 layer among the `kv_source_layer_ids`) times 288 bytes of 512-channel fp4 latent with block scales plus 68 bytes of indexer key, an inferred layout stated as an assumption.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: do the closed forms reproduce the released checkpoints' parameter counts and cache bytes exactly for the families the book's layers cover, and to a named, itemized residual otherwise?
2. Model and data: about a dozen core configurations (the Qwen3 ladder and Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3.5-2B and 35B-A3B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma 4 E2B and 26B-A4B, SmolLM3-3B, gpt-oss-120b, DeepSeek-V3, V4-Flash and V4.1-Flash, Kimi K3) plus extended rows, all from pinned snapshots; no weights are downloaded, headers are read by HTTP range request (first 8 bytes give the header length; sharded indexes handled; packed fp4 and MXFP4 unpacked by a per-format factor).
3. Procedure: derive, compare with the header census at group level (embedding, head, attention, linear mixer, dense FFN, routed and shared experts, router, norms, lookup tables, MTP, vision), print derived, header, difference and "explained by"; compare cache bytes with `d2l.config_memory` (exact for dense; recurrent state within 0.1% for hybrids, a disagreement is a bug report to the 1.1 author) and with `lm-arch-expected`; the `FlopCounterMode` check on a width-256 random instance of the Qwen3-8B plan within 5%; fill the report schema for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Kimi K3.
4. Claim: exact for dense, MoE and MLA families (confirmed on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3-235B-A22B, DeepSeek-V2 at the time of the blueprint); Kimi K3's total within 0.5% of the Hub figure and its active count within 3% of the report's, printed as table entries only; Gemma 4's rows need a new layer plan (`@d2l.register_arch('gemma4')`: per-layer embeddings as a lookup-table group, `layer_types` with 512 or 1,024-token windows) and are the first test of the row procedure.
5. Nothing is empirical here, so there is no noise check; report numbers are expected values and never tune the calculator.
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.config_params(by_group=True)` (1.1; MoE raises and `config_stats` computes those parts itself), `d2l.config_memory`, `d2l.ServingModel` (fed by `ConfigStats` through `kv_bytes_override` and `state_bytes`), `huggingface_hub` metadata calls.
7. T0 throughout; the Transformers `AutoModel.from_config` on the meta device is an independent census for the types it can build (not for `trust_remote_code` types, which stay header-only).
**Figures:** `fig_lm_design_axes` (one decoder block annotated with the axes and the sections that own them); `fig_lm_arch_census` (where the parameters live: backbone, experts, lookup tables, vision, MTP per model on a log axis with the report's headline total marked; cache bytes per token split into growing and bounded, fixed state hatched "per sequence, not per token") (plot); `fig_lm_arch_axes_timeline` (four small multiples over release date) (plot). Tables `tab_lm_arch_axes`, `tab_lm_design_table`, `tab_lm_arch_deepseek`, `tab_lm_arch_schema`.
**Restate / forward:** `tab_modern-recipe` and `sec_scaling-laws` (the 12 L d-squared census, the non-embedding convention and `eq_six_nd`, restated in one sentence each; the table here is the canonical extension); `sec_kv-cache` (`eq_kv-cache-bytes`, `kv_cache_bytes`); `sec_moe` (its hand-run census of Mixtral and DeepSeek-V3, which `config_stats` generalizes); `sec_hybrids` (the cache is paid per attention layer); `sec_read_write` (the safetensors header). Forward: none.
**Exercises:** 7. Derive: the four numbers of one repository (backbone, index elements, active in decode, active in prefill); cache bytes per token for a hybrid with MLA layers (Kimi Linear, Kimi K3); the parameter cost of a latent MoE against full width (K3: 29.6B against 59.2B, plus 0.17% for the projections); the cache with an fp8 indexer (1,040 bytes). Measure: which released indexes disagree with their reports (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's 179,999,981,459 elements against its configuration). Check: a residual census row. Open: a report schema stress test on a new release in at most 200 words.
**Writer notes:**
- "Parameters" has at least five meanings (total, active, backbone, checkpoint elements, bytes); say which every time. The Hub API counts packed fp4 and MXFP4 tensors as elements while the header gives the packed shape; an "off by two" is almost always this (gpt-oss's U8 tensors). Lookup tables (Engram) cost memory and traffic, not FLOPs: V4.1-Flash holds 196.6B elements of tables beyond its 552B backbone. `num_key_value_heads` is meaningless for MLA (128 in V3) and 1 for V4's single KV head; cache bytes come from `kv_lora_rank` plus `qk_rope_head_dim`, or from `head_dim`. `mla_use_nope` does not remove the rope slots from the weights; read shapes. A configuration can lag its report or its weights; print disagreements, never tune. Do not infer a mechanism from a field name: `hc_mult` is the number of residual streams, `compress_ratios` is per layer with extra entries for MTP slots (43 entries for 40 layers).
- Differences from the blueprint: the lookup-memory axis is separate from the feed-forward axis; the DeepSeek line gains the V4 step (the blueprint already added it as a fifth row); Gemma 4 E2B and 26B-A4B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B join the core rows; Kimi K3's disputed active count is a configuration-derived entry; the capstone's `comparators(scenario)` reads this table.
- Library additions: `d2l.config_stats(config, *, kv_bytes=2, state_bytes=4, groups=('text',), plan=None) -> d2l.ConfigStats` (fields `total_params`, `active_params`, `params_by_group`, `flops_fixed`, `flops_per_ctx_token`, `cache_bytes_per_token`, `cache_bytes_bounded`, `state_bytes`, `layers`, `notes`; methods `flops_per_token(ctx, mode)`, `cache_bytes(ctx)`, `to_row()`); `d2l.LayerSpec` (mixer in `gqa`, `swa`, `mla`, `dsa`, `gdn`, `kda`, `lightning`, `csa2`; ffn in `dense`, `moe`, `latent_moe`); `@d2l.register_arch(model_type)` registering a plan of at most 30 lines (the only model-specific code; registered plans listed in blueprint ch14 §14.1, to which `gemma4` is added); `d2l.load_config`, `d2l.safetensors_census`, `d2l.design_table(registry, core_only=True)`, `d2l.ReportSchema`, `d2l.check_report`. An unknown field with no mapping is appended to `notes`, never guessed.
- Risks and fallbacks: a renamed or gated repository keeps its pinned snapshot; packed-dtype unpack factors differ per format (one test each; unresolved cases go to notes and leave the exact-match set); the 68-byte indexer layout is an assumption to revise if the V4 report contradicts it; `config_memory` and `config_stats` disagreeing is filed with 1.1, with `config_stats` authoritative per layer kind; Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has no report and stays a configuration-only row.
- Detail: blueprint ch14 §14.1 (the per-layer closed forms, the numerical test table, the report-schema worked examples) and the chapter's config fact sheet (fetched 2026-10-28).
**Sources:**
- Papers and reports: [Qwen3 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09388) (the dense family; report-against-config worked case); [DeepSeek-V2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434), [DeepSeek-V3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437), [DeepSeek-V3.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02556), [DeepSeek-V4: Towards Highly Efficient Million-Token Context Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348) and [DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.19969v1) (the line of releases; §2 and §4.2.1 of the last for reconciliation); [Kimi K3](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1) (§2; fields read from the configuration, numbers not printed); [Llama 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783) (a dense report-only row; the Hub repository is gated); [gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b Model Card](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.10925) (router biases, MXFP4 experts); [HELM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110) (the evaluation questions a report should answer).
- Code and documentation: [Gemma 4 model card](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/core/model_card_4) (variants, windows of 512 and 1,024, per-layer embeddings, Apache-2.0; the local-to-global ratio is read from `layer_types`, the card gives none); [google/gemma-4-E2B](https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-4-E2B), [Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), [HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM3-3B](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM3-3B), [deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash), [moonshotai/Kimi-K3](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3) (configuration files and headers); [Qwen3.8 README](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3.8) (the 27B and 2.4T rows); [Transformers configuration classes](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main_classes/configuration); [safetensors metadata parsing](https://huggingface.co/docs/safetensors/metadata_parsing) and [Hub API endpoints](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/api) (headers, `createdAt`, `safetensors.total`); the four Transformers modeling files listed under Teaching sources.

### 14.2 Mixture-of-Experts Design at Scale · T2
**Idea:** Sparsity is a design axis with its own scaling law, and the router's score function, normalization and node limits are co-designed with the network the experts live on.
**Opening:** The `sec_moe` model picked 8 experts of 64 by hand; released models choose 256 small experts with 8 active and one shared, or 896 with 16 active behind a latent projection. The concrete example is the opening cell listing expert count, top-k, shared count, expert width over hidden width, score function and dense-prefix layers for six released models (`tab_lm_moe_models`). The open question: what fixes the number of experts, and where does a model keep knowledge that no arithmetic needs?
**Teaches:**
- Total against active parameters, granularity (k experts of width A over k at fixed active width A) and the fitted law L(S, G) with the optimum at fixed training FLOPs; "a 3B-active MoE is a 3B model" is false for memory and decode traffic (Qwen3-30B-A3B reads 61 GB of weights).
- Router design in released models (`tab_lm_moe_routers`): softmax scores with a scaling factor (V2, Qwen3) against sigmoid scores with normalized top-k and a bias controller (V3, K2, K3, GLM, MiniMax) against the square-root softplus of V4; group- and node-limited routing (V3's 8 groups and 4 chosen) co-designed with expert parallelism; dense early layers (`first_k_dense_replace` 3 in V3 and GLM, 1 in the Kimi models, 0 in Qwen3 MoE and gpt-oss) and why models keep them.
- All-to-all bytes per token with and without a latent: the expected number of nodes a token's k experts touch, n(1 minus (1 minus 1/n)^k) with replacement, capped by node limits, times the dispatched width times dispatch and combine bytes; LatentMoE projects to a smaller width before dispatch (K3's 3,584 of 7,168); experts touched per batch, 1 minus (1 minus k/E)^b, sets decode weight traffic.
- Engram's hashed n-gram lookup memory as a sub-block (`subsec_lm_moe_lookup`): a table indexed by hashed n-grams (up to 4-grams, about 384M rows per table, 8 heads of 256) read beside the MoE layer, costing memory and traffic but no FLOPs; a miniature with gated integration in the notebook; shipped in DeepSeek V4.1-Flash and, as `ngram_*` and `ple_*` fields, in Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.
- Expert specialization measured on a released model: routing traces over code, math and prose against a shuffle baseline; load balance is not specialization.
**Derivation:** Optimal sparsity at fixed FLOPs from a parametric law in total parameters, data and sparsity (the Abnar et al. form with its published coefficients used only structurally, since the units are unknown; the Krajewski et al. granularity form), with D equal to C over 6(1 minus S)N and the interior optimum found by root finding, checked against a 200-by-200 brute-force grid; all-to-all bytes per token with and without a latent. Smallest case: hidden 4,096, top-8, 64 experts over 8 nodes, dispatch and combine at 2 bytes, with and without a latent of half width; a Monte-Carlo over one million tokens at E 256 and n 8 agrees to three decimals, and V3's group limit gives at most 4 distinct nodes.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: at fixed active compute and tokens, how does validation loss move with total parameters and granularity, and does the fitted law's optimum sit inside the grid?
2. Model and data: the reference model (138M active) with every FFN after layer 0 replaced by `d2l.MoEFFN` at the dense FFN's active width, no shared expert, sigmoid scores with normalized top-k and the bias controller (rate 1e-3), no auxiliary loss, sorted dispatch; the grid G in {1, 2, 4, 8} by S in {2, 4, 8, 16} plus dense, 17 runs on the same token count (the slowest, E 128, at most 8 minutes), one seed per cell and two extra seeds at (8, 4) and at dense; the fit L equals e plus (a plus g G to the minus gamma) S to the minus alpha in log space with a residual bootstrap.
3. Second measurement (committed): routing traces of Qwen3-30B-A3B over three domains (FineWeb-Edu, FineMath, python-edu; about 100K tokens each, ids and statistics committed, not text) on a T2 pair, with expert load, entropy and a 1,000-permutation shuffle baseline for specialization.
4. Checks: sorted dispatch against `sec_moe`'s dense-gather layer (1e-5 in fp32, 3e-3 in bf16); gradients within 1e-4 relative; `torch._grouped_mm` against the loop (1e-5); the sigmoid and softmax routers against the literal Transformers `Qwen3MoeSparseMoeBlock` and `DeepseekV3MoE` on 256 tokens (1e-5); the latent form against equation 11 of the K3 report (1e-5); root finding against brute force to grid resolution; `config_stats` reproduces an `MoEFFN` layer's parameter count exactly.
5. Claim that survives noise: loss falls with total parameters at fixed active with diminishing returns (an exponent to one digit with its bootstrap interval), and a cell wins only if the gap exceeds two standard deviations of the three-seed cells and the paired interval excludes zero; the paper's exponents are not compared, only the sign.
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.load_reference_model`, `d2l.PackedStream`, `d2l.a2a_bytes` (6.6; the baseline the latent version extends), `d2l.config_stats`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`, the `ffn_factory` seam of `d2l.TransformerBlock`.
7. T1 reduction (`cfg.scale='t1'`): `d2l.GPT` at width 256 with 6 blocks on a 20M-token slice, dense plus (S, G) in {(4, 1), (16, 1), (4, 4), (16, 4)}, two seeds at 90 seconds each, fit skipped; routing on OLMoE-1B-7B (64 experts, top-8, 13.8 GB, which needs a whole 16 GB card or 256-token sequences at batch 2).
**Figures:** `fig_lm_moe_axes` (the sparsity axes on one layer: expert count, top-k, shared expert, latent width, lookup table); `fig_lm_moe_sweep` (loss against total parameters at fixed active, by granularity; tokens per second; load imbalance) (plot); `fig_lm_moe_a2a` (all-to-all bytes per token against top-k with and without a latent and with node limits) (plot). Tables `tab_lm_moe_models`, `tab_lm_moe_routers`; `fig_lm_moe_lookup` (the Engram miniature).
**Restate / forward:** `sec_moe` in one paragraph (routing collapse, `eq_moe-aux`, `eq_moe-bias`, `eq_moe-layer`, shared and fine-grained experts, `tab_moe-experts` reproduced from configurations with expert-count and width columns); `sec_scaling-laws` (`eq_chinchilla_law`, `eq_six_nd`); 6.6's all-to-all volume (not re-derived; the latent width is the addition); 5.3's decode model (total parameters set memory, active parameters set traffic). Forward: none.
**Exercises:** 8. Derive: the inference cost model (bytes read per decode step against batch); the touched fraction under non-uniform routing (Jensen); the latent width that equalizes K3's traffic with V3's (K3 uncapped 7.06 nodes against V3's cap of 4; about 4,061 against the shipped 3,584); an average of 6 of 8 experts with zero-computation experts. Measure: load imbalance against domain skew; router entropy against load; G 1 against G 8 at S 8 with three seeds. Open: zero-computation experts (LongCat-Flash's identity experts) as a variable-compute arm at T1 with three seeds; a hashed, a dense and a learned first layer.
**Writer notes:**
- Differences from the blueprint: Engram's primary paper is verified (arXiv 2601.07372, "Conditional Memory via Scalable Lookup"); cite it, and keep the sub-block in 14.2 unless lookup tables spread across several releases (the editor's four-condition rule); zero-computation experts are an exercise, not body text; LatentMoE stays (shipped in K3).
- Matched active parameters is not matched FLOPs; the dense-gather layer of `sec_moe` costs grow with E, so the sweep needs the sorted dispatch; normalization, scaling factor, score function and bias interact (V2's softmax with scale 16 and V3's sigmoid with scale 2.5 are not interchangeable); a fitted exponent from 16 points has a wide interval, never extrapolate the optimum beyond the grid; expert statistics from 100K tokens are noisy for rare experts (bootstrap, drop experts below a token threshold).
- Memory and fallbacks: if E 128 exceeds 34 GiB halve the micro-batch and double accumulation; if the sorted loop is too slow at E 128 use `torch._grouped_mm` or cap E at 64; Qwen3-30B-A3B does not fit one A100 40 GB (T2 pair with `device_map='auto'`, batch 2 by 1,024 if above 38 GiB per GPU); `num_hash_layers` semantics remain unverified until the V4 report is read; the code corpus is committed as ids and statistics only.
- Library additions: `d2l.MoEFFN(d, num_experts, top_k, width, *, shared=0, shared_width=None, score='sigmoid'|'softmax'|'sqrtsoftplus', norm_topk=True, scale=1.0, n_group=1, topk_group=None, latent=None, zero_experts=0, bias_rate=1e-3, dispatch='sorted')` (a drop-in `ffn_factory` storing `self.stats`, with `route`, `forward`, `update_bias`); `d2l.moe_dispatch_bytes(num_experts, top_k, hidden, *, latent=None, nodes=8, node_limit=None, b_dispatch=2, b_combine=2, exact=False)`; `d2l.expert_stats`; `d2l.fit_sparsity_law(df)`; `d2l.optimal_sparsity(coefs, C, grid)`; `d2l.train_lm_steps(model, batches, steps, *, lr, warmup, decay_frac, seed, eval_every, eval_fn, hooks=())` (about 30 lines over `d2l.pretrain` with `d2l.wsd_lr` and `d2l.param_groups`; the variant-training loop of 14.4 and 14.7). Artifacts `lm-arch-moe-sweep` (JSONL plus `fit.json`), `lm-arch-routing-qwen3-30b` (`.npz`, int16 ids, about 40 MB). Detail: blueprint ch14 §14.2.

### 14.3 Latent Attention and Cross-Layer KV Sharing · T1
**Idea:** A low-rank latent for keys and values can be absorbed into the query and output projections at decode, so the cache holds one small vector per token, if and only if the rotary position is kept out of the absorbed path.
**Opening:** The GQA cache of Qwen3-8B still stores eight heads of keys and values per layer, 147,456 bytes per token; a single latent of width 512 per token would cut that to 1,152 bytes but seems to cost a re-expansion at every step. The concrete example is the opening arithmetic: DeepSeek-V3's expanded keys and values would be 4,997,120 bytes per token over 61 layers; its latent is 70,272, 71 times less and 2.1 times less than Qwen3-8B's GQA. The open question: can an existing GQA model be converted?
**Teaches:**
- MLA: a down-projection to a latent c of rank r with a decoupled rotary slice of width d_r, up-projections for keys and values, and the absorption of the key up-projection into the query and of the value up-projection into the output projection, which turns decode into multi-query attention with one head of width r plus d_r; absorption is a reordering, never a pre-merge (merging W_O with W_UV is 3.7 times larger).
- Why RoPE blocks absorption: after the up-projection the rotation sits between the two factors and depends on the position difference, so the absorbed query would be position-dependent; the decoupled slice carries the rotation separately at a cost of d_r over r plus d_r (64 of 576, about 11%).
- Decode cost per context token per layer and arithmetic intensity for three strategies (expanded cache, latent re-expanded each step at about 120 times the FLOPs, absorbed); prefill is a different trade (absorbed costs about 3.4 times the attention FLOPs of expanded, so prefill runs expanded).
- Cross-layer sharing (one cache read by adjacent layers; the borrower rotates its queries against the owner's keys) and conversion of a trained GQA checkpoint by a joint, optionally activation-aware, SVD of its key and value projections with a short recovery.
**Derivation:** The absorption identity (`eq_lm_mla_absorb`) and why a rotation between the factors breaks it (`eq_lm_mla_rope`); the activation-aware joint low-rank factorization (`eq_lm_mla_awsvd`, a whitening by the Cholesky factor of X-transposed X, reducing to a data-free joint SVD at X equal to I). Smallest case: two heads at dimension 8 with latent 4 in prose; in code d 256, H 8, d_n 32, d_r 16, d_v 32, r 64, r_q 96, seeded, where explicit and absorbed agree to 1e-10 in fp64 and 1e-5 relative in fp32, the three strategies agree, `MLACache.bytes()` equals L(r plus d_r) times bytes times n, RoPE after the up-projection against position-ignorant absorption differs by a relative error of order one, and `config_stats(DeepSeek-V3).cache_bytes_per_token` is exactly 70,272.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: do the explicit and absorbed paths agree in bf16, and at what context and batch does absorbed MLA decode beat an 8-KV-head GQA layer of the same query width?
2. Model and data: one layer at DeepSeek-V3 dimensions (d 7,168, H 128, r 512, r_q 1,536, d_n 128, d_r 64, d_v 128) with random bf16 weights; arms GQA 128:8 (`d2l.GQAAttention`), MLA expanded cache, latent re-expand, absorbed; n in {1K, ..., 32K}, batch in {1, 4, 16}; 50 warm-up and 200 timed steps with CUDA events and graphs, five repetitions; a fit of step time to tau0 plus tau1 n b, and the 5.3 decode model's prediction from `d2l.chip_specs()` (the A100 row predicts MLA about 2 times faster per context token; recompute).
3. Conversion: Qwen3-0.6B converted by joint SVD at ranks r in {32, 64, 128, 256, 512} against its original 1,536 numbers per token, with oracle SVD, data-free joint SVD and activation-aware SVD on a 64K-token calibration slice, keeping the top rope pairs (MHA2MLA's finding, unverified) and GPT-2 124M (no RoPE) as the control where the conversion is clean; 0 and 200 recovery steps (AdamW 2e-5 on the reference data), eight 1,024-token passages, three recovery seeds at r 128. Optional third measurement: MLA, GQA and two-layer sharing trained from scratch at width 256 with two seeds.
4. Checks: prefill expanded then decode absorbed equals a full forward (1e-5 in fp32); `d2l.MLAAttention` against Transformers' `DeepseekV3Attention` with `rope_scaling=None` (1e-5, interleaved-RoPE flag matched); the bf16 deviation of the absorbed chain reported with its tolerance measured; `CrossLayerKV(share=2)` halves the bytes and `share=1` reproduces the outputs (1e-6); `joint_svd_kv` at full rank within 1e-5 relative; `mha_to_mla` at full rank reproduces GPT-2 logits within 1e-4.
5. Claim that survives noise: the paths are equal in bf16 within the measured floor; the latency crossover exists where the arms' min-max ranges do not overlap, with a bootstrap on tau1; the conversion curves carry paired intervals over passages and the activation-aware method may tie (reported as a tie).
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.GQAAttention`, `d2l.rope`, `d2l.load_qwen3`, `d2l.config_stats`, `d2l.chip_specs`, `d2l.ServingModel`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`, the `attn_factory` seam.
7. T1 throughout (at most 10 GiB); artifact `lm-arch-mla-conversion` (JSON: rank, cache elements per token per layer, method, loss with and without recovery, seeds).
**Figures:** `fig_lm_mla_absorb` (data flow of the explicit and absorbed paths with the decoupled rotary slice); `fig_lm_mla_latency` (decode step time against context for the four arms at three batch sizes, with the 5.3 prediction) (plot); `fig_lm_mla_conversion` (loss against rank by conversion method, with and without recovery) (plot). Tables `tab_lm_mla_strategies` (V3 and Kimi K2 dimensions), `tab_lm_mla_cache_released`.
**Restate / forward:** `subsec_kv-cache-low-rank` (the low-rank premise and the oracle SVD of GPT-2's keys and values; MLA named there with its rank, decoupled RoPE named but not derived); `sec_mdl-svd-low-rank` (Eckart-Young, the optimal rank-r error); `sec_positional-information` (the rotation identity R_t-transposed R_s equals R_(s minus t)); 5.3's decode model; 12.6 and 12.7 as the contrast (compression after training). Forward: none.
**Exercises:** 7. Derive: FLOPs per token for both paths; cache bytes of the MLA models (69,120 for V2, 70,272 for V3, 89,856 for GLM-5); the head count at which absorbed intensity crosses an A100's ridge (about 90 heads); the GQA-to-MLA rank argument (r equal to 2 H_kv d_h); the decoupling cost 11.1% and why NoPE MLA (Kimi Linear) avoids it. Measure: latent dimension against loss on the conversion curve; the crossover prediction against the measurement. Open: one latent shared across two layers in the from-scratch arm; partial RoPE on Qwen3-0.6B (keep 8 of 32 pairs).
**Writer notes:**
- The three traps in order: latent caching with re-expansion costs about 120 times the absorbed FLOPs (33.6M against 278,528 per context token per layer at V3 dimensions); absorption is reordering, not pre-merging; absorbed intensity about 242 FLOP per byte at 128 heads makes decode compute-bound on bandwidth-rich chips (K2 with 64 heads sits lower). Validate in fp32 and fp64 before bf16, where the absorbed chain is longer and the error larger.
- Field semantics: `num_key_value_heads` is a compatibility field for MLA; `mla_use_nope` keeps the rope slots (576 numbers per token even in Kimi K3), read the shapes; conversion without recovery is a capability probe, not a result; a cross-layer borrower must rotate queries consistently with the owner's keys.
- Hardware: SDPA has no fused kernel for a 576-wide head on Ada, so the measurement uses the math or efficient backend and says "unfused"; FlashMLA's 2026-09-30 release dropped Hopper and targets Blackwell and Ascend, so measured latencies are upper bounds; if the `chip_specs()` row is missing, measure bandwidth with a large copy and FLOPs with a large matmul; the expanded arm at batch 16 and n 32K may not fit (drop the cell); Transformers' `DeepseekV3Attention` signature may change (small config, pinned version).
- Difference from the blueprint: the conversion target is Qwen3-0.6B (the book's own checkpoint) with GPT-2 as the no-RoPE control, instead of GPT-2 alone; the partial-RoPE handling is decided at authoring (keep the top pairs per MHA2MLA, or convert in NoPE form and recover).
- Library additions: `d2l.MLAAttention(d, num_heads, dn, dr, dv, r, rq=None, *, rope_base=10000.0, nope=False)` with `forward(x, cache=None, mode='expanded'|'absorbed', pos=0)`; `d2l.MLACache` (`append`, `bytes()`); `d2l.mla_decode_cost(H, dn, dr, dv, r, n, *, strategy, bytes_per=2) -> dict(flops, bytes, intensity)`; `d2l.CrossLayerKV(share)` and `d2l.cla_gpt(vocab, d, H, Hkv, L, share)`; `d2l.joint_svd_kv(W_k, W_v, r, *, calib=None)`; `d2l.mha_to_mla(attn, r, *, calib=None)`. Detail: blueprint ch14 §14.3.
**Sources:**
- Papers: [DeepSeek-V2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434) (MLA and decoupled RoPE); [DeepSeek-V3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437) (MLA at scale, the dimensions used); [Reducing Transformer Key-Value Cache Size with Cross-Layer Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12981) (sharing across layers); [MHA2MLA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14837) (conversion with partial RoPE and joint SVD; its reported savings are quoted as the paper's); [TransMLA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.07864) (GQA-to-MLA conversion, the rank argument); [You Only Cache Once](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05254) (decoder-decoder cache sharing, one sentence); [Kimi K3](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1) (NoPE MLA with an output gate; `kv_a_proj_with_mqa` of shape 576 by 7,168).

### 14.4 Softmax Attention Refinements · T2
**Idea:** A softmax head must put its mass somewhere, and each fix for the mass it does not need (a sink, a gate, a window, a partial or absent position) trades something that can be measured at small scale.
**Opening:** Most heads of Qwen3-0.6B dump a third to half of their mass on the first token; Gemma 4 E2B sees only 512 tokens in most of its layers and works at a 128K context. The concrete example is the opening probe: first-token mass, maximum-to-median residual magnitude and the fraction of near-zero gate values for Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3.5-2B and Gemma 4 E2B on the same 2K-token passages, with the disclaimer that differences between released models are pointers, not ablations. The open question: which of these fixes still matters once a model is trained with it from the start?
**Teaches:**
- Sinks: a head with nothing to attend to cannot output zero, since the output lies in the convex hull of the values, so it parks its mass on a token whose value is nearly zero; massive activations are the mechanism; a learned sink logit (gpt-oss) is exactly one extra key with logit s and zero value, and the output is the standard one scaled by sigma(LSE minus s).
- Gates: an elementwise sigmoid gate on the attention output (Qwen3.5's doubled `q_proj`, 8 heads of 256) lets a head emit zero without a sink and adds H d_h d parameters per layer; the T0 toy shows the baseline concentrating, the gate spreading, the sink using its column.
- Positions: partial RoPE (rotate the first fraction of the head's channels; the static pairs are those whose wavelength exceeds the context, 10 of 32 for Qwen3.5-2B at theta 1e7 and 262,144) and interleaved NoPE layers (SmolLM3-3B drops the rotation in every fourth layer) beyond the training length, measured by pure extrapolation without scaling (so that the measurement is of the architecture, not of YaRN, which is 4.5's).
- Local-global layouts as a KV dial: with a fraction f_g of global layers and window w, the cache is 2 H_kv d_h b L (f_g n plus (1 minus f_g) min(n, w)); Gemma 4's windows of 512 (E2B, E4B) and 1,024 (12B, 26B-A4B, 31B) with the ratio read from `layer_types`; gpt-oss's alternating 128-token windows (36,864 growing bytes per token against 4.7 MB bounded). Per-layer embeddings (Gemma 4 E models) in one paragraph: a per-layer input table that buys capacity with memory rather than FLOPs. Differential attention in one sentence.
**Derivation:** A learned sink logit s equals one extra key of logit s and zero value (`eq_lm_sink_equiv`); the sink margin: a zero-value key whose logit exceeds the others by at least ln(nV over epsilon) bounds the output norm by epsilon (`eq_lm_sink_margin`), and the minimum output norm without a sink is the distance from the origin to the convex hull of the values (`eq_lm_sink_hull`). Smallest case: logits (2, 1, 0) with a sink at 3, where the three standard weights are scaled by sigma(LSE minus 3). Check cells: `d2l.attention_with_sink` against a concatenated softmax (exact) and against sigma(LSE minus s) times SDPA (1e-6); the margin bisected for n equal to 2^k at k from 1 to 14 with slope 1 in ln n; the partial-rotary static-pair count against brute force for five released configurations (exact integers).
**Notebook:**
1. Question: what do a learned sink, a gated output and partial RoPE with NoPE layers each change in loss, first-token mass, maximum activation and length generalization when a model is trained with them from the start?
2. Model and data: four arms at the reference model's scale (138M): baseline (GQA, full RoPE, QK-norm), sink, sigmoid gate, partial RoPE at 0.25 with every fourth layer NoPE; the same tokens, seed 0 for all four and seeds 1 and 2 for the baseline to measure sigma; about 30 minutes per run on one A100 (about 3.5 hours).
3. Metrics: validation loss on `lm-fwedu-val`; attention mass on position 0 from query 64; maximum-to-median residual magnitude; copy accuracy against lookback {L/4, L/2, L, 2L, 4L} on `d2l.repeat_copy_task`; loss at positions beyond L against within L; throughput; parameters.
4. Checks: `RefinedAttention(sink=True)` against Transformers' `GptOssAttention` on a small configuration (1e-5); `RefinedAttention(gate='sigmoid')` against a literal transcription of `Qwen3_5Attention` (1e-5); partial RoPE against `apply_rotary_pos_emb` of `modeling_qwen3_5.py` (1e-6); interleaved against half-split layouts exact up to a permutation; the window mask against `sec_attention-at-scale`'s band mask; parameter counts against `config_stats`.
5. Claim that survives noise: first-token mass falls beyond noise in the sink and gate arms; loss ties within two sigma are the expected outcome and are reported as ties with their diagnostics; copy accuracy beyond L is reported per arm with a bootstrap over 64 evaluation sequences; a gain at 4L bought with a loss at L is named as a trade-off.
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.train_lm_steps` (14.2), `d2l.load_reference_model`, `d2l.load_hf`, `d2l.GQAAttention`, `d2l.rope`, `d2l.config_stats`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`.
7. T1 reduction: `d2l.GPT` at width 256 with 6 blocks and context 256, three seeds per variant (12 runs of about a minute), extrapolation to 1,024; the released-model probes fit in 12 GiB with eager attention at 2K. Artifact `lm-arch-refine-logs`.
**Figures:** `fig_lm_sink_gate` (a head's mass with a sink token against an output gate, and the hull picture behind the margin); `fig_lm_attn_variants` (loss, sink mass, residual magnitude and copy accuracy by arm) (plot); `fig_lm_attn_layouts` (cache bytes against context for local-global ratios and windows, Gemma 4 and gpt-oss marked) (plot). Tables `tab_lm_attn_released`, `tab_lm_attn_positions` (theta, rotated channels and static pairs for Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-2B, GLM-4.5, gpt-oss-120b, K3).
**Restate / forward:** `sec_what-attention-computes` and `subsec_kv-cache-sinks` (the sink phenomenon and GPT-2's first-token mass, the sliding window with 0, 1 or 4 sinks; restated in one sentence each, not repeated); the transformers Further Reading's learned-sink and gated-attention paragraphs (named); `sec_positional-information` (RoPE, ALiBi, NoPE and the train-at-L, test-at-4L protocol; YaRN is 4.5's); `sec_attention-at-scale` (`subsec_attn-receptive-field`, the window mask); `sec_transformer-block` (QK-norm); 4.2's logit growth. Forward: none.
**Exercises:** 8. Derive: cache bytes per token for ratio r and window w, and at n 131,072 for gpt-oss-120b (4.83 GB growing against 9.66 GB all-global; 4.72 MB bounded); the sink as a gate sigma(LSE minus s); the margin at 2^20 keys (18.5 against 12.9 at 2^14); the static pairs for r 64 and theta 1e7 (10) and the theta below which none is static (about 5.9e4). Measure: window size against loss at T1; the stable learning-rate range of the gate arm. Check: a window with and without a sink. Open: per-layer embeddings as a fifth arm (a per-layer table of the vocabulary size at a small width) at T1 with three seeds.
**Writer notes:**
- Differences from the blueprint: Gemma 4 replaces Gemma 3 as the local-global exemplar (windows 512 and 1,024, 128K and 256K contexts, Apache-2.0; the ratio from `layer_types`, since the card states none); per-layer embeddings get one paragraph and the open exercise; differential attention is one sentence with its citation; gpt-oss-20b is optional (about 42 GB dequantized on an A100, no MXFP4 kernels there; a T2 pair or skip).
- The sink is not necessarily the first token (`sink_metrics` measures position 0 only), and removing the first token moves the mass onto refused tokens. "Gated attention" (this section's output gate) and "gated DeltaNet" (14.6's decay and write gates) are different mechanisms; name both. The unrotated channels of partial RoPE are not NoPE heads; a NoPE layer drops the rotation for the whole layer. The book's `_rope` rotates adjacent pairs while Transformers rotates half-split; the loader of 1.2 permutes, `RefinedAttention` carries the flag and a permutation test, and the partial rotary applies to the first `rope_frac` times `head_dim` channels. Extrapolation without scaling measures the architecture, not YaRN.
- Fallbacks: the reference recipe differs from the papers', so compare only within the notebook; effects below noise give ties plus diagnostics plus the T0 toy; fused sink kernels on A100 and Ada are unconfirmed (use the LSE-gate identity or an explicit fp32 softmax); if copy accuracy is near zero, score the loss on the second copy or train longer.

### 14.5 Learned Sparse Attention · T1
**Idea:** A learned indexer selects which blocks of the context a query reads, the selection is paid for by scoring every key cheaply, and training and inference must agree on the same selection.
**Opening:** 12.7's eviction threw tokens away for good; a model could keep everything and learn which blocks each query needs. The concrete example is the opening cell: DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 read 2,048 of 131,072 keys (1.56%), MiniMax-M3 reads 16 blocks of 128 plus a local block (0.21% of a million), and V4 reads 512 of its compressed entries plus a 128-token window. The open question: what does the selection itself cost, and when is it cheaper than reading everything?
**Teaches:**
- Block selection: keys pooled per block and scored against the query (MoBA), or a compressed branch plus a selected branch plus a window, shared across a GQA group (NSA); page bounds as a cheaper score (Quest); token-level selection by a lightning indexer whose heads score every key with a ReLU kernel and keep the top 2,048 (DSA), with the main attention in MLA's multi-query form.
- Train-inference consistency: the indexer is trained first to match the dense head-summed attention (a KL warm-up), then frozen into a sparse stage where it receives no language-model gradient and the loss is restricted to the selected set; the selection kernel at training and at inference is the same; inference-time top-k on a dense model is a different regime (12.7).
- Cost: selection scores all n keys, so sparse attention is not O(k); the crossover n above k a over (a minus b) and the speedup cap a over b (V3.2: cap 17.0, 13.4 at 131,072, break-even about 2,176); per-head selection reads the union of heads' sets while group-shared selection pays k at a worse per-head optimum; index reuse across layers (V4.1's `index_source_layer_ids`, GLM-5.3's 21 full and 57 shared indexers) and hierarchical compression (V4's ratios 4 and 128) as the shipped answers.
- Selection quality: the error of attending to a set S is bounded by twice the maximum value norm times the omitted mass, so top-k of the true attention is the oracle; mean-pooled keys can hide a sharp key.
**Derivation:** FLOPs per query for full attention against scoring plus k blocks (`eq_lm_sparse_cost`, `eq_lm_sparse_cap`) and the omitted-mass error bound (`eq_lm_sparse_err`). Smallest case: a 64K context with blocks of 64 and k 16; at V3.2's dimensions a equals 2H(2r plus d_r), 278,528, b equals 2 H_I d_I, 16,384, k 2,048. Check cells: the formula against `config_stats(...).flops_per_token(n)` on V3.2 and GLM-5 for n from 4K to 1M (1e-9 relative); the bound over 1,000 random sets on a seeded Dirichlet of 512 keys; the expected union size n(1 minus (1 minus k/n)^G) against a Monte-Carlo at n 4,096, k 256, G 4.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: does window plus top-k blocks match full attention on retrieval, how much head-summed mass does each selection rule capture at a fixed budget, and what does selection cost in time?
2. Three measurements at T1. Selection quality on frozen Qwen3-0.6B: two layers (largest and smallest head-summed attention entropy), 4,096-token documents from the book corpus (200 train, 50 held-out, no chapter overlap), a `LightningIndexer` with 4 heads of 64 trained by the KL warm-up (1,000 steps at 1e-3) then 300 sparse steps, budgets k in {64, 128, 256, 512} against MoBA's block gate (blocks of 32) and Quest's page bounds (pages of 16), two indexer seeds. Trained-in sparsity: width 256 with 6 blocks at context 2K on `d2l.recall_task` (64 pairs, vocabulary 512) mixed 1:1 with language-model batches; arms full, window 128, window plus top-4 blocks of 64; two seeds, recall at 2K, 4K and 8K. Selection overhead: one layer at V3.2 dimensions in bf16 MQA form; arms dense absorbed, token top-k (64 indexer heads of 128, top 2,048), block top-k (blocks of 128, top 16); n from 4K to 64K at batch 1 and 8; score, top-k, gather and attention times from the profiler, five repetitions, a fit of tau0 plus tau1 n.
3. Checks: gather against mask implementations (1e-5 in fp32); top-k covering every block equals causal SDPA (1e-5); token top-k with k at least n (1e-6); causality exact; the indexer against the literal einsum of DSA's equation 1 (1e-6); `d2l.indexer_kl_loss` equals `F.kl_div` (1e-6) with zero gradient to the fixed target; the oracle set captures at least as much mass as any set.
4. Claim that survives noise: the trained indexer captures more head-summed mass than the block gate or the page bound, with the gap widening as the budget shrinks (bootstrap over documents); the windowed arm sits near chance beyond its window and the block arm in between (reported "did not converge" if the one-minute runs do not); selection time is reported as measured, with FLOP speedups never presented as wall-clock.
5. Reused pieces: `d2l.MLAAttention` (14.3), `d2l.RefinedAttention` (14.4), `d2l.load_qwen3` (1.2), `d2l.book_corpus` (2.4), `d2l.config_stats`, the window mask of `sec_attention-at-scale`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`.
6. T1 throughout (at most 12 GiB, about 14 minutes); artifact `lm-arch-sparse-profiles` (per n and arm, kernel-category times, memory, selection recall). `config_stats` gains the `dsa` and `csa2` layer kinds here.
**Figures:** `fig_lm_block_select` (a query, the block summaries, the selected blocks and the window; the four rules side by side); `fig_lm_sparse_recall` (captured mass against budget per rule) (plot); `fig_lm_sparse_profile` (time per category against context for the three arms, with the FLOP cap drawn) (plot). Tables `tab_lm_sparse_released`, `tab_lm_sparse_union`.
**Restate / forward:** `sec_attention-at-scale` (fixed windows and `subsec_attn-receptive-field`, taken as given); `sec_kv-cache`; 14.3's absorption (`eq_lm_mla_absorb`); `sec_mdl-divergences-distances` (the KL of the warm-up); 12.7's eviction as the contrast; 5.3's decode model. Forward: none.
**Exercises:** 7. Derive: the block size that balances scoring and reading; the cap for GLM-5 (a 139,264, b 8,192, cap 17.0); the union size under correlated heads; MiniMax-M3's attended fraction (0.21%). Measure: a budget sweep on the frozen-model cell; a post-hoc indexer fitted to a dense model against the trained-in arm. Check: V4.1-Flash's `index_source_layer_ids` and `kv_source_layer_ids` against its cache formula. Open: 14.3's latent as the substrate (index over the latent) and index reuse at GLM-5.3's 21-to-57 ratio.
**Writer notes:**
- The three claims that go wrong: "sparse attention is O(k)" (the indexer scores all n); "the FLOP speedup is the wall-clock speedup" (measure); "top-k on a dense model is the same thing" (a sparse model is trained or retrofitted; the inference-time regime is 12.7's). The compression ratio changes the unit of selection (V4's top-512 at ratio 128 covers 65,536 tokens). The indexer gets no language-model gradient in DSA; say so when the reader asks why it does not drift.
- Precision: DSA scores in fp8 at inference per the V3.2 report; the notebook uses bf16 for training and inference alike and states the convention (2 H_I d_I FLOPs per scored key). The V4.1 hierarchy's "compression divides the scanned entries" is an assumption checked against the report's §2.3.

### 14.6 Hybrid Models at Scale · T3 (T1 load)
**Idea:** A released hybrid is the Advanced recipe, one attention layer in a few, at scale, and its serving cost follows from the attention fraction and the fixed state of the linear layers.
**Opening:** The `sec_hybrids` model had two layers; Qwen3.5-2B has gated DeltaNet in three positions of four and gated attention in the fourth, 18 linear and 6 full layers. The concrete example is the opening cell listing the layer counts of released hybrids read from their configurations (Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5-2B and 35B-A3B, Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B, Kimi Linear's 20 KDA and 7 MLA, Kimi K3's 69 and 24, MiniMax-M1's 70 lightning and 10 softmax, GLM-5.3-Flash's 34 KDA and 11 sparse, Nemotron's `hybrid_override_pattern`, and MiniMax-M2's 62 of 62 softmax as the reminder that the choice is not monotone). The open question: where does the fixed state stop paying?
**Teaches:**
- The released recipe: where the attention layers sit (`full_attention_interval` 4 in the Qwen line; never first), what the linear layer contains in practice (a depthwise causal convolution over the projected q, k, v, L2-normalized queries and keys, a decay gate from a softplus with a learned log-scale, a write gate beta from a sigmoid, head replication when value heads outnumber key heads, a gated RMSNorm before the output projection), and what the chunked kernel does: a unit-lower-triangular solve per chunk with gamma ratios kept in log space.
- Loading Qwen3.5-2B into the book's code: `d2l.Qwen35Hybrid` composed from the book's `d2l.GatedDeltaNet` (extended by the pieces above in a subclass) and `d2l.Qwen3Attention` with 14.4's output gate and partial RoPE, with the mismatch table (`tab_lm_hy_mapping`: the (1 plus w) norm convention folded at load, the gated norm applied before the SiLU gate, SwiGLU at width 6,144, the doubled query projection split into query and gate, half-split RoPE on the first 64 of 256 channels at theta 1e7, the vision tower and MTP head skipped by name prefix) and a layer-by-layer logit match.
- Cache bytes at context L for attention fraction f: M(n) equals L_f c_kv n plus L_l c_st with the fixed state c_st equal to H_v d_k d_v b_s plus the convolution state, the crossover n-star where the state equals the cache, and the ratio to an attention-only peer; prefix caching needs state snapshots, and a cached state cannot be truncated or extended backwards (13.4).
- Relatives in one difference each: Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.8 (the same layout at 27B dense and 35B-A3B or 2.4T-A95B MoE), Kimi Linear and K3 (KDA with a lower-bounded, full-rank gate and NoPE MLA in the attention layers), Nemotron 3 (Mamba-2 plus MoE, trained in NVFP4), Mamba-3 (trapezoidal discretization, complex state, multi-input heads; the layer belongs to `chap_modern_rnn`, which gets the same pointer).
**Derivation:** The gated chunked delta rule (`eq_lm_hy_chunked`): the recurrence S_t equals a_t(I minus beta_t k_t k_t-transposed)S_(t minus 1) plus beta_t k_t v_t-transposed is computed chunk-wise exactly by one triangular solve, with outputs from the chunk-start state plus a masked intra-chunk term; and the state-against-cache arithmetic (`eq_lm_hy_state`). Smallest case: Qwen3.5-2B with 6 full layers at 2,048 bytes per token and 18 linear layers at 1,085,440 bytes of state each gives M(n) equal to 12,288 n plus 19,537,920, n-star about 1,590, and 9.3 times less than Qwen3-1.7B at long context; at 128K, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B holds 2.75 GB per sequence against 12.88 GB for Qwen3-30B-A3B, about 4.7 times less. Check cells: chunked against recurrent in fp64 (1e-10 relative for chunks of 16, 64, 256); both against Transformers' `torch_chunk_gated_delta_rule` and `torch_recurrent_gated_delta_rule` in fp32 (1e-5); against `fla`'s kernel when it imports (tolerance measured); the gate at zero reduces to the book's `chunked_delta_rule` (1e-6); `HybridCache.bytes()` after an n-token prefill equals M(n) exactly on the loaded model.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: does the book's class reproduce Qwen3.5-2B's logits, and how do memory and throughput scale with context for a released hybrid against an attention-only peer of similar active size?
2. T1 (the loading half): Qwen3.5-0.8B in fp32 on three 512-token prompts with first-divergence localization (`output_hidden_states=True`; the first layer whose relative error exceeds three times the previous layer's is flagged; the likely culprits in order are the norm convention, the half-split RoPE and the gate split); Qwen3.5-2B in bf16 with the noise-floor rule (the book's maximum absolute logit difference is at most twice the difference between Transformers in bf16 and in fp32 on the same prompts) plus top-1 agreement over all positions; stateful decode equals the full forward in fp32 (1e-5); a kernel micro-benchmark of one layer (recurrent loop, PyTorch chunked at 64, `fla` chunked) for T from 1K to 32K; a T1 serving comparison of Qwen3.5-2B against Qwen3-1.7B through Transformers `generate` at 2K, 8K and 32K.

### 14.7 The Residual Stream across Depth · T2
**Idea:** Pre-norm dilutes each layer's contribution as the residual stream grows with depth, and learned mixing across several streams or over earlier layers restores it only when the mixing is constrained to preserve the identity path.
**Opening:** The hidden-state norm of Qwen3-0.6B grows layer by layer while each layer's update stays about the same size, so late layers change the stream by a smaller fraction. The concrete example is the opening cell: residual RMS and update RMS per layer for the loaded Qwen3-0.6B, with the ratio falling with depth. The open question: is depth being wasted, and would width have been the better purchase?
**Teaches:**
- Norm growth under pre-norm: the expected squared norm after L layers grows like L for independent updates and like L-squared for aligned ones, so the RMS grows between the square root of L and L, and a layer's contribution is diluted by the inverse; post-norm and the off-stream variant (`tab_modern-recipe`'s OLMo row) as the alternatives that give up the identity path.
- Hyper-connections: n parallel residual streams mixed by token-wise learned matrices (expansion, mixing, write-back); the product of unconstrained mixing matrices across depth grows or vanishes geometrically; the manifold-constrained version (mHC) projects the mixing matrix onto the doubly stochastic set with a few Sinkhorn iterations, which keeps the product's spectral norm at most one and preserves the stream mean; the traffic cost (about 20d against 3d per token for the plain residual at n 4) and the kernels that hide it.
- Attention Residuals: each layer's input is a convex combination of all earlier outputs, with weights from a pseudo-query against normalized keys, in a blocked form (Kimi K3's 8 blocks of 12 layers plus the embedding source) that stores N d instead of L d; the inputs are convex combinations, so there is no identity path unless the attention puts weight on the previous output.
- DenseFormer's depth-weighted averaging and value residuals as pointers (one difference each; the Further Reading notebook has their sources).
**Derivation:** Doubly stochastic matrices are closed under products, have spectral norm at most one and fix the uniform vector (`eq_lm_res_ds`); unconstrained products are bounded below by the spectral radius to the power L (`eq_lm_res_growth` for the norm). Smallest case: n 4 streams over L 96 layers with seed 0: unconstrained B_l equal to I plus 0.1 times Gaussian noise (log of the product norm over L printed, singular values shown); Sinkhorn with 20 iterations on exponentiated Gaussian logits (column sums within 1e-6, the row residual r_20 against the iteration count), with the product's spectral norm at most 1 plus L r_20 and the mean drift at most L r_20 times the norm; the constrained product's second singular value decays. Sinkhorn itself is an exercise.
**Notebook:**
1. Question: does the constraint widen the stable learning-rate range and flatten the norm profile at equal tokens, and what does it cost in traffic?
2. Model and data: the reference model's recipe at 138M; two arms, pre-norm and mHC with four streams and 20 Sinkhorn iterations, with unconstrained hyper-connections and blocked Attention Residuals (N about L over 8, at least 4 blocks) as optional third and fourth arms on committed logs; three peak learning rates ({1, 2, 4} times the recipe's; the blueprint's {0.5, 1, 2, 4} if the budget allows), identical tokens (about 8 minutes per run), seed 0 everywhere and seeds 1 and 2 for the baseline at the recipe's rate; instability is pre-registered as a non-finite loss or a loss exceeding its earlier minimum by more than 0.5 nats after step 100 (4.2's criterion).
3. Metrics: final loss against rate; residual RMS and gradient norm per layer; tokens per second and peak memory relative to pre-norm; `d2l.stable_lr_range` (rates whose final loss is within two sigma of the variant's best and stable).
4. Checks: `HyperConnection(n=1)` with identity maps equals the pre-norm `d2l.TransformerBlock` (1e-6); the n-copies expansion with identity-like initialization reproduces the baseline (1e-5); mHC column sums (1e-6), nonnegativity, row residual reported on 1,000 random tokens; the product closure; `AttnRes` convexity, block size 1 equal to the full form, the online-softmax merge equal to the direct computation (1e-6); parameter counts against `config_stats` with the `hc_mult` and `attn_res` extensions.
5. Claim that survives noise: a flatter norm profile under mHC; the stable range differs only when resolved beyond a factor of two; loss ties within two sigma are ties; unconstrained mixing is unstable at the higher rates only if the pre-registered criterion fires.
6. Reused pieces: `d2l.train_lm_steps` (14.2), `d2l.load_reference_model`, `d2l.load_qwen3` (the opening probe), `d2l.TransformerBlock`, `d2l.GPT`, `d2l.config_stats`, `d2l.paired_bootstrap`.
7. T1 reduction: width 256 with 12 blocks on a 20M-token slice, two rates per variant and two baseline seeds (about 15 minutes); HC arms at T2 run at half micro-batch with doubled accumulation (four streams multiply residual activations about four times). Artifact `lm-arch-residual-logs`.
**Figures:** `fig_lm_residual_mixing` (one stream against several with mixing matrices, and the blocked attention over earlier outputs); `fig_lm_res_variants` (loss against rate, residual RMS against layer, gradient norm against layer, throughput and memory) (plot); `fig_lm_res_product` (the product norm across depth, unconstrained against doubly stochastic) (plot). Tables `tab_lm_res_cost`, `tab_lm_res_released` (`hc_mult`, `hc_sinkhorn_iters`, `mhc`, `hc_count`, `attn_res_block_size` by model).
**Restate / forward:** `sec_transformer-block` (pre-norm against post-norm and the signal-propagation argument, one sentence); `sec_init_param` and `subsec_variance_across_depth` (variance growth and the 1 over the square root of 2L residual scaling, taken as given); 1.6's residual stream as a workspace; `tab_modern-recipe` (the OLMo row); 4.2's instability criterion. Forward: none.
**Exercises:** 8. Derive: norm growth for independent against aligned updates and the dilution factor at layer 64 (about 0.18 of layer 2's); the traffic per token for multi-pass against single-pass mixing (20d, 10d, 3d); the closure and spectral-norm proof; the blocked Attention Residuals cost against block count; Sinkhorn's convergence in two or five iterations. Measure: streams in {2, 4, 8} against traffic at T1; the second singular value of the product. Open: depth against width at equal parameters under mHC; a memo comparing depth-weighted averaging, value residuals and Attention Residuals.
**Writer notes:**
- Differences from the blueprint: two arms plus an optional third (the blueprint ran four variants at four rates, 16 runs); three rates; DenseFormer and value residuals are pointers with sources in the Further Reading notebook. Shipped evidence is read from configurations only: `hc_mult` 4 with 20 Sinkhorn iterations in DeepSeek V4-Flash, V4-Pro and V4.1-Flash, `mhc` in GLM-5.3-Flash, `hc_count` 4 in Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, `attn_res_block_size` 12 in Kimi K3; the mHC paper predates the V4 releases.
- More streams are not free capacity (activations scale with n). A finite Sinkhorn is only approximately doubly stochastic and the residual compounds over depth; the constraint preserves the stream mean, not each stream. Residual RMS is not comparable across n-stream variants; compare the mean read-out. Attention Residuals' granularity (layer against sublayer) and the zero-pseudo-query initialization (uniform weights) are modeling choices; read arXiv 2603.15031 §2 before implementing, since no public reference implementation was located (the K3 repository may carry modeling code).
- Fallbacks: if the exact mHC parameterization cannot be matched, test properties and document deviations (paper §3); if HC arms exceed 38 GiB, quarter the micro-batch, then n 2, then fewer layers or `torch.compile`; if stability events are rare, extend the rate grid by 8 for the baseline only or use 24 blocks at T1; if 16 runs exceed the budget, drop the lowest rate for all but the baseline.
- Library additions: `d2l.sinkhorn(logits, iters=20, eps=1e-6)`; `d2l.HyperConnection(n, d, mode='hc'|'mhc', sinkhorn_iters=20)` (X of shape B by T by n by d; token-wise expansion, mixing and write-back as in V4.1's equation 2; asserts properties, not constants); `d2l.AttnRes(num_layers, d, block=None)`; `d2l.ResidualGPT(variant, vocab, d, H, Hkv, L, ...)` with variants `prenorm`, `hc`, `mhc`, `attnres`, `attnres_block`, `dwa`, `value_residual`; `d2l.depth_diagnostics(model, batch)`; `d2l.stable_lr_range(runs, tol)`. Detail: blueprint ch14 §14.7.
**Sources:**
- Papers: [Hyper-Connections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.19606) (several residual streams with learned mixing); [mHC: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24880) (the doubly stochastic constraint by Sinkhorn; §3 for the parameterization); [Attention Residuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031) (attention over earlier layers' outputs, the blocked form; §2 for granularity and initialization); [Value Residual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17897) and [DenseFormer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02622) (pointers); [Kimi K3](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1) (§2.2, §5.2.2: block Attention Residuals at 93 layers); [DeepSeek-V4: Towards Highly Efficient Million-Token Context Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348) (mHC shipped with four streams) and [DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.19969v1) (§2.4.1, the single-pass form and equation 2).
- Code and documentation: [Kimi-K3 repository](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/Kimi-K3) (artifacts; check for modeling code); [moonshotai/Kimi-K3](https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3) and [deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash) (the configuration fields).
- Courses, tutorials and blogs: [Smol Training Playbook](https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceTB/smol-training-playbook) (stability ablations and learning-rate sweeps); [Stanford CS336, Spring 2026](https://cs336.stanford.edu/) (architectures and hyperparameters lecture); Sebastian Raschka, [The Big LLM Architecture Comparison](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/the-big-llm-architecture-comparison) (normalization placement across releases).

### FR Further Reading: Architectures · T0
**Idea:** The reading notebook holds what dates fastest, the open-weight release calendar and the designs not yet in the core, and the design-under-a-budget checklist that hosts the capstone.
**Opening:** A reader who has worked through seven axes wants to know what else released models tried in the last year, and what to try first with a budget of their own. The concrete example is the calendar's most recent row with its configuration-derived numbers. The closing names the next axis the four-condition rule would admit.
**Teaches:** The open-weight release calendar (names, Hub `createdAt` dates and configuration-derived numbers from the 14.1 registry; no prose claims about ranking, and a refresh procedure per edition). Byte-level patching: entropy-based patches (BLT) and dynamic chunking (H-Net), with the compute-per-byte comparison against a BPE model at equal FLOPs (no production adoption found by November 2026). Diffusion language models: masked diffusion scaled to a 16B and a 100B-total model (LLaDA2.0), parallel unmasking and its speed-quality trade, with the text-scale example requested from `sec_diffusion-discrete` once that chapter settles. Depth aggregation (DenseFormer, value residuals) as 14.7's pointers. Zero-computation experts (LongCat-Flash) as 14.2's exercise. Test-time training and memory layers in one paragraph (Titans; Memory Layers at Scale) as the one course topic with no core home. The design-under-a-budget checklist (task distribution, data, compute, hardware, context, serving objective, quality gate), the experiment-ranking rule (prior uncertainty times decision sensitivity over cost) and the dossier format of the capstone (`sec_lm_capstone`): one measured baseline, one rejected design with a pre-registered rule and evidence, no verdict from a difference inside two sigma.
**Derivation:** none (the capstone's binding-resource formula is 5.3's decode model with 14.1's per-token bytes and state; the compute-per-byte identity of patch models is one line).
**Notebook:** none (reading); the capstone's starter (`load_scenario`, `check_design`, `predict_decode`, `comparators`) ships with the chapter data and runs at T0, with its measured baseline at T1.
**Figures:** none.
**Restate / forward:** 14.1's table as the data source; `sec_diffusion-discrete` (`eq_diffusion-masked-loss`, the unmasking sampler) and `sec_text-sequence` (byte-level BPE) in one sentence each. Forward: none.
**Exercises:** the capstone only.
**Writer notes:**
- Placement: this notebook covers byte patching and diffusion language models (multi-token prediction is in 12.5) and hosts the budget checklist and the capstone, the blueprint's optional sections. Keep it at 1,000 to 2,000 words, no training run, every citation with a clause saying what it adds, and refresh it with the 14.1 registry each edition.
- The capstone is self-contained: scenario B (one 16 GB GPU, at most 1B total parameters, Qwen3-0.6B against Qwen3.5-0.8B as the measured pair) is the T1 path; the autograder checks hand-derived claims to 0.5% (exact cache bytes for GQA, MLA and GDN layers), measured peak memory within 15% and decode throughput within 25% of `predict_decode` (or a profile localizing the gap), a pre-registered `rules.yaml` whose hash the run log carries, and a verdict consistent with the interval; the human rubric penalizes any conclusion from a difference within noise and any number without a source. The capstone uses 16 GB, not the blueprint's 24 GB scenario text.
- Diffusion exemplar: LLaDA2.0-mini (16B) does not fit a 16 GB card; LLaDA-8B-Instruct does, and either is a pointer only; Mercury is closed. The text-scale masked-diffusion example is requested from `sec_diffusion-discrete` and this notebook does not duplicate it.
- Library: `d2l.Scenario`, `d2l.load_scenario`, `d2l.check_design`, `d2l.predict_decode` (a `ServingModel` plus `config_stats` composition), `d2l.design_matrix`, `d2l.rank_experiments` (about 100 lines, exact unit tests). Detail: blueprint ch14 "Assignment: Design under a budget", §14.8 and §14.9.
**Sources:**
- Papers: [Byte Latent Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09871) (entropy-based patches) and [H-Net](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07955) (dynamic chunking); [LLaDA2.0](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.15745) (masked diffusion at 16B and 100B total) and [LLaDA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09992) (the 8B formulation); [Mercury](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17298) (a commercial diffusion LM, closed); [D3PM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03006) (discrete diffusion foundations, taught in `sec_diffusion-discrete`); [DenseFormer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02622) and [Value Residual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17897) (depth aggregation); [LongCat-Flash](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01322) (zero-computation experts); [Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00663) (a neural memory updated at test time) and [Memory Layers at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.09764) (trainable key-value memory in place of FFN compute); [Better and Faster Large Language Models via Multi-token Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.19737) (the pretraining objective, now 12.5's; cited for the calendar's heads column).
- Code and documentation: [BLT repository](https://github.com/facebookresearch/blt); [LLaDA repository](https://github.com/ML-GSAI/LLaDA) and [GSAI-ML/LLaDA-8B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/GSAI-ML/LLaDA-8B-Instruct); [Hub API endpoints](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/api) (the calendar's `createdAt` source); [nanochat](https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat) (a complete small-model recipe for the capstone's baseline).
- Courses, tutorials and blogs: [Ultra-Scale Playbook](https://huggingface.co/spaces/nanotron/ultrascale-playbook) and [Smol Training Playbook](https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceTB/smol-training-playbook) (budget reasoning and experiment selection); [Stanford CS336, Spring 2026](https://cs336.stanford.edu/) (the end-to-end assignment discipline the capstone copies); Alex Smola, [MLSS efficiency lecture](https://alex.smola.org/posts/45-mlss-efficiency/) (inference-budget reasoning); [CMU 11-711, Spring 2026](https://cmu-l3.github.io/anlp-spring2026) (diffusion and flows lecture).
